<meta>This page is the dedication leaf of Jean Tarin’s 1618 edition of works by Origen and other early Christian fathers. It follows the title page which introduced the treatises of Zacharias Scholasticus and Anastasius of Sinai. Here, the editor Tarin addresses his patron, Jean de Gondi, justifying the scholarly labor of recovering and correcting ancient manuscripts for the public good.</meta>

<page-type>dedication</page-type>
<sig>ã ij</sig>

<image-desc>A decorative rectangular woodcut headpiece featuring elaborate foliate scrolls, floral motifs, and two small animal or hybrid figures.</image-desc>

### TO THE VERY
# REVEREND
## AND ILLUSTRIOUS LORD,
### LORD JEAN DE GONDI, DEAN
### of the Church of Paris, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Aubin
### of Angers, Patron. <note>Jean de Gondi (1567–1623) was a powerful French cleric from the influential Gondi family; he served as the Dean of Notre-Dame de Paris and later became the first Archbishop of Paris.</note>

->JEAN TARIN SENDS GREETINGS.<- <note>Jean Tarin (1586–1666) was a French classical scholar and rector of the University of Paris. The "S. D." in the original stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends health/greetings."</note>

<image-desc>A large square woodcut initial 'V' decorated with intricate foliate patterns and a grotesque mask at the top.</image-desc>

*Those who recall*
*the writings of ancient*
*authors (MOST DISTINGUISHED*
*PRELATE) from neglect and dust*
*to light and splendor,*
*even if they provide no other benefit to the public, I believe they certainly serve both their contemporaries and posterity in this one way: that they make public property those things which were held in private custody—not without a certain injury to the public—so that works written and labored over for everyone might at least serve the interests of many. To this benefit, those who add another—namely, restoring to health things that were at first correctly established but later distorted and corrupted, by correcting faults—are certainly both considered and truly are worthy of public gratitude for their industrious zeal* <note>original: "vitia emendando" — Tarin is referring to the process of textual criticism, where a scholar compares different manuscript copies to remove errors introduced by previous scribes.</note>

---

<summary>In this formal dedication, Jean Tarin presents his editorial work to Jean de Gondi, arguing that rescuing ancient Christian texts from obscurity and correcting manuscript errors is a vital service to the public and future generations.</summary>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication by Jean Tarin to Jean de Gondi. Tarin is discussing the hierarchy of scholarly labor: the primary work of original composition and discovery, the secondary work of emendation, and the "third-rank" work of translation (interpretation). He explains why the greatest scholars often avoid translation despite its utility.</meta>

...perceive the fruit of their labor. Indeed, no others in any age have performed these roles—which have always been held as primary—except those who, in addition to the highest natural talent <term>ingenium: innate intellectual ability or genius</term>, possessed those resources in abundance: I mean leisure <term>otium: the productive freedom from public business required for scholarly study</term> and the other supports by which these studies are sustained. Those who were abandoned by such aids, while they were pursuing those primary goals, nonetheless took an honorable stand in those secondary ones. 

Between these two, the work of interpreters <note>In this context, "interpreters" refers specifically to translators who render a text from one language (like Greek) into another (like Latin or French).</note> seems to be positioned. To these men, though weary from a rich and fertile harvest, the glory that follows is by no means equal to the fruit of their labor. This is perhaps because people think it a shameful thing to admit they have spoken through an interpreter with an author whose own voice it would be much more honorable to hear and respond to directly. Or perhaps it is because these translators, while they lessen the labor of others by interpreting, actually take away from the industry of many; for when that "citadel of erudition" <note>Tarin refers to the original, difficult language of a text—likely Greek—as a "citadel" that requires effort to scale.</note> is, so to speak, leveled and brought down into the soil of a more familiar language, people are accustomed to relax their minds. Where there is no need for sharp exertion, men generally cease to strive for anything great. 

From this, I believe, it follows that the most eminent men have left these third-rate shares of praise to others, while they themselves sought the path to the primary ranks. They did not feel they were acting in accordance with the greatness of their own talent unless they devoted themselves to that glory which was considered the greatest. For no one will wonder that they avoided a risk to their own reputation, if one considers <note>original: "re-" (catchword for "reputaverit")</note> their prudence amidst such great dexterity and skill of mind...

<vocab>talent, leisure, studies, interpreters, erudition, glory</vocab>

<summary>Tarin discusses the challenges of translation, arguing that while it is useful, it is often undervalued compared to original scholarship because it makes the material "too easy" for the reader and lacks the prestige of primary research.</summary>
<keywords>translation theory, scholarship, Jean Tarin, Jean de Gondi, academic hierarchy, erudition, intellectual labor</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s dedication to Jean de Gondi. Having previously discussed how translation "levels the citadel of erudition" by making difficult Greek texts accessible in more common languages, Tarin now addresses the personal and professional risks translators take, as well as the heated rivalries that often plague the scholarly world.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>ã iij</sig>

...will recognize. Nor, however, did this reality deter others from entering upon this steep and slippery path as well, even extending a hand to others—clearly at mutual risk, for if one should slip, both must fall together. And indeed, since it is a human thing for most to happen to stumble, who would wonder at it? That it does not happen to everyone is more a matter of admiration. Truly, I see it is right to rejoice that very many have stood firm and progressed quite far—even if those who thought they had stumbled the least were later found by those who would correct their slips; and there was certainly no lack of people who would say that these men had not stood quite upright. 

Either we are so bleary-eyed in our own affairs while seeing sharply in those of others, or time and chance always bring something with them which—as the author says—might defeat the **wisdom of a hundred learned men** <note>original: "centum... doctûm hominum consilia"</note>. And certainly, those who have engaged in this labor so purely and holily that they intended no detraction from others, but only to note faults or reshape what was corrupted, seem to me to have truly found a way by which they might find others equally fair-minded. By attesting that they are mindful of humanity <term>humanitas: the quality of being humane, refined, and empathetic toward the shared human condition</term>, they might most easily obtain forgiveness. 

If all had maintained this balance <term>temperamentum: a proper proportion or moderating restraint</term> as much as the most modest did, those quarrels would not be heard in the **Temple of the Muses** <note>original: "Musarum fano"; a metaphorical reference to the scholarly community or the university</note>, nor would we hear such intemperate brawling between peers fighting like gladiators. For my part, I neither...

<summary>Tarin discusses the inherent risks of translation, noting that while errors are human, they often invite harsh criticism from peers. He advocates for a spirit of "humanitas" and moderation to end the bitter rivalries that frequently disrupt the scholarly community.</summary>
<keywords>translation risks, scholarly criticism, humanitas, Temple of the Muses, Jean Tarin, academic rivalry</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s dedication to Jean de Gondi, Archbishop of Paris. Having previously argued that scholars should be forgiven for unintentional errors, Tarin now contrasts willful ignorance with the "human" mistakes made in the pursuit of learning. He advocates for a collegial "royal road" of scholarship and introduces his specific project: the restoration of ancient texts.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

...can be said with enough vehemence or bitterness against those who not only act intentionally in a way for which they are rightly criticized, but who even love their own fault and defend it with the stubbornness of a defiant mind. However, I do not see why those who have committed some human error in literature <note>original: "humanitus aliquid in literis commiserunt"</note> should be attacked and torn apart with the drawn blade, as it were, of the pen—and certainly much less so than the former. 

For truly, a heavy and wretched condition would be established for the cultivators of these studies if they alone were to err without hope of pardon; and if—while they love the whole **humanity of letters** <term>humanitas literarum: the refined culture, empathy, and classical learning that define a civilized scholar</term>—they were to be received inhumanely and harshly by their own associates and companions, which is by far most unworthy. 

Therefore, it ought to be held especially sacred and solemn that those walking the **royal road** <note>original: "regiâ viâ"</note> of the sciences should kindly warn those who wander from it through ignorance or lack of consideration. They should call them back to the straight path or lead the way graciously until the wanderers reflect upon themselves and reconsider their position—something they almost always do of their own accord. 

Yet, in this matter, the charge of rashness must not be refused by those who, poorly supplied with the necessary resources, gird themselves for a task that requires great assistance in every way and cannot be maintained except by the strongest defenses: the **restoration of ancient books** <term>instaurationem: the process of editing, correcting, and reviving ancient texts for a modern audience</term>. When I first began to think of this work, following your **authority** <note>original: "autoritatem"</note>, there came to mind what was said both cleverly and truly...

<summary>Tarin argues that scholars should treat each other's unintentional errors with kindness rather than vitriol, distinguishing between stubborn ignorance and "human" mistakes. He then introduces the daunting but necessary task of restoring ancient texts, which he undertook under the patronage of Jean de Gondi.</summary>

<keywords>scholarly ethics, humanitas, restoration of texts, Jean de Gondi, academic rivalry, ancient books, literary criticism</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s dedication to Jean de Gondi. Having argued that scholars should be guided gently back to the path of truth rather than harshly criticized, Tarin now reflects on his own internal struggles—his youth, his lack of experience, and the sheer weight of the scholarly task he has undertaken—while expressing how Gondi’s kindness ultimately emboldened him to publish his work.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

...no one would deny that in praiseworthy matters, the effort itself is counted as praise; and for one who has thought well, even if things succeeded less well for him than he wished, the outcome is not condemned, and the **intention** <note>original: "voluntatem"</note> is even loved. 

But there were greater and more powerful things occurring to me that led me away from that thought: my age, which is neither sufficiently seasoned by experience nor strengthened by practice; although my spirit urged me on, it felt itself carried away by impulse rather than guided by counsel. 

Then there is the condition of my life—so full of toil, immortal God!—and unless hope for the future consoles us and the approval of good men lightens the burden, it is a thankless one. It claims us men, who have been handed over to this **scholarly leisure** <term>otium: in the classical sense, this is not "laziness" but the dedicated time required for high-level study and reflection, which Tarin paradoxically describes as "laborious"</term>, entirely for itself, and does not suffer us to be devoted to any other work. 

There is also the magnitude and weight of the matter, which I did not sufficiently weigh when I took this burden upon myself—I have long since realized this, and lest anyone think me worthy of a heavier **criticism** <term>animadversio: a formal scholarly or legal censure or "noticing" of a fault</term>, I display it myself and openly announce it. 

I have no need to mention the other things that have often held me back, though I was incited to these **studies** <note>original: "studia"</note>. Indeed, that last point would have been the most serious, had not a certain ambitious haste propelled these still-unripe studies to the point where, thinking of your extraordinary **kindness** <note>original: "benignitate"</note> toward me, my spirit was emboldened; it preferred to appear grateful to you—to whom it owes so much—rather than humble before everyone else. And so it has happened, as occurs in [daily]...

<meta>catchword: quoti- (likely "quotidie" meaning daily)</meta>

<summary>Tarin confesses his feelings of inadequacy due to his youth and the heavy burden of scholarship, but explains that he chose to publish his "unripe" work out of a sense of gratitude for Jean de Gondi's patronage.</summary>
<keywords>scholarly toil, otium, intellectual modesty, patronage, Jean de Gondi, academic ambition, effort vs. outcome</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory preface by Jean Tarin to Jean de Gondi, the Archbishop of Paris. The previous page ended with Tarin describing how his youthful impulses and the weight of his scholarly duties were pulling him in different directions. The text here completes the thought that his desire to honor his patron overcame his hesitation.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>

...daily, so that what we love and desire most, we might consider less difficult. I greatly desired to testify to that most favorable goodwill of yours toward me—to everyone, if it were possible, but certainly to declare it to as many as possible—so that those who saw you surrounded by a choir of all great virtues might recognize you as the most kind patron of my studies, more surely by no other way than by my own most truthful public praise. I did not begin to reflect upon this in my mind until I ceased to be afraid; for that youthful desire, an ill-advised counselor, was driving me, and the sense of duty repeatedly reminded me, lest I seem ungrateful any longer, and led me as if I were entirely bound to it. 

I yielded not so much to shame as to necessity, since I had taken it upon myself to give a sign of a mindful soul by whatever means I could. An opportunity presented itself—one that was not slight and by no means to be regretted, if I knew how to use it—yet the times barely offered it to one busy with other things. 

At hand was the **Philocalia of Origen** <term>Origenis Philocalia: A 4th-century anthology of Origen’s writings on the interpretation of Scripture, compiled by Basil and Gregory. The title literally means "Love of the Beautiful/Excellent."</term>, a work most pleasing even by the recommendation of its own name, were it not also shining with the splendor of **Basil the Great** <term>Basilius Magnus: St. Basil (c. 330–379), a Greek bishop and foundational figure in Eastern monasticism</term> and **Gregory the Theologian** <term>Gregorius Theologus: St. Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–389), an orator and philosopher-saint renowned for his defense of the Trinity</term>—and what great lights they are! This work looked to you alone out of the **Sacred Order** <term>sacrus ordo: referring to the high-ranking clergy; here, the hierarchy of the Church in which Jean de Gondi held a prominent place</term>—I will say freely what I feel—it looked to you especially, to whom it should be returned as a dedication and a debt, not by one hesitating or delaying, but by one managing the task diligently. No—

<summary>Jean Tarin explains how his desire to show gratitude to his patron, Jean de Gondi, overcame his youthful hesitations, leading him to dedicate his edition of Origen’s Philocalia to the Archbishop.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Tarin, Jean de Gondi, Origen, Philocalia, St. Basil the Great, St. Gregory of Nazianzus, patronage, scholarly duty, dedication</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory preface by Jean Tarin to Jean de Gondi, Archbishop of Paris. Tarin is transitioning from discussing his own hesitation to praising the specific virtues and noble lineage of his patron, specifically noting the connection between the patron's character and the themes of the "Philocalia" by Basil and Gregory.</meta>

which I now touch upon, things that in most others are found in isolation, but in you are accompanied by a most ample retinue: the dignity of the most honorable affairs, the nobility of a most famous lineage, the splendor of your household, and the greatness of honor within the Church of God. You hold a rank closest to that most exalted seat <note>original: "celsissimam sedem" — referring here to the Archbishopric of Paris</note> of which you have always been most worthy, though you were never in the least bit a seeker of it. Nor do I speak of this honor as something recent, but as a debt long overdue, which has returned to your family to the applause of France—and perhaps even with the approval of foreign nations—namely, the summit of Church honors bestowed upon your most sweet brother, a prince in every kind of praise, the Most Illustrious **Cardinal de Retz** <term>Cardinalis Retzio: Henri de Gondi (1572–1622), the first Cardinal de Retz and predecessor to Jean de Gondi as Bishop/Archbishop of Paris</term>. Indeed, now that he has been clothed in the purple, the purple itself <note>The "purple" refers to the distinctive red robes and the rank of a Cardinal</note> seems to me to have become more adorned.

I shall not speak of unknown things, but of those which clearly turn the eyes and devotions of all toward you: that true and genuine **Philocalia** <term>Philocalia: From the Greek "love of the beautiful/excellent." Tarin is punning on the title of the book he is dedicating, suggesting the patron embodies the very "love of virtue" described in the text</term> of all that is honorable and good—which seems so natural to you it might have been born with you—and that inner elegance arising from the adornment of all virtues. Because this elegance overflows most purely into all your words and deeds, this refined and choice apparatus of theological matters <note>original: "Theologicarum... supellex" — referring to the scholarly work at hand</note> was seeking you out. It required the examples of those most excellent peaks of the Church, **Basil and Gregory** <note>St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus, the compilers of Origen's Philocalia</note>, whose vigilance, piety, religion, and mercy you so greatly love and so ardently embrace. Your loftiness of mind shows itself in despising those things which men far unlike you look up to, caught as they are by the enticements of empty things. Finally, there is that singular [quality] in every part of your life...

<summary>Tarin praises Jean de Gondi’s noble lineage and the ecclesiastical honors of the Gondi family, specifically mentioning his brother, the Cardinal de Retz. He draws a parallel between de Gondi’s personal "love of beauty and virtue" (Philocalia) and the patristic texts of Basil and Gregory.</summary>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s dedication to Jean de Gondi. Having previously praised his patron’s lineage and character, Tarin now shifts to justifying his own labor on this edition of the Philocalia. He portrays the work as a humble return for his patron’s many favors, carved out of his rare moments of leisure.</meta>

glory, dedicated this to you as your own, however small a gift <term>muneris: a gift, duty, or contribution</term> it may be. Now, if anything has been able to proceed from me—I who have been overwhelmed by so many favors from you in return for a single benefit—it is all yours, all yours, I say! Thus, I am not so much offering you something new as returning a debt long owed. For this reason, I have labored more to appear grateful toward you than to seek praise for my own industry <term>industriæ: diligent labor or hard work</term>.

Therefore, although many things held me back from this undertaking, and others urged me to approach it, these latter reasons seemed far superior. This was because they combined the declaration of my duty <term>officij: duty or moral obligation</term> with an increase in the common utility <term>vtilitatis: usefulness or public benefit</term>—which, it seemed to me, was not insignificant. Nor was it a task unworthy of carving out small portions from my daily allowance <note>original: "demenso" — refers to a measured portion, like a ration of food or time</note> (not of my affairs, but of myself) and thinking those few holiday hours, which were very rare indeed, were not badly spent on this work.

And so, as much as I was permitted to breathe from my constant duties, I devoted that much time to this study—time which I stole from myself. If others are not at least disappointed by it, I certainly shall never regret it. For I am not the kind of man who, having placed my apprenticeship <note>original: "tirocinio" — the first stage of training for a soldier or scholar</note> here, would seek even third place in that noble race of learned men who present themselves as the bravest champions of all antiquity <term>antiquitatis: ancient times or the study of the past</term>, either by uncovering, purging, or—in a way that harms no one and perhaps benefits many—interpreting the monuments <term>monumentis: records, writings, or physical remains of the past</term> of the ancients. If I were to desire any place among them, [I would find myself] so far away from—

<summary>Tarin describes the production of this book as a personal sacrifice of his limited leisure time, intended as a grateful "repayment" to his patron Jean de Gondi rather than a pursuit of scholarly fame.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, patronage, scholarly labor, public utility, Jean de Gondi, translation of antiquity, gratitude</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>Jean Tarin continues his dedication to Jean de Gondi. Having just discussed his own modest "apprenticeship" in scholarship, he now defines his role not as a primary actor, but as a facilitator providing materials for the "Republic of Letters." He specifically addresses the need for this bilingual edition of Origen's Philocalia, lamenting the modern necessity of providing Latin translations alongside the original Greek.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>e ij</sig>

...I might seem to be, as I understand how far removed I am from them. What, then, is my role? To act? Certainly it is to assist others in what they may do for the <term>Reipubl. literarum: Republic of Letters; the international community of scholars</term>, which is especially useful, and truly glorious for themselves. For I also foresee that this will be no slight incentive to someone: that since these two exceptional specimens have been brought to light from the infinite labors of **Origen**, inviting the reader, they might take up the same plan concerning all the best works. Thus, they may very appropriately join to the Latin works—which, deprived of their own spirit, have long wandered alone—the very voice of **Origen**, and not merely an image of his voice, which is mute in comparison to the original.

For how many people are there who would not prefer to speak face-to-face with the one they value most, rather than through the intervention of a man who is little known or perhaps even unwelcome? Therefore, if the study of literature were held by everyone in the place it deserves, this practice which has almost become an established custom in our way of <term>interpretationis: translation or interpretation</term>—a sort of "two-horse team" <note>original: "bigae coniugatio" — refers to the practice of publishing Greek and Latin text side-by-side</note>—would not have been necessary. For what successful course, I ask you, can there be in such an unequal yoke? 

But we must obey, even against our will, an authority more powerful than it is just, which one would resist in vain. For he who wishes to publish these <term>monimenta: monuments; here referring to the enduring written works</term> "naked" <note>meaning in the original Greek without a translation</note>, since so few can read them, would seem to look out too little for his own interests and, as they say, for the benefit of the many. And so it has plainly become the custom, just as formerly for Roman <term>Magistratibus: Magistrates; high-ranking government officials</term> in their entourage...

<summary>Tarin explains that his role is to provide scholars with the original Greek "voice" of Origen, though he begrudgingly includes a Latin translation to satisfy the modern reader's needs. He compares the bilingual format to an "unequal yoke" but acknowledges it is necessary for the work to be widely useful.</summary>
<keywords>Republic of Letters, Origen, translation theory, bilingual editions, Greek scholarship, Jean Tarin</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>Jean Tarin continues his address to Jean de Gondi. He has just argued that while a "two-horse team" of side-by-side Greek and Latin text is an "unequal yoke," it has become a necessary evil for modern readers who cannot engage with the original Greek directly.</meta>

...not with that honorary interpreter, though sometimes a necessary one was provided, who might attend to them both in private and in public. In the same way, for the most distinguished authors, especially the **Greeks**, a kind of attendant <note>original: "apparitor"; in ancient Rome, an "apparitor" was a public servant or official assistant to a magistrate</note> is assigned. This attendant is not always a confidant of their inner secrets or a companion allowed into their private chambers; rather, he is one who attempts to sketch the magnitude and majesty of his master’s speech in a more familiar style of language. He strives for this with all his strength, though he may scarcely ever fully achieve it. 

Truly, if anyone has achieved this by means of an excellent intellect, let them be granted well-deserved praise and congratulations. For my part, I shall consider myself abundantly satisfied if, instead of praise, I might obtain from others—following your example—the pardon which your singular <term>humanitas: a Latin concept combining kindness, cultural refinement, and philanthropy</term> so easily promises. In this particularly difficult turning point of a most hindered journey, I have looked for nothing greater or more fruitful than this. 

Let applause delight others; let others be captured by pomp and spectacle or the allurements of glory. Let the fruit of my labor be simply not to have completely failed in this performance. On this I will sustain myself for the present, and for the future I will nourish the best hope of attempting greater works—a hope which holds me firm, fixed and rooted in your kindness. May that kindness lead the way and preside over these premature and hurried works. Their <term>festionatio: haste</term> is surely to be forgiven, for they rushed to please all good men for your sake and under your illustrious name. And why not indeed...

<summary>Tarin describes the humble role of the translator as a mere "attendant" to the great Greek authors and asks his patron, Jean de Gondi, for pardon regarding the hurried nature of his work.</summary>

...was it not necessary to hurry, so that these insignia, these lights, this flower, this selection, this treasure of more hidden Theology <note>original: "Theologiæ"</note>, this instrument of more abstruse wisdom, these choice gems—excerpted from the immense riches of Origen by divine men <note>Tarin refers to St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus, who compiled the *Philocalia*, a collection of Origen's most beautiful and important passages</note>—might be brought to a man such as everyone knows you to be, most liberal Bishop Theodore <note>original: "Theodorum Episcopum"</note>, as a monument of a grateful mind? Was it not right that they be placed in a good light—that is, in the sight of all those who are more refined in the humanities? 

But this was no less desired by those excellent and chosen companions: the most eloquent Zacharias Rhetor <note>A 6th-century Christian philosopher and bishop known for his dialogue against the eternity of the world</note>, a most faithful champion of Christian truth; that famous Anastasius <note>likely Anastasius Sinaita, a 7th-century monk and theologian</note>, shaped by a certain heavenly discipline; and those fragments of more splendid and ancient purple, <term>ON THE SOUL <gloss>De Anima</gloss></term>. I have brought these forth so that they might no longer remain hidden—being entirely worthy to flow into the knowledge of all. And I have brought them into that innermost sanctuary, most holily dedicated by your pious ardor of prayer, so that they might seek the auspices of public commendation from you. 

I do not doubt that there will be a place for them there, where all things noble and excellent hold their own—that is, the highest and first—place. Both their own splendor and dignity, as well as your liberal inclination toward these letters, most kindly show that there will be a most ample place for them. Farewell.

->Paris. From our Harcourt College. September 6th,<-
->in the Year of Salvation 1618.<-

# TO THE KIND READER, <note>original: "LECTOR CANDIDE"</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap initial 'Q' decorated with intricate floral patterns and a bird or creature intertwined with the foliage.</image-desc>THAT you see my own translation everywhere in this work is something done as much against my will as it was restricted by the constraints of time. I truly wish that necessity had not driven me to a point where I must either flee the resentment of others' criticism or dread the reputation of being thoughtless. Indeed, I hope no one interprets my actions less kindly than I intended; I acted with no other thought than to take all the labor and struggle upon myself, and to stand alone under the weight of any severe judgment, having invited no partner to share the burden. 

And certainly, as I was reviewing and reflecting, several things occurred to me that brought to mind that ancient proverb: **to think ahead is better than to regret** <note>original Greek: "προνοεῖν ἢ μετανοεῖν" (*pronoien e metanoien*), a common Greek maxim emphasizing foresight over hindsight</note>. However, just as it is the mark of a man to acknowledge his own fault, it is the mark of humanity to freely forgive the faults of others. I offer no excuse for failing to do the former; as for the latter—that you might forgive me willingly—the following reasons will appeal to your kindness. When I undertook to publish the <term>Philocalia <gloss>an anthology of the works of Origen compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus</gloss></term> as quickly as possible, I believed I had taken on no other burden than ensuring it was produced in its most corrected form. The hope of this was making me—

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page where Jean Tarin explains his decision to translate the Philocalia alone, he now describes the specific sources he used and the intense pressure he faced from the printing house to finish the work quickly.</meta>

...the reliability of the **Royal Manuscript** <note>original: *Regij Codicis*; likely referring to a Greek manuscript in the library of the King of France</note> was paramount, and I relied upon it in most cases of doubt, especially since it could be supported by the published editions of the books *Against Celsus* and two other writings. I also placed my trust in that famous translation by a well-known **Theologian** <note>likely referring to a previous Latin translator of Origen</note>, whose reputation and authority had kept me from examining his work too critically. 

Meanwhile, the printing equipment was prepared and the **type was set** <note>original: *formae componuntur*; literally "the forms are composed," referring to the physical layout of metal type for the press</note>. It was only then, when I finally saw that previous translation for what it was, that I snapped out of my gullibility. I began to beg for a delay so that I could hammer out a new or at least a revised translation. 

However, those whose financial interests were at stake in this market argued that all their preparations would go to waste if I frustrated their expectations with a postponement. They told me I had only a small amount of time to stay ahead of the rapid pace of the printing presses. I pleaded that my life was already far too busy; they kept pushing until I finally accepted the burden. 

In the meantime, the work never stopped. Every day they dragged from me my **nighttime studies** <note>original: *lucubrationes*; a term for scholarly work produced by candlelight</note>—writings that were neither polished nor even fully claimed by me—so that I am forced to admit that almost everything was produced "under the hand" <note>meaning written hastily as the printer waited for the next page</note>. This is why I wasn't able to compare my work carefully with other published books at first. 

Now that the project is finished, I am reconsidering these points more thoroughly. I honestly fear that I may have caused some boredom, and I felt it was better to leave these revisions to the **Notes** as a sort of second thought. In these notes, I have applied a painstaking diligence to even the smallest details and doubts. I have included **variant readings** <note>original: *variantes lectiones*; differences in text found between various manuscript copies</note> drawn from the **Holy Bible** and many points I marked out with perhaps too much anxiety. I would offer an excuse for this if I didn't trust in your fairness. By acting this way, as you can clearly see, I chose to invite criticism upon myself rather than criticize the work of others...

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Jean Tarin describes the intense pressure of the printing process. He concludes his explanation of why he worked so hastily ("under the hand" of the press) and now transitions into his editorial philosophy regarding the specific texts included in this volume, such as the works of Origen, Zacharias, and Anastasius.</meta>

I chose this path, believing that by asking for what I seem to have a right to demand, others might in turn show me greater fairness. For no one who is convinced that a person does no harm if they refrain from giving offense will think that the things I have passed over were also things I had actually noted. I followed this principle not only with **Origen**, but also with **Zacharias** and **Anastasius**. 

As for those **Selections** <note>original: *Eclogas*; chosen excerpts or passages</note> *On the Soul*, which were quite messy due to very corrupt manuscripts and thus not easy to "clean up" <note>original: *defaecare*; a philological term for refining a text and removing errors</note>, I felt it a matter of conscience not to leave them separated from their "companions," as it were. This is because they seemed to call for inclusion and did not differ much from the subject matter of **Anastasius** <note>likely referring to Anastasius Sinaita, a 7th-century scholar</note>. 

And perhaps there will be those who find relief in this shortcut—those weary of the longer works of **Plato and Aristotle**—since this path seems to have been discovered by someone who had spent a long time treading and deeply exploring both philosophers. He followed nearly the same method as the **collectors of oracles** <note>original Greek: *chresmologountes* (χρησμολογοῦντες)</note> and **compilers** <note>original Greek: *eklogeis* (ἐκλογεῖς)</note> of former times. These men would record the opinions of the best authors, sometimes using the authors’ own words and sometimes their own; at times they would interject their own judgment, offering praise or expressing indignation. 

Nevertheless, any slightly more thoughtful reader will judge that this man was no common scribe, but clearly a learned and practiced scholar. He was one whose own spirit prompted him to bring the complex and difficult treatment of the Soul by the ancient philosophers—especially **Aristotle**—into a single view. Like a **dividing thread** <note>an allusion to Ariadne’s thread, used to navigate the Labyrinth in Greek mythology</note> through those twists and narrow passages, he guides and assists those who have lost their way by his leadership and 

help.

...fore. I would greatly wish for you to experience this, as I believe it was established with that very intention. In them, you will find certain substitutions of "second thoughts that are better" <note>original Greek: *deuteron ameinonon* (δεύτερων ἀμεινόνων); a proverbial expression for refined corrections</note>, and—what will please you not a little—you will realize that this edition brings quite a lot of fuller, and perhaps better, material than is found in other books. As for the remaining matters, which are perhaps neither trivial nor non-existent, you will surely grant them—if not to the man himself, then certainly to the spirit of humanity and scholarship. 

If you find any stumbling block in **Origen Adamantius** <note>Adamantius, meaning "Man of Steel," was a common nickname for the 3rd-century scholar Origen, referring to his tireless work ethic</note>, listen, I pray, to what he himself says concerning the "stone of stumbling" <note>a biblical reference to Romans 9:33 or 1 Peter 2:8; Tarin is likely referring to Origen’s controversial reputation in the Church</note>. And these works, such as they are, were sent by the truest and greatest theologians—who have called Origen the "whetstone of all theologians" and the greatest teacher of the churches after the Apostles (and they were not the only ones to say so). They were sent to a man—what more can I say?—who is truly a Bishop, as a most beautiful gift. Receive them in such a way that, like **Jerome**, you pluck different flowers from many sources, not intending to approve of everything, but rather to choose the good things. Finally, yield to the immortal voice of the divine Apostle: "Test all things; hold fast to what is good" <note>original Greek: *panta dokimazete, kalon katechete* (ΠΑΝΤΑ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΖΕΤΕ, ΚΑΛΟΝ ΚΑΤΕΧΕΤΕ); quoting 1 Thessalonians 5:21</note>.

<margin>20</margin> Against those who claim that the entire world and the human race were created not for the sake of man, but for the sake of irrational animals. Their argument is that irrational animals live with less toil than we do; and that, being wiser than us, they are more beloved by God, possess an awareness of the Divine, and have foreknowledge of future events. This section also addresses the transmigration of souls <term>transmigration of souls: *metempsychosis*, the belief that a soul can be reborn into a different body, including that of an animal</term>, as well as the practice of augury <term>augury: *oionistikē*, the ancient practice of predicting the future by observing the flight or sounds of birds</term> and the deception associated with it.

<margin>21</margin> Regarding free will <term>free will: *autexousion*, literally "self-power" or the innate capacity for self-determination</term>, and an explanation and resolution of those Scriptural passages which seem to negate it.

<margin>22</margin> What is the "dispersion" of rational or human souls on earth? This is hidden and revealed through the account of the building of the Tower, and the subsequent confusion of languages; including a discussion on the many "lords" assigned to those who were scattered, according to the specific condition of each group. <note>Origen interprets the Tower of Babel as a spiritual event where souls were assigned to different nations and angelic overseers based on their previous choices.</note>

<margin>23</margin> Regarding Fate <term>Fate: *Heimarmene*, the concept of an inescapable, pre-determined destiny</term>, and how, while God has foreknowledge of what will be done by each person, our own free choice is still preserved. Furthermore, in what way the stars are not causes of human affairs, but merely signs. Also, why humans cannot have an exact knowledge of these things, as the signs are set out for divine powers; and what the reason for this is. Included in this is a passage from Clement, Bishop of Rome, in his discourse to his father in Laodicea, regarding a most necessary theory on why astrology sometimes appears to be true. <note>original: "Clementis Episcopi Romae," referring to the *Clementine Recognitions*, a popular early Christian narrative attributed to Clement of Rome.</note>

<margin>24</margin> Regarding Matter: that it is not uncreated <note>original: *agennetos*, meaning without a beginning or source</note>, nor is it the cause of evil.

<margin>25</margin> That being "set apart" due to God’s foreknowledge does not negate our free will.

<margin>26</margin> Regarding what things are truly good and what things are truly evil. Also, that these categories exist within the realm of our choices and outside of our choices <term>within our choices: *proairetikois*, things dependent on the will; *aproairetois*, things independent of the will</term> according to the teaching of Christ, and not as Aristotle thinks. <note>Aristotle argued that external "goods" like wealth or health were necessary for happiness, whereas Origen emphasizes that only the state of the soul truly matters.</note>

<margin>27</margin> Concerning the passage: "The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh." <note>Exodus 9:12. This was a central problem for Origen: how can a just God harden a heart and then punish the person for it? He argues it is like the sun hardening clay while softening wax.</note>

19. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Against those who claim that both the world and mankind were created not for the sake of man, but for the sake of irrational animals <term>irrational animals: *bruta*, creatures lacking the human capacity for reason</term>, because animals live with less toil than we do, and since they are supposedly wiser than us, they love God, possess a sense of the Divine, and foreknow future events. This section also discusses the migration of souls <term>migration of souls: *metempsychosis*, the belief that a soul can be reborn into different bodies, including animals</term> and the practice of augury <term>augury: *augurali disciplina*, the ancient method of foretelling the future by observing the flight or sounds of birds</term> and its deceptive nature. 216.

20. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Concerning the freedom of the will <term>freedom of the will: *liberum arbitrium*, the capacity for moral choice</term>; and the solution and interpretation of those passages of Scripture which seem to take that freedom away. 264.

21. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What the "dispersion" of rational or human souls upon the earth might be, which is obscurely declared through the building of the Tower and the confusion of languages that occurred there; also concerning the many "lords" who, by reason of the specific arrangement of things, were placed over those who were scattered. <note>Origen often interpreted the Tower of Babel as a spiritual descent where souls were assigned to different nations and angelic guardians based on their merit.</note> 312.

22. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Concerning fate, and how—since God foreknows the things done by every individual—the freedom of the will remains intact. Also, in what manner the stars do not cause human affairs, but only signify them; that men cannot have exact knowledge of these things, but these signs exist within the divine powers; and what the cause of these things might be. A certain necessary observation by Clement, Bishop of Rome, in a sermon to his father at Laodicea, regarding those who think that Astrology is true. <note>Clement of Rome was an early Church Father; the sermon mentioned is likely from the *Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions*, a popular early Christian philosophical "novel."</note> 330.

23. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Concerning matter; that it is not uncreated <term>uncreated: *ingenitam*, something that has always existed without a beginning</term>, nor is it the cause of evils. 377.

24. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Predestination and setting apart based on foreknowledge <term>foreknowledge: *praenotione*, God's prior knowledge of what will happen</term> does not take away the freedom of the will. 398.

25. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which things are truly good and which are evil: these are freely chosen or avoided according to the doctrine of Christ, but not as Aristotle supposes. <note>Aristotle viewed virtue as a habit often influenced by external circumstances; Origen emphasizes the radical freedom of the soul granted by Christ.</note> 408.

26. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Again, regarding the verse: *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh.* <note>original Latin: "Indurauit Dominus cor Pharaonis." This is a key text from Exodus used by Origen to explain how divine action interacts with human stubbornness.</note> 428.

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN.

The present book contains a selection of Scriptural questions and solutions, drawn from various books of Origen. This collection was compiled and gathered by those wise in divine things, Gregory and Basil. In a small notebook <term>small notebook: *pyktion*, a portable writing tablet or bound book</term> which he had prepared, Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–389 AD), a central figure in early Christian theology known for his eloquence</note> sent it to Theodore, who was at that time the Bishop of Tyana, just as the letter written to him shows, which reads as follows:

A festival is what your letter brought—and even better, because you anticipated the proper season with your eagerness, granting us the joy of celebrating in advance. Such are the things that come from your Piety; for our part, we have nothing greater to return to you than our prayers. However, so that you may have a souvenir from both myself and the holy Basil, we have sent you a small volume of Origen’s *Philocalia* <term>Philocalia: Literally "Love of the Beautiful," here referring to a collection of the most "beautiful" or excellent excerpts from Origen's vast works</term>, containing selections useful to those who love learning <term>those who love learning: *philologoi*, students of literature and divine wisdom</term>. Please deign to accept this, and show us proof of its benefit through your diligence, being helped by the Spirit.

---

*This book contains a choice selection of questions on the Scriptures and their solutions, drawn from various commentaries of Origen and compiled by those most expert in divine matters, Gregory and Basil. One of them, Gregory the Theologian, sent it in a small volume to Theodore, the Bishop of Tyana at that time, as this letter written to him declares.* <note>original: "Delectum hic liber continet..." This section is a 16th or 17th-century Latin translation of the Greek text above, standard in early modern scholarly editions.</note>

*Your letter represents for us the joy of a feast day; and what is far more excellent, you outrun the time itself, and by your generous will and inclination, you provide an early celebration. These are the things that proceed from your piety; for our part, we respond with prayers as much as we can. And so that you may also have from me and from the holy Basil a monument of our friendship, we have sent you this little book of selections from Origen, in which excerpts are held that are useful to scholars. Do not be burdened to receive these; then, show what fruit you have gathered from them, aided by your study and the spirit.*

<meta>This page continues Origen’s critique of scriptural interpretation. While the previous page addressed heretics who rejected the Creator God of the Old Testament entirely, this page turns its focus to "simple" Christians within the Church. Origen argues that while these believers are right to worship the Creator, their literal reading of difficult passages leads them to attribute "cruel" and "unjust" traits to God. He proposes the "Apostolic Rule" as the necessary corrective.</meta>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER I.

<columns>

...devised. But furthermore, even the more <term>simple-minded</term> <note>Original Greek: *akeraioteroi*; Latin: *simpliciores*. Refers to believers who lack advanced theological training or allegorical insight.</note> among those who boast of belonging to the Church, though they have supposed none to be greater than the **Creator**—acting soundly in this regard—nevertheless hold such views about him as one would not even hold regarding the most cruel and unjust of men. And the cause for all the aforementioned false opinions, impieties, or ignorant words concerning God seems to be nothing else than that the Scripture has not been understood according to its **spiritual** meaning, but has been interpreted according to the <term>bare letter</term> <note>original: *psilon gramma*. The literal or "naked" meaning of the text without looking for deeper spiritual truths.</note>. Therefore, for those who are persuaded that the sacred books are not the compositions of men, but were written by the inspiration of the **Holy Spirit**, by the will of the Father of all things through Jesus Christ, and have come down to us, the apparent ways of understanding must be pointed out; while we hold to the **rule** <note>original: *kanonos*. The "Rule of Faith" or standard of orthodox interpretation used by the early Church.</note> of the heavenly Church of Jesus Christ according to the **succession of the Apostles**. And that there are certain <term>mystical economies</term> <note>original: *oikonomiai mystikai*. These are the secret arrangements or "plans" of God’s interaction with humanity revealed in the Bible.</note> revealed through the divine Scriptures, all believe, even the simplest of those who have [clung] to the Word...

<column-break/>

...devised. Moreover, some simpler ones who boast that they are of the church, think nothing greater than the **Founder**, indeed embracing a sound opinion in that; but they suspect such things of him as they would not even think of a most cruel and unjust man. To all these, no other cause of false opinions, impiety, and foolish talk about God appears to be than that the scripture is not understood according to the **spirit**, but is accepted according to the <term>naked sound of the letter</term>. ### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER I.

In the writings of Solomon, within the book of Proverbs, we find a certain instruction of this kind concerning the divinely written doctrines:

Therefore, one ought to transcribe the meanings of the Holy Scriptures into one’s own soul in a threefold way. The purpose is that the simpler person may be built up by what we might call the **flesh** of the Scripture—this is the name we give to the obvious and literal interpretation <note>original: "πρόχειρον ἐκδοχήν" (procheiron ekdochēn). # PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER I.

[The spiritual sense] belongs to the person who is able to demonstrate of what heavenly things the Jews according to the flesh <note>original: *kata sarka*. Origen uses this term to refer to those who follow the literal, physical requirements of the Law without seeking a deeper spiritual meaning.</note> served as a pattern and a shadow; and of what future good things the Law holds a shadow. And somewhere the same Apostle says, using phrases from the books of **Exodus** and **Numbers**, that these things happened to them as **types** <note>original: *typikōs*. ### ->PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER I.<-

...[to distinguish] the sense of the **Scripture** scattered everywhere from that which is impossible according to the letter. Since, therefore, as will be clear to those who encounter it, the literal sequence <note>original Greek: "εἱρμός" (heirmos); meaning the logical connection or flow of the words.</note> is at times impossible, while the primary meaning is not only possible but true, one must strive to grasp the whole mind [of the text]. This involves connecting the account of what is impossible according to the letter with those things that are not only possible but historically true, interpreting them **allegorically** <term>allegory: a method of interpretation that finds a hidden spiritual meaning behind the literal words.</term> alongside those events that did not literally happen. For we assert regarding the whole of **Divine Scripture** that while all of it has a **spiritual sense**, not all of it has a **bodily sense** <term>bodily sense: the literal, historical, or physical meaning of the text.</term>; for in many places the bodily sense is proved to be impossible. Therefore, the one who approaches the **Divine Books** with reverence as divine writings must apply great care and attention, for the character of their understanding appears to us in this way: The words report that a certain nation upon the earth was chosen...

<column-break/>

...the sense of **Scripture** diffused everywhere, to judge it from that which cannot be done according to the letter. Since therefore, as will be manifest to those reading attentively, there can be no continuity in those things which pertain to the letter; yet there can be, and indeed truly is, a principal order which strives to comprehend the whole mind of **Scripture**. This order connects the reason of those things which cannot happen according to the letter, through the **spirit**, to those things which are not only not impossible, but are also true according to history; and these, along with the things that did not literally happen, include an interior sense and are spoken through **allegory**. For thus we have determined concerning the whole of **Scripture**: that all its passages have the sense of the **spirit**, but not all have the **bodily** [sense]. For we have frequently shown by arguments that the bodily sense cannot always be. Wherefore, it is necessary for him who dwells cautiously and religiously in the **Divine Books**—as in divine writings—to apply much care and attention. To us, the form of their understanding appears as follows: The **Scripture** records that God chose a certain nation from the earth...

<meta>This page continues Chapter 1 of the Philocalia, a collection of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus. On the previous page, Origen argued that every detail of Scripture, down to the smallest stroke of a letter, is filled with divine wisdom. He now explains how this "Fullness" is perceived by the faithful and how to handle passages that seem difficult or "offensive" to the reader.</meta>

# OF ORIGEN

...from the <term>fullness</term> <note>original: "πληρώματος" (pleromatos) / "plenitudine". A technical theological term referring to the totality of divine powers and the complete presence of God within the Word.</note>, it breathes fullness upon those who have eyes to see the things which belong to the fullness, and ears hearing those things that come from the fullness, and a sense-organ for perceiving the most sweet odor exhaled from the fullness. But if, while reading the Scriptures, you should sometimes trip over a thought which is, as it were, a <term>stone of stumbling</term> <note>original: "λίθῳ προσκόμματος" (lithō proskommatos). A reference to Romans 9:33 and Isaiah 8:14, describing a obstacle that causes one to trip; Origen uses it here to describe difficult biblical passages.</note> and a <term>rock of offense</term> <note>original: "πέτρᾳ σκανδάλου" (petra skandalou). Similar to the stone of stumbling, this refers to something that "scandalizes" or traps the reader's understanding.</note>, blame yourself. For you must not despair that these thoughts contain this stone of stumbling and rock of ruin, so that <margin>Romans 9</margin> what was said may come to pass: *He who believes shall not be put to shame.* First, believe; and beneath that which is thought to be a stumbling block, you will find a great deal of holy benefit.

---

*From the commentaries on the 40th Psalm. After he has directed the beginning of the history concerning <term>Uriah</term> <note>Uriah the Hittite, whose story is found in 2 Samuel 11. Origen is explaining his method of "allegorizing" or looking for a hidden spiritual meaning in this historical narrative.</note> toward a hidden sense, he adds:*

If, however, it seems to anyone to be a "violent" <note>In this context, "violent" means forced or unnatural interpretation.</note> thing that I have transferred a part of the history to an abstruse sense, and have not interpreted it in a uniform way, it is clear that such a claim is made rashly, and that other things must be sought for in this passage; unless, indeed, there is someone who has very accurately weighed the details of this place...

<column-break/>

...from the fullness, it breathes of the fullness for those who have eyes seeing the things of the fullness, and ears hearing the things from the fullness, and a sense-organ breathing in the sweet odor of the things from the fullness. But if ever, while reading the Scripture, you should stumble at a thought which is a "stone of stumbling and a rock of offense," blame yourself. For do not lose hope that this stone of stumbling and rock of offense possesses [divine] thoughts. So that what was spoken might come to pass: *And he who believes shall not be put to shame.* Believe first, and you will find much holy benefit beneath that which is considered a stumbling block.

---

*From the explanatory notes on the 40th Psalm, in the section where he has allegorized the beginning of the history concerning Uriah, he adds:*

If it seems to anyone to be forced to allegorize a history in part, but not to smooth it out [consistently], it is clear that these things will have been said in vain, and other things must be sought for the passage. Unless, perhaps, someone who has further examined the details of the passage...

<summary>Origen explains that while Scripture is filled with divine "fullness," readers may encounter difficult passages that act as "stumbling blocks." He argues that these difficulties are tests of faith and that an allegorical, spiritual interpretation—such as his treatment of the story of Uriah—reveals hidden holy benefits.</summary>

...wishes to restore all things, both concerning the murdered man and his apparent goodness—in that he was unwilling to go into his own house and rest while the people were in camp and in the midst of the struggle. A method of interpretation that looks for a deeper spiritual or symbolic meaning beneath the literal "letter" of the text.</note> in these matters, and who think the wording was recorded for its own sake, will represent the will of the Holy Spirit who deemed these things worthy of record. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding those who misunderstand the relationship between the Old and New Testaments. It follows the fragment of Origen's "Homilies on Leviticus" quoted in the Philocalia, specifically addressing the Gnostic error of separating the God of the Law from the God of the Gospel.</meta>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER I.

...from Judaism and from the God who gave these scriptures and the whole Law, and they fashioned **another God** <note>original: "ἕτερον θεόν" / "aliú Deum". Origen is refuting the Marcionite and Gnostic claim that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser or different deity than the Father of Jesus Christ.</note>, apart from the God who gave the Law and the prophets, apart from the one who made heaven and earth. But this is not the case; rather, the one who gave the Law also gave the Gospel; the one who made the things that are seen also gave the things that are not seen. And the things seen and the things not seen possess a kinship; and they have such a kinship that "the invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made" <note>This is a quotation of Romans 1:20, used here to justify the allegorical interpretation of the physical world and the physical text of the Law.</note>; there is also a kinship between the visible things of the Law and the prophets and the things that are not seen, but are understood, of the Law and the prophets. Since, therefore, the Scripture itself is composed, as it were, of a **body** <note>original: "σώματος" / "corpore". The literal or historical sense of the text.</note> which is seen, and a **soul** <note>original: "ψυχῆς" / "animâ". The moral or intellectual sense.</note> which is understood and perceived within it, and a **spirit** <note>original: "πνεύματος" / "spiritu". The highest, mystical, or "heavenly" sense.</note> which is according to the patterns and **shadow of heavenly things** <note>original: "σκιὰν τῶν ἐπουρανίων" / "vmbram cœlestium". A reference to Hebrews 8:5, suggesting that the Old Testament rituals prefigure spiritual realities.</note>; come then, let us call upon Him who made for the Scripture a body, soul, and spirit—a body indeed...

<column-break/>

...from Judaism and from the God who was the author of these scriptures and the whole Law, they fell away and fashioned **another God** <note>original: "aliú Deum". See the note in the preceding column regarding Gnostic dualism.</note> besides the one who had given the Law and the prophets, and who had made heaven and earth. This is certainly most foreign to the truth. For the God who gave the Law also gave the Gospel: He who made those things which are seen also gave those things which are not discerned by the eyes: and those things which are seen and those which do not appear to the eyes have a kinship between themselves. Moreover, they have such a kinship that the works of God which cannot be seen may be seen and known through the things made from the creation of the world: those things which are seen in the laws and prophets have a kinship with those things which are not seen, but are understood in the Law and the prophets. Since, therefore, the Scripture itself also consists as if of a **body**, which is discerned, and of a **soul**, which is understood and conceived within it, and then of a **spirit** through the patterns and **shadow of heavenly things**: Come, having called upon Him who made the body, soul, and spirit of the Scripture, the body indeed...

<summary>Origen argues for the unity of the Old and New Testaments, asserting that the same God created the physical world, the Law, and the Gospel. He introduces his famous tripartite theory of scriptural interpretation, comparing the text to a human being composed of body (literal), soul (moral), and spirit (spiritual).</summary>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER II.

->And after other things.<- <note>original: "Καὶ μεθ᾿ ἕτερα" / "Et post alia". A standard formula indicating an excerpt taken from a larger work.</note>

As we are about to begin the interpretation of the Psalms, we will first set forth a most graceful tradition handed down to us by a Hebrew <note>This likely refers to one of Origen’s Jewish teachers in Caesarea, whom he frequently cites for traditional interpretive insights.</note> regarding the whole of Divine Scripture in general. For that man used to say that the whole of divinely-inspired Scripture, because of the obscurity found within it, is like many rooms locked within a single house. Next to each room lies a key, but not the one that fits it. Thus, the keys have been scattered around the rooms, not matching the individual rooms where they are placed. He said it is a very great task both to find the keys and to fit them to the rooms they are able to open. Therefore, the Scriptures, being obscure, do not receive the starting points for being understood from anywhere else but from one another, since they contain the method of explanation scattered within themselves. I believe that the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> also hints at such an approach to understanding the divine words when he says: "Which things also we speak, not in the taught words of human...

<column-break/>

->And after other things.<-

As we are about to begin the interpretation of the Psalms, we shall propose a most excellent document regarding the Scripture handed down to us by a Hebrew: for he used to say that the entirety of Scripture, inspired by God, was—on account of the obscurity within it—similar to many chambers enclosed within a single building. To each chamber was placed a key that did not belong to it, and thus the keys were scattered among the chambers, each not corresponding to the chambers where they were placed. Truly, he said, it is a far more difficult task to find the keys and to fit them to the cells which they are able to open. Therefore, even those hidden Scriptures are understood by taking the arguments for understanding from nowhere else than from one another, for they hold within themselves the scattered logic of exposition. I think, therefore, that the Apostle was opening this path for understanding the divine discourses when he said: <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> *Which things we also speak, not in the taught [words] of human...*

<note>The text cuts off here, continuing Paul's thought from 1 Corinthians 2:13: "...wisdom, but in those taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual." This aligns with Origen's point that Scripture explains Scripture.</note>

<term>Hebrew</term>: A reference to a Jewish scholar; Origen often sought Jewish tradition to better understand the Old Testament.
<term>Hermeneutics</term>: The theory and methodology of interpretation, especially of biblical texts.

<summary>Origen introduces the "Allegory of the Keys," a famous metaphor suggesting that while the Bible is obscure, the solution to understanding one passage is often found hidden in another. This establishes the principle that "Scripture interprets Scripture."</summary>

## On the solecism and unrefined phrasing of Scripture.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin>
*Also that: "And we have this treasure in earthenware vessels, so that there may be an overflowing of the power of God, and not from us."* We have understood this as if "treasure" refers to that which is taken from elsewhere—the treasure of cognition and hidden wisdom. # What constitutes "much speaking," and what defines "many books": divine scripture is one book.
## CHAPTER 5.
*From the fifth volume on the Gospel of John. In the preface.*

Since you are not content to have taken this work upon yourself for the sake of my absence, acting as my monitor and task-master <note>original: "laboris exactor". ## On the Distinctive Characters of the Divine Scripture.

### CHAPTER VII.

*From the small volume on the Song of Songs <note>The "Song of Songs" (or Canticle of Canticles) is a book of the Bible written as a series of poetic dialogues</note>, which he wrote in his youth.*

To the one who has not understood the distinctive character of the "persons" <note>In this context, Origen uses the term "persons" (prosopon) to mean the "voices" or "characters" in a dialogue</note> of the divine Scripture—both those who are speaking and those to whom the words are addressed—what is said causes great confusion. This happens when the reader asks who the speaking person is, what kind of person is being addressed, and when the speaking person has stopped speaking—for the person being addressed is often kept in view while another person [is addressed]...

<column-break/>

...saving voice from these sounds <note>original Latin: sonis</note> for those who wish to learn, quieting and restraining all power of the evil spirit, just as David’s music calmed the evil spirit that had invaded Saul and was suffocating him. You see, then, even in this third way, the peacemaker: the one who sees the peace and harmony of this entire Scripture in a consistent way, and brings it together for those seeking rightly and debating with sincerity.

## On the Proper Identification of Characters in Divine Scripture.

### CHAPTER VII.

*From the small volume on the Song of Songs, which he wrote as a young man.*

To the person who has not perceived the specific character of the "persons" <note>original Latin: personarum</note> in the divine Scripture—both of those who speak and those to whom words are directed—the things being said will bring much confusion. This occurs when one seeks to know who the speaking character actually is, what kind of person they are addressing, and where the character who was speaking has left off, since often the one to whom the words are addressed is being observed along with another...

...as he himself is speaking, or the one to whom the speech was directed is no longer listening, but another receives the words, while the speaker nonetheless remains. What need is there to seek examples of each of these, when the writings of the prophets are filled with such an abundance <note>original Latin: copia</note> of them? It is the habit of Scripture to leap instantly from one discourse to another, and the prophets do this in a very obscure and confused manner.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of a specific problem in biblical interpretation: the identity of the speaker in the Psalms. Origen is addressing the apparent contradiction in the book of Acts, where Peter attributes the words of a Psalm to the Holy Spirit speaking through David, even though the words themselves seem to be spoken by Christ (the Savior). This page introduces the concept of "prosopopoeia" or personification as the solution to this mystery.</meta>

->PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER VII.<-
->83<-

...saying: "O God, do not pass over my praise in silence; for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me," and what follows, until, "and let another take his office." <note>original Greek: ἐπισκοπὴν (episkopēn). Origen is quoting Psalm 109:1–8 (Psalm 108 in the Septuagint). In Acts 1:20, Peter quotes this to justify replacing Judas Iscariot among the apostles.</note> How then, if it is the Savior who is saying these things, does Peter say, "It was necessary for the Scripture to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David"? Could it be that what we are being taught here is something like this? The Holy Spirit <term>personifies</term> <note>original Greek: προσωποποιεῖ (prosōpopoiē). This is a rhetorical term for when a writer or speaker adopts the character of another person.</note> in the prophets, and if He personifies God, it is not God Himself who is speaking, but the Holy Spirit speaking from the persona of God. And if He personifies Christ, it is not Christ who is speaking, but the Holy Spirit speaking from the persona of Christ. Thus, even if He personifies the prophet, or that ancient people, or this current people, or whatever else He personifies, it is the Holy Spirit who is the spirit doing the personifying.

<column-break/>

<margin>Psalm 108</margin>
*it is: "O God, do not hold back my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the fraudulent is opened against me," and the words that follow, up to those words: "and let another receive his office." How then, if it is the Savior who says these things, does Peter say, "It was necessary to fulfill the scripture, which the Spirit had foretold through the mouth of David"? Is it not then that what we are taught here is such: the Holy Spirit <term>fashions personas</term> <note>original Latin: personas fingit. This translates the Greek concept of acting or speaking in character.</note> in the prophets; and if He takes on the persona of God, it is not God who speaks, but the Holy Spirit speaks from the persona of God. If He introduces Christ, it is not Christ who speaks, but the Holy Spirit speaks from the persona of Christ. So also, if He exhibits the persona of a prophet, or of this or that people, whatever persona He finally introduces, it is the Holy Spirit who fashions all those personas.*

->OF ORIGEN<-
->84<-

Nothing is to be corrected among those things which, in the Scriptures, have the appearance of a <term>solecism</term> <note>A solecism is a grammatical mistake or an intentional breaking of the rules of syntax.</note>, and which seem to be inconsistent according to the literal letter, provided they maintain the sequence of understanding among those who are endowed with intelligence.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### *From the commentaries on Hosea.*

Since those things in the Scriptures which have the form of a solecism confuse the reader by the wording itself—causing one to suspect that the divine writings were not written correctly or as they should be—some even dare to change them under the pretext of "correction." They attempt to rearrange the meaning contained within those words that seem to lack consistency. Therefore, since something of this sort has necessarily occurred here, as far as can be gathered from the phrasing in the words set before us, let us look at the meaning lying hidden within them. For when he spoke in the plural number, <margin>Hosea 12</margin> *They wept and they prayed to me*, and again set out what follows in the same number, *while I was in the house, they found me*, he utters the remainder in the singular number, saying:

<column-break/>

Concerning the fact that one must not attempt to correct the expressions of Scripture which appear as solecisms and do not preserve the literal sequence, when they preserve the logical sequence of the thought for those capable of understanding.

## CHAPTER 8.
### From the commentaries on Hosea.

SINCE whatever things are spoken in the manner of a solecism throughout the Scripture confuse the reader in their wording, so that one suspects the texts were not written correctly, nor consistently, nor as they truly are; such that some even dare to alter them under the pretext of correction, displacing the sense dwelling within those words that seem to be written inconsistently; it is necessary, as we have fallen upon a similar case here regarding the wording of the words before us, that we see the sense dwelling within them. For having spoken in the plural, *they wept and they prayed to me*; and again having indicated what follows in the plural, *being in the house they found me*, he brings in what follows in the singular, saying:

<summary>Origen argues that apparent grammatical errors (solecisms) in the Bible are intentional and contain hidden depths, warning readers not to "correct" the text to make it follow standard rules of human language. He uses a grammatical shift from plural to singular in the Prophet Hosea to illustrate how these linguistic anomalies require spiritual rather than editorial interpretation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen's defense of the "solecisms" (grammatical irregularities) in the Bible. Having established in the previous page that these are not errors to be corrected but intentional features of the text, he now provides specific examples from Hosea and Genesis to show how the Holy Spirit moves between singular and plural forms to convey deeper meaning.</meta>

->PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER VIII.<-

"and there it was spoken to him." <note>original: καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτόν. This refers to Hosea 12:4.</note> For if someone looks only at the bare wording <term>bare wording</term> <note>The "bare" or "naked" wording refers to the literal grammatical surface of the text without considering its spiritual or logical depth.</note> and thinks a mistake has been written, he might eventually write it in the plural, or change the preceding words to the singular. For having read, *They wept and they prayed to me*, and *While being in the house they found me*, he would say that what follows should be: *There it was spoken to them*—that is, to those who wept and prayed and, while in the house, found God. But through a careful observation of similar phrases, we will show that this too has been spoken consistently. In Genesis, God, when giving the commandment to Adam, says: *Of every tree in the paradise you [singular] shall surely eat, but from the tree of knowing good and evil, you [plural] * <note>Origen is noting that in the Greek Septuagint, the command shifts from the singular "thou" to the plural "ye."</note> *shall not eat of it; for in whatever day you [plural] eat of it, you [plural] shall die the death.* For having begun there also from the singular by saying, *Of every tree in the paradise you [singular] shall surely eat*, He then introduces the plural, saying, *But from the tree of knowing good and evil, you [plural] shall not eat of it; for in whatever day you [plural] eat...*

<column-break/>

*And there he spoke to him.* <note>Latin: Et ibi locutus est ad ipsum.</note> If anyone observes the bare wording, thinking it written by error, he will even write the latter part in the plural number, or reduce the former parts to the singular. For he who reads: *They wept and prayed to me, and while I was at home, they found me,* will assert that the following things should be read thus: *there he spoke to them:* that is, to those who wept and prayed and found God at home. But from an observation of similar words, we shall show that those things also were spoken coherently. In Genesis, God, giving a commandment <margin>Genesis 2</margin> to Adam, says: *Of every tree that is in paradise, eat [singular]; but of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, you [plural] shall not eat of it: for on whatever day you [plural] eat of it, you [plural] shall die the death.* For since there also he had begun from the singular, *of every tree which is in paradise, eat [singular],* he joins it to the plural number, saying, *but of the tree of knowing good and evil, do [plural] not eat of it: for on whatever day you [plural] shall have eaten...*
