### CHAPTER IX.

From the ninth volume <note>original: "tome," referring to a specific book or section of Origen's larger commentary</note> on the Epistle to the Romans: on the passage, "What then is the law of sin." <note>original: "Quid igitur lex peccati" / "Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτίας"</note>

Just as "law" is one name, it is not the case that the discourse concerning "law" is one and the same everywhere in Scripture. Therefore, in every single place, there is a need to accurately track and contemplate it: to weigh what is signified by the name of "law" now, and what it might mean in another instance. But this principle must also be maintained for many other words. For there are words in Scripture that, though they have been assigned the same name, signify different things; these confuse those who think that because there is one word, there is also one single meaning, wherever that name might appear. Now, regarding the fact that the word "law" is applied not to the same meaning but to several, we shall pass over many points—which would require much effort and zeal to resolve the complex meanings they contain—and we shall set forth those things which could persuade anyone...

### CHAPTER IX.

From the ninth volume on the Epistle to the Romans, on the passage: "What then is the law of sin."

Just as "law" is one name, it is not the case that the teaching regarding "law" is one throughout the whole of Scripture. Therefore, in every place, it is necessary to carefully apply oneself and observe: what is signified by the sound of the word "law" in this instance, and what should be understood in that instance. Therefore, it is necessary for the person reading the divine scripture to carefully observe that the scriptures do not always use the same words to refer to the same things. They do this sometimes because of **homonymy** <note>original: ὁμωνυμίαν; a term for when one word has multiple distinct meanings, like "bank" of a river vs. "bank" for money</note>, sometimes because of etymology, and sometimes because the **context** <note>original: σύμφρασιν</note> requires a word to be used differently in certain instances than it is found in others. <column-break/>

Therefore, the law of nature by no means confirms with its testimony the righteousness of God which was declared by Jesus Christ, for it is lesser than it. But the law of Moses [does]; not the letter, but the spirit, and the prophets who correspond to the spirit of the law, and the spiritual discourse that is in them. Wherefore, it is necessary for him who pores over the divine scriptures to observe diligently that they do not always use the same terms for the same things; which they do sometimes by **shared naming** <note>original: cognominationem; the Latin equivalent of homonymy</note>, sometimes by figurative reasoning, and sometimes because of the context of the phrasing, which requires that a word be used differently in some places than it is placed in others. If we observe this attentively, we shall avoid many slips and misguided interpretations. the prophets? Was it not that every word that came forth from their mouths was effective? It is not to be wondered at if whatever word the prophets sent out achieved a result consistent with the words; but I also believe that every marvelous letter written among the divine oracles is effective. There is not one iota, nor one stroke <note>original Latin: "apex"; Greek: "κεραία" (keraia) — the smallest mark or serif on a letter. And it is not wonderful if every word spoken by the prophets worked a work fitting to the word; but indeed I think that also every wonderful letter written in the oracles of God is effective. And there is not one iota, nor one stroke written in the Scripture, which does not work its own work for those who understand how to use the power of the letters.

Just as with herbs, each one has a power, whether for the health of bodies or for whatever else; but it is not for everyone to understand for what each of the herbs is useful. Rather, if some have received knowledge, these are the ones who spend their time among the herbs, so that they might see both when it is to be taken, and where on the body it is to be applied, and in what manner it is prepared to benefit the one using it. Thus, the holy and spiritual man is like a sort of herbalist <term>botanikos (βοτανικός) — a gatherer of herbs; here used as a metaphor for an expert interpreter of the "medicinal" properties of words</term>, collecting from the sacred writings every iota, and every ordinary element <term>stoicheion (στοιχεῖον) — meaning both a fundamental physical element and a letter of the alphabet</term>...
</columns>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 104 regarding the spiritual efficacy of Scripture. Origen is addressing the "usefulness" of the Bible, responding to critics who argue that if a text is not understood, it cannot be inspired.</meta>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XII <note>The *Philocalia* is a 4th-century collection of Origen’s writings compiled by St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus. This chapter focuses on how the "divine power" of the biblical text works on the human soul.</note>

...of the scriptures: either that they are not **God-breathed** <note>original Greek: θεόπνευστοι (*theopneustoi*) — a term used in 2 Timothy 3:16 to describe the divine inspiration of Scripture</note>, since they are not useful—as an unbeliever might suppose—or, as a believer, you must accept that because they are useful, they are indeed God-breathed. You must know, however, that our benefit often occurs without us even noticing it. For example, we are often prescribed a certain food to eat to sharpen our eyesight, and surely while eating we do not perceive that we are benefiting our eyes. But after a second or third day has passed, the distribution of the nourishment that benefits the eye makes us believe through experience that our eyesight has been improved. This can also be seen with other foods that benefit specific parts of the body. So, believe this also regarding the **divine scripture**: that your soul is benefited even if your mind does not grasp the fruit of that benefit from the words themselves, through the mere act of reading. For the things within us are charmed <note>original: ἐπᾴδεται (*epaideta*) — Origen uses the metaphor of an "incantation" or "song" to explain how the words of the Bible act directly on the spiritual nature of the reader</note>; the better parts of us are nourished, while the worse parts are neutralized.

<column-break/>

...scriptures: either they were not **divinely given** <note>original Latin: *divinitus datas*</note> because they are not useful—as an unbeliever might suspect—or, as a believer, admit that they were divinely given because they are useful. We must realize, therefore, that benefit very often comes to us without our even feeling it. In the same way, we are often ordered to take some food for sharpening the eyes, yet while taking it, we do not yet feel the eye being relieved; but on the second or third intervening day, the distribution of the food that helps the eye makes us believe, having experienced it, that we have been relieved in our sight. This may also be observed in other foods useful to certain parts of the body. Thus, therefore, hold it as certain regarding the **divine scripture** that the soul is helped, even if the mind does not perceive the fruit of that utility which flows from the words through the bare reading alone. For the things that are within us are charmed; the better things are nourished, and the worse things are rendered powerless.

<header>OF ORIGEN</header>

Those who wish to avoid wandering from the truth in understanding the divine Scriptures must, of necessity, have mastered the liberal disciplines <note>In the ancient world, the "liberal arts" (such as grammar, logic, and rhetoric) were considered the essential training for a free person's mind and a prerequisite for philosophy.</note> that are suited to this purpose, serving as the first instructions <term>propaedeutics: introductory or preparatory studies</term>; without these, we cannot achieve an accurate understanding of the things being signified.

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*From the 3rd volume of the commentaries on Genesis.*<-

<margin>Gen. 1</margin>
And God made the two great lights: the greater light for the rule of the day, and the lesser light for the rule of the night, and the stars. And God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth and to rule over the day and the night. Now, we must ask whether the phrase "for the rule of the day" is the same as "to rule the day," and whether "for the rule of the night" is the same as "to rule the night." For Aquila <note>Aquila of Sinope was a 2nd-century translator who produced an extremely literal Greek version of the Hebrew Bible to assist those who found the standard Septuagint too loose.</note> maintained a consistent phrasing: in place of "for the rule," he substituted "into power," and for "to rule," he put "to exercise power"

<column-break/>

That for those who wish not to stumble regarding the truth when perceiving the divine Scriptures, it is most necessary to know the fitting logical lessons—that is, the preparatory studies—for this use; without which the accuracy of the meanings cannot be presented in the manner that is required.

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*From the 3rd volume of the commentaries on Genesis.*<-

And God made the two great lights: the greater light for the rule <note>The Greek *archas* can mean both "beginnings" and "rules/powers."</note> of the day, and the lesser light for the rule of the night, and the stars. And God set them in the firmament of heaven, so as to shine upon the earth, and to rule the day and the night. It must be sought whether "for the rule of the day" is the same as "to rule the day," and "for the rule of the night" is the same as "to rule the night." And Aquila indeed preserved the correspondence, making instead of "for the rule," "into authority," and instead of "to rule," "to exercise authority."

<header>PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIV.</header>

...to exercise power <note>original: "exousiazein." The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the word "power."</note>. For those who have concerned themselves with the examination of meanings say that in those passages which contain a pairing of names <term>appellations: nouns or naming words</term> and predicates <term>predicates: words describing an action or state</term>, the things belonging to the names exist first, and the predicates follow from the names. Or, they say that while they have a name, there is a corresponding predicate; for example, "wisdom" <note>original: "phronesis"</note> is the name, but "being wise" <note>original: "phronein"</note> is the predicate. Likewise, "temperance" <note>original: "sophrosyne"</note> is the name, and "being temperate" <note>original: "sophronein"</note> is the predicate. And they say that wisdom exists first, and then the predicate follows: "being wise" comes from "wisdom." Even if we seem to some to be acting against the intent of the Scripture in doing this, we have observed these things: since God, who makes the lights, makes the great one for the rule <note>original: "eis archas" (literally: for the beginnings/rule)</note> of the day, and the lesser one for the rule of the night; but He places them in the firmament of heaven no longer "for the rule" of the day and the night, but "to rule" <note>original: "eis to archein"</note> over the day and the night. For that which is ordered and consistent with technical logic <note>original: "technologoumeno"</note>, the names are placed first in the passage...

<column-break/>

...to have power <note>original Latin: "habeant." This column provides the Latin translation of the Greek text on the left.</note>. They say, moreover, those who have more diligently pursued the meanings, that in those places in which there is a joining together of names <term>appellations: the Latin "appellatio" refers to nouns</term> and of those things which are said of something <term>predicates: the Latin "praedicatum" refers to what is said of a subject</term>, that those things of which they are names come first, and those things said of them follow. For example, that which has a name is like "understanding" <note>original Latin: "intelligentiam"</note>; but that which is said of it is like "to understand" <note>original Latin: "intelligere"</note>. Similarly, the name is "temperance" <note>original Latin: "temperantiam"</note>; the predicate is "to be temperate" <note>original Latin: "temperatum esse" </note>. And they say that understanding precedes, and that which is said from understanding—"to understand"—follows after. We have observed these things even if we seem to some to be acting outside the mind of the Scripture: for since God, who makes the lights, makes the great one for the rule of the day, and the lesser for the rule of the night, He places them in the firmament of heaven, not for the rule of the day and night, but so that they might preside over <note>original Latin: "praesint"</note> the day and night. Because, in an orderly way and in agreement with the opinion of one who teaches the art of Logic, the names are placed first in that location...

Let the person who finds these things difficult to accept consider whether he can correctly understand a proposition about morals, the nature of things, or theology without an accurate knowledge of meanings and those things illustrated in the study of dialectic <term>dialectics: the branch of logic used to examine the truth of meanings through reasoned discussion</term>.

For what is absurd about listening to those who investigate the properties of words in each language and diligently stick to their meanings? For is it absurd to listen to those who speak of proper terms in languages and to attend carefully to meanings? ### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIV.

Regarding those to whom the phrase applies, "the world lies in the power of the evil one" <note>original: "ὁ κόσμος ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται" (1 John 5:19)</note>; that this was spoken by John to refer to earthly and human things instead of the physical universe. For those who think that "world," according to the word itself, signifies the system <term>system: from the Greek 'systema,' referring to the cosmos as an organized, physical whole</term> composed of heaven and earth and the things within them, express themselves most boldly and impiously concerning God. They are in no way able to show through actual fact how the sun, moon, and stars—which move in such an orderly fashion—could "lie in the power of the evil one." Furthermore, if we present to them the verse, "This is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" <note>original: "ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου" (John 1:29)</note>, demonstrating that "world" is used in these instances to mean where sin abounds—that is, in the earthly regions—those who are fair-minded will accept these arguments. But those who are argumentative or who behave foolishly will persist in the wretched judgments they have once made because of their ignorance of the shared name <term>homonymy: the linguistic phenomenon where one word has multiple, distinct meanings</term>. Again, if it is said, "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself" <note>original: "θεὸς ἦν ἐν Χριστῷ κόσμον καταλλάσσων ἑαυτῷ" (2 Corinthians 5:19)</note>, they will no longer be able to maintain what they have assumed about...

<column-break/>

<margin>1 John 5</margin> What it signifies, that *the world is placed in the power of the evil one*, because John used it in that place for the earthly orb and human affairs. For having thought that "world" through that word signified the orb of heaven and earth and what is contained in them, they pronounce most audaciously and—more wickedly than can be said—against God, since they cannot demonstrate in reality in what way the sun and moon and stars, which move in such a fit order, are placed in the evil one. But we say these things by way of digression, to show that we also believe the knowledge of the liberal arts <term>liberal arts: here referring to the "trivium" (grammar, logic, and rhetoric) which Origen viewed as essential tools for biblical scholarship</term> to be entirely necessary for those who wish to hold the truth in understanding the divine Scriptures and not stumble. # OF ORIGEN

...lead to [the truth], as much as they are able, anyone at all—not only the sharp and clever, but also the dull-witted. And not only Greeks or Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarian" simply refers to anyone who did not speak Greek or participate in Greco-Roman culture.</note>, but what is truly the goal of our mission: if one can turn even the most rustic and completely uneducated toward the truth, then it is necessary to hold to that form of speaking which is of common benefit, can be understood by all who hear it, and can captivate the ears of all. However, those who bid a long farewell and reject the unlearned as if they were slaves—those who do not lend their ears to the structure and sequence of polished and elegant speech—and who instead only took account of those trained in eloquence and the disciplines, they have surely forced the commonality of things into the tightest of straits. These things have been said by me for the purpose of defending the humble style <note>original Latin: "tenuitatem"; referring to a "thin" or "simple" literary texture.</note> of the scriptures, which seems to be eclipsed by the splendor of composed oratory, from the blame of Celsus and others; since our prophets, Jesus, and his Apostles followed one method of preaching, which contains not only the truth, but...

<column-break/>

...to lead [people] to it as much as is possible through a love for humanity <note>original Greek: "philanthropian"</note>—anyone at all, not only the wise, but also the foolish. Again, not only Greeks, and not only Barbarians; but what is much more our own practice: if someone is able to convert even the most rustic and unlearned <term>idiōtas: originally meaning a private citizen or someone lacking professional skill, here referring to those without a formal education</term>, it is clear that he must care for a style of speaking that is of common benefit and capable of drawing in every ear. But those who have bid a long farewell to the unlearned as if they were slaves—to those not able to follow the sequence of words and the order of things being announced in refined speech—and have cared only for those raised in rhetoric and learning, these men have contracted the common good into a truly narrow and small space. These things have been said by me as a defense against the charge made by Celsus and others concerning the "imperfection" <note>original Greek: "ateleias"</note> of language in the scriptures, which seems to be darkened by the brilliance of the composition of words in Greek philosophy, since our prophets, Jesus, and his apostles, held to a single way of proclamation, which contains not only what is true, but...

...they began, from the creation of the world and things perceived by the senses, from which one ascends to those things seen by the intellect; and having known His eternal power and divinity not inaptly, nonetheless they became vain in their reasonings, and so their foolish heart wallowed in darkness and ignorance of the worship of the divine power. ...[starting] from the creation of the world and the things of sense, from which they ascend to the things of the mind; having seen His eternal power and divinity not without knowledge, no less were they made vain in their reasonings, and as their foolish heart wallows in darkness and ignorance concerning the service of the divine. For it is clear to those who read <note>original Greek: "τοῖς ἀναγινώσκουσι" (tois anaginōskousi). ### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XV.

->**[PAGE 137]**<-

It is clear, then, that he <note>Referring to the critic Celsus.</note> is forced to accept the words from the prophecy <note>Isaiah 53:2.</note> as being true concerning Christ. This no longer allows the accusations against Jesus to proceed. Furthermore, to the one who says: "Since a divine spirit was in a body, it surely ought to have differed from the rest, either in size, or voice, or strength, or awe-inspiring presence, or persuasiveness"—how did he not see the variation in His body? It appeared to those who saw Him in a way that was possible for them to perceive, and for this reason, it appeared in a way that was useful, showing itself to each person as they needed to see it. It is not surprising that matter—which is by nature changeable and alterable, and transformable into whatever the Creator <note>original Greek: *dēmiourgos*.</note> wishes, and receptive of every quality the Craftsman <note>original Greek: *technitēs*.</note> desires—should sometimes have the quality of which it was said, *He had no form nor beauty*, and at other times be so glorious, awe-inspiring, and wonderful that the spectators fall on their faces before such great beauty.

<column-break/>

...the Gospels nor the Apostles declare that he had no form or beauty, he is indeed forced to admit from the prophecy <note>The Latin text here specifies "David’s prophecy" (*Dauidis vaticinio*), though the quote "no form nor beauty" is actually from Isaiah 53:2. Ancient authors occasionally grouped various prophetic books together under prominent names.</note> that it is true regarding Christ, which certainly restrains all accusations and reproaches against Christ, and does not allow them to spread. Again, when he says, *If indeed a divine spirit was in a body, he ought to have differed from the rest in size, or voice, or strength, or grandeur, or in the power of persuasion*: how did he not see the difference of his own body, as much as those who saw him could perceive? For that reason, it appeared in a useful way, just as it was necessary to be seen by each person. Nor is it a wonder that matter—which is able by nature to be turned, varied, and moved into all things whatever the Maker <note>original Latin: *opifex*.</note> wishes, and which admits every quality that the Craftsman wishes—should sometimes be affected by that quality of which it is said: *He had no appearance, nor beauty*, and at other times be so illustrious and stupendous and admirable that the spectators of such great beauty [fall down]...

We do not call the more diligent readers to a bare and irrational faith, but wish to demonstrate that there is a need for fairness in those who read, and much examination—and, if I may call it so, an entrance into the mind of the writers—so that it may be discovered with what purpose each thing was written. # ORIGEN

<page-num>140</page-num>

...he refuses to accept the apparent divinity announced in those very books, he withdraws credit from the Gospels. For if they were not seekers of truth but had written fictions (as Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Platonic philosopher and the first major intellectual critic of Christianity.</note> thinks), they would never have written that Peter denied Jesus, or that the disciples were <term>scandalized</term> <note>From the Greek *skandalizo*, meaning to be tripped up or to have one's faith shaken by an obstacle.</note>. Indeed, it would seem these things should have been shrouded in silence, especially by men who wished to teach their readers to despise death for the sake of the Christian faith. But now, seeing that the divine word would subdue men by its virtue and power, they included these things as well, which somehow would not harm the reader, yet would not offer an excuse for denying the faith. But the Gospel history holds something secret, declaring the various forms of Jesus Christ according to the nature of the divine word...

<column-break/>

...he refuses to accept the apparent divinity announced in these same books, he distrusts the Gospels. Yet he ought to have seen the love of truth in the writers from their recording of the darker details, and thus believed the more divine parts as well. For if they were not lovers of truth, but—as Celsus imagines—were recording fictions, they would not have recorded Peter denying him, or the disciples of Jesus being led into a stumbling block. For even if such things had happened, who would have challenged the account by claiming it occurred this way? Perhaps, in all likelihood, these things should have been kept silent by men who intended to teach those reading the Gospels to look down upon death for the sake of the confession of Christianity. But now, seeing that the Word <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos). But the account also has something mystical in it, announcing that the various forms of Jesus are to be referred back to the nature of the Divine Word...

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XVII.

->V ii<-

...having grasped this, he will be cautious about applying different names to different things. He must avoid the error of those who mistakenly bestow the name **God** upon lifeless matter, or who drag down the title of **the Good** from the First Cause <note>original: "tou prōtou aitiou" — In early Christian and Platonic philosophy, this refers to God as the ultimate source of all existence.</note>. Indeed, the danger is perhaps no less for the one who degrades the name of God to things he ought not, than for the one who alters names that possess a certain secret logic <note>original: "aporrhēton logon" — This suggests that names are not arbitrary labels but have an inherent, mystical connection to the power they represent.</note>, applying titles of the lesser to the greater, or titles of the greater to the lesser. I do not mean to say that as soon as the name Zeus is heard, one immediately understands the son of Cronus and Rhea, the husband of Hera, the brother of Poseidon, the father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who lay with his daughter Persephone. Or that with the name Apollo, one immediately hears the son of Leto and Zeus, and the brother of Artemis—along with all the other tales brought forward by the wise fathers and ancients who follow the teachings of Celsus...

<column-break/>

...perceived, he will be afraid to impose other names on other things, lest he fall into the error of those who, through blindness of mind, confer the name **God** upon inanimate matter, or tear away the name of **the Good** from the First Cause, or from virtue and honor to blind Pluto <note>The Latin text uses "Plutonem," referring to the god of the underworld, here used interchangeably with the god of wealth.</note>, or to that fit constitution of flesh, blood, and bones found in health and a good physical condition, or to that which the common people think is noble birth. 

Perhaps there is no less danger if one refers the name of God to those things which are not fitting, than if one changes those names in which a secret reason <note>original: "arcana ratio" — The Latin equivalent of the "secret logic" mentioned in the Greek column.</note> dwells, and imposes those attributed to inferior things upon the superior, or conversely, attributes those said of the superior to the inferior. # PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XVII.

->V iij<-

Those skilled in such matters know that the same **incantation** <note>original: "epōdēn" — a ritual chant or spell.</note>, when spoken in its native dialect, is capable of performing what the incantation promises. However, if it is changed into any other language whatsoever, it can be seen to become weak and to have no power at all. Thus, it is not the things signified by the words, but the specific qualities of the sounds themselves that possess a certain power within them for this or that purpose. 

This is also how we shall defend the Christians, who struggle even unto death so that they do not proclaim **Zeus** <note>original: "Dia" (Greek) / "Iouem" (Latin) — the king of the Olympian gods.</note> as God, nor name Him by any other dialect. For they either acknowledge the common name "God" in an indefinite sense, or they use it with the addition of "the Creator of all things," "the Maker of heaven and earth," who sent down certain wise men to the human race in former times. When the name "God" is applied to the names of these men <note>Origen refers to the practice of calling the Lord "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob," arguing these specific combinations of names hold spiritual power.</note>, it accomplishes a certain power among men. Many other things could also be said on this topic of names against those who think we should be indifferent about their use. And if—

<column-break/>

They know that the same song <note>original: "carmen" — here used in the sense of a formula or incantation.</note>, if one incants it in its proper tongue, accomplishes what the song promises; but if it is changed into any other voice, it appears sluggish, languid, and of no virtue. In this same manner, it is not the meanings of the things, but the qualities and properties of the voices that have something effective in them toward these or those ends. 

Thus also we shall respond concerning the Christians, who contend unto death lest they call **Jupiter** God, or name Him by any other tongue. For they either confess the common name, "God," indefinitely, or with this added: "the Founder of the universe," "the Maker of heaven and earth," who sent these wise men to the human race, to whose names the name of "God" being adapted performs a certain virtue among men. <meta>This page continues the argument from page 158, where Origen challenges Aristotle's theory that names are merely arbitrary conventions. <page-num>159</page-num>
<header>PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XVII.</header>

Human dialects have a specific origin, as is clear to those capable of considering the nature of <term>incantations</term> <note>original: "ἐπῳδῶν" (epōdōn) — rhythmic chants or ritual spells believed to have inherent power.</note> which are adapted to different dialects and to the various sounds of names according to each language. We have briefly discussed these matters in the preceding sections, stating that even those things which naturally possess power in a particular dialect no longer <term>have any effect</term> <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖ" (energei) — meaning the spiritual efficacy or "energy" is lost when the sound changes.</note> when they are translated into another tongue, as they did when uttered in their own native sounds. This same principle is even found to apply to human beings. For if a person has been called by a certain name in the Greek dialect since birth, we could not—by changing that name into the Egyptian or Roman dialect, or any other—make him experience or do the very things he would experience or do when called by the name first given to him. Indeed, even one who was called from the beginning in the Roman tongue, if we were to change his name into the Greek dialect, we would not be able to achieve what the incantation promises to do, as it relies on preserving the name first bestowed upon him.

<column-break/>

Human languages have an origin, as is clear to those who are able to understand the nature of <term>incantations</term> <note>original: "carminum" — literally songs or verses, but used here in the sense of ritual chants.</note> which, according to different languages and the different sounds of names, are adapted to the authors of those languages. We have briefly disputed these things in the sections above, teaching that those things which have power in one language, if they are changed into another, do not produce the same effect as they did with their own proper voice. This is also found to be the case among men: for he who from birth has been called by a certain name in the Greek tongue, never—by changing his name into the Egyptian, Roman, or any other dialect—will we bring it about that he is so affected or acts as if he were called by the first imposition of his name. Neither can we, for one who from the beginning is called by a Roman voice, if we change his name into the Greek language, do that which the incantation itself promises, since it preserves the name first imposed upon him.

<summary>Origen argues that names and languages possess an inherent, natural power rather than being mere human inventions, noting that ritual incantations and personal names lose their efficacy when translated. He uses this "linguistic realism" to explain why specific names for the Divine must be preserved in their original form.</summary>

<summary>Origen argues that the names of the Hebrew patriarchs possess inherent spiritual power that is lost when translated into their literal Greek meanings. -> # ORIGEN <-

...nor do we call Apollo the sun, nor Artemis the moon. Instead, we practice a pure piety toward the **Creator** <term>Creator; original: "δημιουργὸν" (Greek) or "conditorem" (Latin). Indeed, we have a true fear regarding the name of God and His beautiful creations, so that we do not admit any myth—even under the pretext of **allegory** <term>allegory; original: "τροπολογίας" (Greek) or "figuratæ dictionis" (Latin). <column-break/>

...nor Apollo as the sun, nor **Diana** <note>original: "Dianam"; the Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, equivalent to the Greek Artemis</note> as the moon; rather, practicing pure piety toward the Creator and celebrating His beautiful works, we do not defile divine matters even by name. We approve of Plato's speech in the *Philebus*, who refused to confess that "pleasure" is a God. *“My fear, O Protarchus, concerning the names of the gods is so great, and such is my dread.”* But we hold a righteous fear regarding the name of God and His glorious works, so that we do not admit any myth—even under the appearance of **figurative language** <gloss>referring to "tropologia" or allegorical interpretation</gloss>—to the detriment of those who are less experienced.

->ORIGEN<-

And just as he prefers a man of *one wife* over one who has married a second time for the Episcopate, and one who is *without fault* over one worthy of reproach, and the *sober* over the one who is not, and the *temperate* over the intemperate, and the *honest* and somewhat grave over the unrefined: so he wants the one who is to be primarily placed in the Episcopate to be a teacher, and powerful in convincing those who resist. Does Celsus <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and the first known critic to write a comprehensive polemic against Christianity.</note> therefore rightly reproach us, as if we say: "Let no educated person approach, no one wise, no one prudent"? How then does Celsus unreasonably accuse us by claiming we say: "Let no educated person approach, no one wise, no one prudent"? ### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XVIII.

->ORIGEN<-

Bb iij

The Word <note>original: "ὁ λόγος" (ho logos) — referring here both to the teaching and to Christ himself as the Divine Reason.</note> promises to heal those who come to it, making everyone worthy of God. It is also a lie that those who teach the divine Word wish to persuade only the foolish, the low-born, and the insensitive, or slaves, women, and children. For the Word calls these people indeed, in order to improve them; but it also calls those who are far superior to them, since Christ is the Savior of all people—and especially of believers, whether they are intelligent or more simple. And he is the propitiation <term>propitiation: a sacrifice or offering that brings reconciliation and restores a relationship with God</term> before the Father for our sins, and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world. Therefore, it is unnecessary to want to defend ourselves further against the words of Celsus <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century critic of Christianity whose work is known primarily through Origen's point-by-point rebuttal.</note>, which are as follows: "For what is otherwise bad about being educated and attending to the best reasoning, and being and appearing to be prudent? What does this hinder in regard to knowing God? Why is it not rather a help, and something through which one might better be able to reach the truth?" Indeed, to be truly educated is not—

<column-break/>

—[if they] have approached, the divine Word promises that he will care for them and will render everyone worthy of God. It is also false that they wish to lead away only the fatuous, the ignoble, those lacking sense, and slaves, women, and little boys—those who teach the divine Word. -># THE WRITINGS OF ORIGEN #<-

...regarding them as dead: these people mourn those who have been overcome by shameful lust or any other outrage as if they were lost and dead to God, just as they would mourn those who have passed away. > *who display the most shameful things in the marketplace and gather a crowd—he says that they would never come into a meeting of prudent men, nor would they dare to show off their fine doctrines among them: but where they see young boys, and a crowd of slaves, and a circle of coarse and uneducated people, there they thrust themselves in, and there they hunt for applause and glory.*

In this, Celsus does nothing else but slander and heap insults, in the manner of women at a **crossroads** <note>original Latin: "triuio"; Greek: "τριόδοις". A crossroads was a typical place for gossip and low-class arguments.</note> who [exchange insults with one another].

<column-break/>

...considering them to have become dead. These men mourn those who have been overcome by licentiousness or any absurd act as if they were lost and dead to God, grieving for them as if they were deceased. And as if they were **risen from the dead**, if they demonstrate a worthy change over a longer time than those who are being introduced for the first time, they eventually admit them. However, they do not appoint to any office or leadership in the so-called Church those who, after having already approached the **Word** <term>Word: (Greek: "Logos") Here referring to the Christian faith or the teachings of Christ.</term>, have stumbled. Regarding these people to whom Celsus likens us—those who in the marketplaces show off the most unspeakable things and gather a crowd—he says:

> *Into a gathering of sensible men they would never enter, nor would they dare to show off their "fine things" among such people. But wherever they see youngsters, and a mob of house-slaves, and a company of foolish people, there they push themselves in and make a show.*

And in this he is doing nothing other than abusing us, much like the women in the **crossroads** who make it their aim to [shout at each other].

<column-break/>

...to heap insults with reproaches is his purpose. For we, as much as we are able in strength and spirit, strive to ensure that our gathering is a gathering of prudent men, and that all our matters are, as much as possible, honorable and divine. Then we dare to bring into the midst those discourses which we hold for the community, when we have prudent listeners; but we hide all the most profound things when we see that the unrefined have come together, who rather have need of those discourses which are figuratively called **milk** <note>original Latin: "lac". ### PHILOCALIA, CHAP. XVIII.

<columns>
...by the providence of God, who willed it to change into an ethereal and divine quality? It is not as Celsus said—speaking as a mere debater—when he compared the human flesh of God to gold, silver, and stone, claiming that the former is more perishable than the latter. For according to strict logic, one incorruptible thing is not "more incorruptible" than another; nevertheless, we shall respond to this: if it is possible for <term>matter: "hyle" — the underlying substance of the universe</term>—which underlies all qualities—to change its qualities, why is it not possible for the flesh of Jesus also to have changed its qualities and become such as was necessary for one dwelling in the ether <note>original: "aither." In ancient science, ether was the "fifth element," a pure substance that made up the stars and heavens, unlike the heavy elements of Earth.</note> and the regions above it? Having no longer the characteristics of fleshly weakness, and those things which Celsus called "more defiled"? In this, he is not even acting like a philosopher. For that which is truly "defiled" is such because of moral vice. But the nature of the body is not defiled; for the nature of the body—including the power of procreation—does not possess the vice of defilement in its own nature.

<column-break/>

...by the providence of God, who willed it to pass into a heavenly and divine nature? It is not as that disputant Celsus said; comparing the human flesh of God with gold, silver, and stone, [claiming] that it is certainly more akin to corruption than these. For in truth, no incorruptible thing is more incorruptible than another incorruptible thing. Nonetheless, we shall reply to this: if matter, which is subject to all qualities, can change its qualities, why can the flesh of Jesus not also have been such—once its qualities were changed—as it ought to be when dwelling in heaven and the higher places? Having now cast aside those things which are proper to human infirmity, and which Celsus called "viler" <note>original: "improbiora." Celsus, a pagan critic, mocked the Christian idea of a physical resurrection, viewing the functions of the human body as "filthy" or unworthy of divinity.</note>? Nor is he surely acting as a philosopher in this. For that which is absolutely faulty is of such a kind because of malice; for the nature of the body is not wicked. For the body, insofar as it has the power of procreating by nature, does not possess the malice and faultiness of wickedness.

</columns>

<summary>Origen argues that Jesus's physical body was transformed into a divine, "ethereal" state after the resurrection, using the philosophical concept that matter can change its qualities. He further rebukes the critic Celsus for suggesting that the natural functions of the human body are inherently "evil" or "filthy."</summary>

First, he thinks that thunder, lightning, and rain are not the works of God, clearly acting the part of an Epicurean <note>original: "epikourizōn" — behaving like a follower of Epicurus, a philosopher who taught that the gods do not intervene in human affairs</note>. Second, he says that even if one were to grant that these are the works of God, they are no more for the nourishment of us humans than for plants, trees, herbs, and thorns. He claims this by assigning it to chance and not truly to providence, acting in an Epicurean fashion. For if these things are useful no more to us than to plants, trees, herbs, and thorns, it is clear that they either do not come from providence at all, or they come from a providence that does not care for us any more than for trees, herbs, and thorns. Both positions are inherently impious <term>asebes: lacking proper respect for the divine</term>; and to argue against such claims while standing before one who accuses us of impiety is foolish. For it is clear to everyone from what has been said who the truly impious one is. Next, he says that even if you say these things—namely plants, trees, herbs, and thorns—grow for humans, why would you say they grow for humans any more than for the wildest of the irrational animals? <column-break/>

For he opines that thunder, lightning, and rain are not the works of God, clearly speaking now as an Epicurean. Then he says, even if someone grants these are the works of God, they are no more for the nourishment of humans than for plants, trees, herbs, and thorns; confessing, as if he were a genuine follower of Epicurus, that these things happen by chance and rashly, not providently. For if these are of use no more to us humans than to plants and trees and herbs and thorns, it is manifest that these neither come from providence; or they come from that providence which provides for us no more than for trees or herbs or the bramble. But both of these views are impious; just as it is foolish to contradict these things and stand against him who objects to our impiety: for from those things which have been said, it is manifest who the impious one is. Then he adds, *“Even if you say these things grow for the sake of humans—namely plants, trees, and herbs and thorns—why will you say they grow for humans more than for the fiercest of brute animals?”* Clearly, therefore...

This Latin term carries the sense of foresight and the practical application of reason.</note></term>, has been given to us, and it is more powerful than whatever weapons the animals are seen to be equipped with. From this, it is clear that what Celsus stated is also a lie: namely, that in this regard, God subjected humans to the beasts. For God did not subject humans to the beasts, but through human intelligence He made the beasts catchable, as well as through the skills derived from intelligence used against them. For it was not without God’s help that humans devised their own safety from the beasts and achieved dominion over them. From this, it is clear that Celsus is also wrong when he spoke in such a way that God rather subjected humans to the wild beasts. For God did not subject humans to the beasts, but gave the beasts to be captured by human prudence and by the arts devised by prudence against them. # ORIGEN

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.

...to those who have been deemed worthy of reason <note>original: *logou*; referring to both human logic and the Divine Word.</note>. Cities, therefore, among men were established with many skills and the arrangement of laws; but political systems, offices, and commands among men are either those properly so called—certain virtuous habits and activities—or are named so in a more figurative sense <note>original: *katachrestikoteron*; a rhetorical term for using a word in an extended or non-literal way.</note> according to an imitation of those [ideals] as far as possible. For, looking toward those [ideal patterns], those who have systematically legislated have established the best political systems, offices, and commands. None of these are to be found among the irrational creatures, even if Celsus applies these rational names—assigned to things done with reason—such as "city," "political systems," "offices," and "commands," even to ants and bees. In these instances, one must by no means accept the comparison to the ants or the bees, for they do not act with reasoning. Instead, one should marvel at the divine nature, which has extended as far as the irrational creatures a sort of imitation of rational beings—perhaps to put rational beings to shame <note>original: *dysōpian*; literally "to make one turn away their face" out of embarrassment or a sense of duty.</note>, so that by looking at the ants, who are more industrious...

<column-break/>

...to whom He granted the gift of reason. Cities, therefore, were established by many human skills and the ordering of laws; but republics, commands, and powers among men are so named for certain honorable habits and actions, or less properly, those which are fashioned into an imitation of those others as far as possible. For by looking into those [patterns], those who brought forth laws established the best forms of the republic, the magistracies, and the powers. None of these things will you find among the [irrational] animals; even if Celsus attributes names belonging to reason—and imposed upon things done with reason—such as cities, republics, magistracies, and powers, to ants and bees. This is by no means to be accepted concerning ants and bees, for they do not act with counsel and reason. Rather, let us admire the divine nature, which has extended even to those lacking reason a certain imitation, as it were, of rational beings, and this perhaps so that men might be put to shame as they behold the ants, and become more diligent in their work...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s counter-argument against the philosopher Celsus. ### ORIGEN

...see someone struggling, they lighten their loads. A person who is not at all trained in the discipline of **reason** <note>original: *logou*; referring to the divine faculty of reason that distinguishes humans from animals</note> and does not listen to it will say: "Since we differ in no way from ants when we bring help to those who are struggling, why do we do this in vain?" Furthermore, ants—being irrational animals—are never puffed up with arrogance when their own works are compared to those of men. But men, who by virtue of their reason are able to hear how their **social nature** <note>original: *to koinonikon*; the inherent human drive toward community and mutual benefit</note> is being degraded, would be seriously harmed—as far as Celsus and his arguments are concerned. He does not see that while he wishes to turn his readers away from Christian piety, he is also discouraging them from showing compassion toward those who carry the heaviest burdens, a virtue not exclusive to Christians. It would have been proper for him, if he were indeed a philosopher who perceived the value of community, not to abolish what is useful to mankind along with Christianity. Instead, he should have, if possible, promoted those good things which the Christian way of life <note>original: *Chrestianismo*; Origen highlights that Christian ethics often align with universal human virtues</note> shares in common with other men. But if...

<column-break/>

...see someone struggling, they take hold and help. A person who stands in need of the education provided by **reason** <note>original: *logou*</note> and who in no way listens to it will say: "Since we differ in no way from ants even when we help those who are struggling, why do we perform such actions to no purpose?" And while the ants, being irrational animals, would not be lifted up toward pride when someone compares their works to those of men, men—who through reason are able to hear the way in which their **social instinct** <note>original: *to koinonikon*</note> is being diminished—would be harmed. This is the result of Celsus and his words; he does not realize that in his desire to alienate those who read his writing from Christianity, he also turns them away from the sympathy Christians show toward those bearing the heaviest of burdens. It would have been right for him, if he were truly a philosopher and sensitive to the **social bond** <note>original: *tou koinonikou*</note>, not to sweep away the useful things among men along with Christianity, but to work together, if possible, with the things that are good in Christianity and common to other men. But if...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s rebuttal of Celsus’s claims regarding animal intelligence. On the previous page, Origen discussed the social cooperation of ants, arguing that while they appear to act with human-like virtue, they are actually driven by instinct rather than the divine gift of reason. Here, he specifically addresses the complex behavior of ants storing grain and Celsus's underlying Platonic philosophical assumptions about the nature of the soul.</meta>

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.

<columns>

Ants break off the sprouts of the fruits they store away so that they do not germinate; instead, they remain as food for them throughout the year. We must not suppose that **reason** <note>original: *logismos*; the faculty of logical calculation or deliberation</note> in ants is the cause of these actions, but rather Mother Nature herself, who has ordered even the irrational creatures so that not even the smallest part is left without a trace of the **reason derived from nature** <note>original: *tou apo tes physeos logou*; the inherent order or logic found in the natural world</note>. Unless, of course, through these arguments Celsus secretly wishes to "Platonize" <note>to follow the philosophy of Plato, who suggested that souls could be reincarnated into different types of living beings depending on their conduct</note> in many respects, suggesting that every **soul** <note>original: *psyche*</note> is of the same kind, and that the soul of a human differs in no way from that of ants and bees. Such a view brings the soul down from the **vaults of heaven** <note>original: *apsidon tou ouranou*; a reference to the celestial spheres from which souls were thought to descend into the physical world</note> not only into the human body, but into the others as well. But Christians will not be persuaded by these things, having previously embraced the belief that the human soul was made **in the image of God** <note>original: *kat' eikona theou*; the core Christian belief in human dignity and uniqueness based on Genesis 1:27</note>. They see that it is impossible for a nature created in God's image to entirely lose its distinct characteristics and take on those of **irrational creatures** <note>original: *alogous*; literally "without reason" or "without speech"</note>.

<column-break/>

Ants strike off and set aside the sprouts of the fruits they have hidden away, lest they should germinate, so that they may serve them as food through the year. The cause of this must not be thought to lie in their own **reason** <note>original: *ratione*</note>, but in the parent of all, Nature, who has so adorned even the irrational animals that not even the smallest part would be left without a vestige of the reason that comes from Nature. Unless, therefore, in these matters Celsus follows Plato <note>original: *cum Platone sentit*</note> in a somewhat obscure way, and wishes every soul to be of a single form, so that the human soul differs nothing from that of ants and bees. This is the opinion of one who would lead souls down from the **celestial citadel** <note>original: *caelesti arce*</note> not only into human bodies, but into the rest as well. Christians will never assent to these views, for they have perceived that the human soul is made **in the image of God** <note>original: *ad imaginem Dei factam*</note>, and they see it to be impossible that a nature created in the image of God should utterly cast away its forms and marks to receive those of **brute animals** <note>original: *brutorum*</note>.

</columns>

He asserts the Christian doctrine of the "imago Dei," which maintains a fundamental distinction between the human soul and the rest of the animal kingdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen’s critique of the philosopher Celsus. On the previous page, Origen discussed the Christian belief that humans are uniquely made in the image of God. Here, he addresses Celsus’s counter-argument: that animals like ants exhibit such high levels of social organization and "reason" that they might be equal to humans, or even possess souls that have "fallen" from a higher state.</meta>

# OF ORIGEN

<columns>

...uncertain after whose images [souls are stripped] in the **brute animals**. Regarding his claim that living ants set aside a specific place for the dead, and that these are their ancestral monuments: it must be said that the more he pursues praises of the irrational creatures, the more—even if he does not wish to—he extols the work of the **Word** <note>original: *Verbi* (Latin) / *Logou* (Greek). In this context, Origen uses the term to mean both the Divine Reason of God and the second person of the Trinity who ordered the universe.</note> which adorned all things. He shows that human cleverness can, with reason, adorn the excellence found in the nature of brutes. But why do I call them "brute" or "devoid of reason"? Since to Celsus they do not seem to lack reason, even though they are called "irrational" by the common sense of all people. Therefore, he does not think ants are devoid of reason—he who professes to speak concerning the whole of nature and proclaims "**The Truth**" <note>A jab at the title of Celsus's book, *The True Word* or *The True Account*.</note> in the very title of his book. He even speaks of ants as if they converse among themselves: *Indeed, when they meet one another, they converse, which is why they do not stray from their paths.* Thus, the perfection of reason is in them, as are the **common notions** <term>Common notions (Greek: *koinai ennoiai*): basic, self-evident concepts that all rational beings are born with, according to Stoic philosophy.</term> of certain general things, and speech, and...

<column-break/>

...I know not according to the images of whom they have been stripped <note>Origen is likely referring to souls being "stripped" of their higher celestial form to inhabit animal bodies, a Platonic idea he is mocking.</note> in the **irrational creatures**. Since he also says that for the dying ants the living set apart a special place, and that this place is for them their ancestral tombs: it must be said that the more he speaks praises of the irrational creatures, the more—even if he is unwilling—he magnifies the work of the **Word** <note>original: *Logos*</note> that ordered all things. He shows the power existing among humans that is able to adorn with reason even the advantages found in the nature of irrational animals. But why do I say "irrational"? Since to Celsus those things called "irrational" according to the common notions of everyone do not even seem to be irrational. At any rate, he does not think that ants are irrational—he who promised to speak about the whole of nature and boasted of "**The Truth**" in the title of his book. For he says regarding ants that they converse with one another in this way: *And indeed, when meeting one another they converse, which is why they do not even miss their ways.* Therefore, there is a fulfillment of reason among them, and **common notions** of certain universal things, and speech, and...

</columns>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.

<columns>

...meanings being signified. # PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.

<columns>

...[diminishing] the greater [humanity], he says that **sorcery** <term>Sorcery (Greek: *goēteia*): In this context, it refers to the use of magic or supernatural knowledge, which Celsus attributes to animals to lower human status.</term> is also found in some irrational animals, so that humans should not pride themselves on this as something unique, nor should they claim superiority over the irrational creatures. And he says these things: *"But if humans take pride in sorcery, then in this regard snakes and eagles are already wiser; for they know many **antidotes** <note>original: *alexipharmaka* (Greek). Remedies that ward off poison or disease.</note> and protections against harm; and indeed, they know the powers of certain stones for the protection of their young; which, if humans happen to find them, they believe they possess a marvelous treasure."* 

And first, I do not know why he called the experience of animals regarding natural remedies, or a certain natural perception, “sorcery.” For the term “sorcery” is applied to something else entirely. Unless, perhaps, he secretly intends—like an **Epicurean** <note>A follower of Epicurus; here Origen implies Celsus is being skeptical of all spiritual or "hidden" powers by labeling them as mere trickery or "sorcery."</note>—to disparage the use of all such things as if they were nothing but the empty promises of sorcerers. But nevertheless, let it be granted to him that humans think highly of themselves because of this knowledge, whether they are sorcerers...

<column-break/>

...wishing to leave [the matter], he says that **incantation** is also found in some of the brutes, so that humans do not glory in it as something unique, nor should they claim any excellence over other animals. *"But if humans glory in the name of **magic tricks** <note>original: *præstigiarum* (Latin). Deceptive illusions or "prestige."</note>, certainly in this both serpents and eagles are wiser, for they know many remedies for repelling poisons and evils; moreover, they know the powers of certain stones for the health of their chicks, which if humans find them, they think they possess a most precious thing."* 

And first, I do not know for what reason he named the experience or a certain natural insight of animals regarding natural remedies "incantation." For the usage of that word is different; unless indeed, secretly, like an **Epicurean**, he wishes to condemn the use of such things, as if it belonged to the promises of **charlatans** <note>original: *præstigiatorum* (Latin). Deceivers or stage-magicians.</note>. Furthermore, let it be granted to him that humans lift up their spirits through the knowledge of these things, whether they be sorcerers...

</columns>

<meta>This page continues Origen’s rebuttal of Celsus's argument from the previous page. Having just questioned why Celsus labels animal instinct as "sorcery," Origen now moves to dismantle the idea that animals are "wiser" than humans because they possess natural remedies. He distinguishes between human "reason" and animal "nature."</meta>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS

<columns>

...whether they are [sorcerers] or not, how is it that snakes are wiser than humans in this regard, using **fennel** <note>original: *foeniculum*. Ancient naturalists believed snakes consumed fennel to restore their sight after hibernation or to help shed their skin.</note> for sharpness of sight and speed of movement? They have received this alone as an innate quality of nature, not from reason, but from the very act of creation. 

Humans, however, do not seek this kind of aid solely by the guidance of nature as snakes do, but sometimes by experience, sometimes by reason, and occasionally by calculation and science. 

In the same way, if eagles carry the found **eagle-stone** <note>original: *aëtites*. A "stone of the eagle," often a geode with a loose pebble inside. In the ancient world, it was thought to protect the nest or assist in birth.</note>, as it is commonly called, to their nests for the safety of their chicks, does it follow that eagles are wise—even wiser than humans—who have found through experience and reasoning the very aid that was imparted to eagles by nature, and have used it with intelligence? 

But so be it; let it be granted that brute animals also know other remedies. Does this prove that these brutes found these things by reason rather than by nature? For unless reason had been the discoverer, nothing would ever have been definitely found in snakes. Let it be also...

<column-break/>

...whether [they are sorcerers] or not; how is it that snakes are wiser than humans even in this, using **fennel** <note>original: *marathron*. The Greek term for fennel, mirroring the Latin *foeniculum* in the parallel column.</note> for sharpness of vision and swiftness of movement? They perceive this alone through a natural instinct, not from calculation, but from their physical constitution. 

But humans do not come to such things merely from a bare nature in the way snakes do; instead, they arrive there partly from experience, partly from reason, and sometimes from calculation and systematic knowledge. 

It is just as if eagles, for the salvation of the chicks in the nest, having found the so-called **eagle-stone**, carry it to them. How does this show that eagles are wise, and even wiser than humans, who through reasoning discovered the natural aid given to eagles by experience and used it with an understanding mind? 

But let it be that other **antidotes** <note>original: *alexipharmaka*. Protective remedies or "warding-medicines."</note> are known by animals; what then does this have to do with proving it is reason and not nature that discovers these things in animals? For if it were not reason that was the discoverer, such a thing would never have been found in snakes in a definite, assigned way. Let it be also...

</columns>

<summary>Origen argues that animal instincts, such as a snake's use of fennel or an eagle's use of the eagle-stone, are products of their created "nature" rather than the deliberate "reason" and "science" used by humans. He refutes Celsus's claim that animals are wiser than humans by showing that human knowledge is intellectual and learned, while animal knowledge is merely biological.</summary>

<columns>

# ORIGEN

...to show that they [the birds] have knowledge, whenever—having foretold what the birds said, that they are going somewhere and will do this or that—they show them going there and doing what they had predicted. From these points, see how many questions of the philosophers—not only of the Greeks but also of the <term>Barbarians</term> <note>original: *barbarorum* / *βαρβάροις*. He discusses whether these animals discovered these things themselves or learned from <term>daimons</term> <note>original: *daemonibus* / *δαιμόνων*. To a 2nd-century writer like Celsus, *daimons* were not necessarily evil "demons" but intermediary spirits or divine beings that could communicate hidden knowledge.</note> the dispositions of birds and other animals from which prophecies are said to come to men; he turns these to his own use. For first, it is asked whether there is even such a thing as an art of <term>augury</term> <note>original: *augurandi* / *οἰωνιστικὴ*. <column-break/>

...to show that they know, whenever, having foretold what the birds said—that they are going somewhere and will do this or that—they show them going there and doing what they had foretold. The Greek text implies a knowledge of the Divine specifically.</note>. # PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.

...into different flights and different voices, and to the rest into these or those movements. Others say that their souls are more divine and suited for this purpose—which is highly improbable. Therefore, Celsus, wishing by the matters before us to prove that <term>irrational animals</term> <note>A philosophical term for animals that do not possess human reason (logos).</note> are more divine and wiser than humans, ought to have established through more evidence that such <term>divination</term> <note>original Greek: μαντικήν (mantikēn); the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note> exists among them. For in that way, we would have opposed his plausible claims with a philosophical disposition concerning such great matters to the best of our ability—overturning his claim that irrational animals are wiser than humans, and proving false his assertion that they even have holy concepts of the divine...

...into different flights and different chatterings, and for the rest into these and those movements. It was necessary, therefore, for Celsus—who from the matters proposed wished to show that irrational animals are more divine and wiser than humans—to show and prove through more evidence such divination; then afterwards more strongly and with demonstration, to reject the sayings of those who take away such prophecies. He should have also overturned with firm arguments the discourses of those who said that such movements for divining are excited in animals by gods or demons. Then, finally, he should have proved that the soul of brutes is more divine than the human soul. For thus, against the disputation of one who acts as a philosopher in such matters, we have proceeded as far as we were able; and we have subverted that claim that brutes are wiser than humans, as well as the claim that they have thoughts about God...

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.

For Celsus, being a man, though he "was in honor, did not understand" <note>original Greek: ἐν τιμῇ ὢν, οὐ συνῆκε; Origen is quoting Psalm 49:20 (LXX 48:21), which says man in his pride is like the beasts that perish.</note>; therefore, he has not even been compared to the cattle and the irrational animals to which he believes the power of <term>divination</term> <note>original Greek: mantikē; the art of foretelling the future.</note> belongs. Instead, by yielding the first place to them—even beyond the Egyptians who worship irrational animals as gods—he has subjected himself and, as far as he is able, the entire human race, as if humans had an inferior and lesser understanding of the divine than the irrational beasts. First, therefore, let us investigate whether there truly exists in birds and the other animals believed to possess it, a power of divination, or not.

<column-break/>

...would free men from their errors concerning God, by sharing with them that clear insight which they themselves have perceived. For he who is a man, and is Celsus, "when he was in honor, did not understand; therefore he has not even been compared to the beasts of burden" <note>original Latin: cùm in honore esset, non intellexit, ideo neque comparatus est iumentis; a Latin rendering of the same Psalm reference used in the Greek column.</note> and other various animals to which he attributes the power of prophesying. First, therefore, let it be asked whether, through birds and the other animals which are said to prophesy, there is a science of <term>augury</term> <note>original Latin: augurandi; the Roman practice of divining the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note> or not.

For the argument being pursued on either side is not to be despised, as it at one time fears to admit such a thing, lest a human being—having abandoned these [divine ways]—should use birds instead of the oracles of spirits <note>original Latin: dæmoniorum; in this context, it refers to the intermediary spirits or "daimons" that pagans believed delivered oracles, which Origen considers lesser or deceptive entities.</note>. -> ### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX. <-

...the will of the one called in our discourses the **prince of this age** <note>original: *archontos tou aiōnos toutou*. A title for the Devil or a ruling demonic power in early Christian thought.</note>; while others manifest it through another species. And see how defiled the demons are, in that they are even used by some in the form of cats <note>original Greek: *galais*. This can refer to weasels, polecats, or domestic cats, all of which were sometimes used in folk divination.</note> to reveal things to come. You should judge for yourself which is better to accept: that the God over all and His Son move the birds and the rest of the animals toward divination <note>original: *mantikēn*</note>, or that those who move such animals—and not to humans, but in the presence of humans—are wicked demons, and as our sacred scriptures have named them, **impure**. If the soul of birds were indeed divine because the future is predicted through them, why should we not rather say that the soul of those humans through whom omens <note>original: *klēdones*. These are "vocal omens"—random words spoken by others that the listener interprets as a prophetic sign.</note> are heard is divine? For then that mill-woman in Homer <note>Referring to *Odyssey* 20.115-119, where a servant grinding grain prays for the suitors' end; Odysseus takes her words as a lucky omen.</note> would be some divine being for speaking these words concerning the suitors:
> *May they now for the very last and final time dine here.*

<column-break/>

...the will of him who in our oracles is called the **prince of this world**, while others signify it through another species. Furthermore, observe the fraud and malice of the demons, some of whom use cats to foreknow the future; and weigh within yourself whether it is better to confess that the God and Lord of all things and His Son move the birds and the remaining living creatures for the purpose of augury <note>original Latin: *augurandum*. The Roman practice of interpreting the will of the gods from the flight of birds.</note>, rather than those [demons] who move these animals and not humans. Truly, in the presence of humans, these are evil demons and, as our sacred writings call them, **impure**. But if the soul of birds is divine because future things are predicted through them, why shouldn't we rather say that the souls of those from whom omens are heard are divine, since omens are taken from humans? Therefore, that woman grinding grain in Homer is divine, who made this omen against the suitors:
> *Let them take this meal for their last, and these their last drinks.*

...[they] have knowledge of God. For I know of many wonderful things recorded about the nature and **tameness** of this animal; however, I have never read anyone who wrote about the **oaths** of elephants, unless perhaps he chose to call their tameness and a kind of **covenant** with humans—once they have come into their power—a "keeping of faith." This claim itself is false; for though it happens rarely, I have read in history that after elephants appeared to be tamed, they turned savage against humans and crushed them. For this reason, the use of elephants was condemned and abolished as being harmful. And because Celsus later brings up the stories told about the **stork**—specifically how they return the favor of nourishment to their parents—in order to prove his opinion that storks are more **pious** <note>original Latin: "pietas"; Greek: "eusebeia". ...have knowledge of God. Rather, this is the speech of a man who desires to corrupt and **adulterate** the notion of **free will**. If we should interrogate him as to what freedom of choice is, he would respond: it is that which impels me in the opposite direction, provided that nothing from without should occur while I am proposing and deciding upon something. Furthermore, he who transfers the blame for his actions to the weak constitution of the body resists clear reason. For reason, when instructing and commanding, takes hold of even the most **lustful** <term>lustful<note>original Latin: *libidinosiores*. Those heavily inclined toward physical desires and passions.</note></term> and the most **uncivilized** <term>uncivilized<note>original Latin: *agrestissimos*. Literally "men of the fields," referring to those who are unrefined or wild.</note></term>. If they obey the warnings, they are so transformed that a conversion and a change for the better frequently occurs. Often, from the most **unrestrained** <term>unrestrained<note>original Latin: *incontinentissimis*. Those who cannot contain their urges or exercise self-mastery.</note></term>, better men emerge—even those who previously did not seem to be such by nature. Those who were of the harshest character become so **tame** <term>tame<note>original Latin: *mansuefiant*. To become gentle, like a wild animal that has been domesticated.</note></term> that those who were never so hard or harsh seem fierce and cruel in comparison to the one who was converted to mildness, while the latter appears most calm and grave...

<summary>Origen argues that human free will is not merely the absence of external pressure, but the internal capacity to choose. He points to the radical moral transformation of "wild" or "licentious" people through reason as proof that our nature can be overcome by our choices.</summary>

<summary>Origen argues that humans are morally responsible for their actions because reason allows them to choose how to respond to external circumstances. ## XX ORIGENIS

...thorns in the earth. It is harsh, yet true: for if the rain had been missing, neither the crops nor the thorns would have come forth; but when it had flowed down seasonably and in moderation, both the crops and the thorns sprang up. Therefore, that land which, after it has often drunk the rain sent down into it, brings forth thorns and thistles, is rejected and near to a curse <note>A reference to Hebrews 6:8.</note>. Was it not, then, that the benefit of the rain also fell upon the inferior land? But its soil, being neglected and uncultivated, produced thorns and thistles. In that same manner, the wonders which God performed are a kind of rain; but the differing wills are like cultivated and uncultivated land, which are of one nature. It is as if the Sun sent forth a voice and said: "I liquefy and I dry," which are opposites. He would say nothing false regarding the subject matter, since by one and the same heat, wax is liquefied, and mud is dried <note>original Latin: "exsiccatur" — the transcription ends with "ex-", but the Greek context completes the word.</note>.

<column-break/>

...thorns in the earth; but even if it sounds ill-omened <note>original Greek: "δύσφημον" (dysphemon) — meaning scandalous or sounding like a bad omen.</note>, it is nevertheless true. From the one heat, wax is melted while mud is dried.

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XX.

...[these things have been] revealed to babes, to those who, after their infancy, have progressed to better things and who remember that they reached such a great height of blessedness <note>original: μακαριότητος (makariotētos) — a state of supreme happiness or divine favor</note> not so much by their own effort as by God’s unspeakable beneficence. By a purposeful design, the one who is abandoned is left to divine judgment, and God is patient toward some of those who sin—not without reason, but because it will eventually benefit them. With a view toward the immortality of the soul and the infinite age, it is sometimes better not to be quickly helped toward salvation, but to be led to it more slowly after having experienced many evils. For just as physicians, even when they are able to heal a patient quickly, will—whenever they suspect a hidden poison <note>original: ἰὸν (ion) — poison or venom; here used metaphorically for deep-seated sin</note> exists within the body—do the opposite of healing. They do this because they truly *desire* to heal, and they make the process more certain by doing so. They consider it much better to keep someone for a long time in a state of inflammation and sickness so that they might regain their health more firmly, than to have them recover more quickly...
