<meta>This page continues Origen's explanation of the Parable of the Sower, specifically addressing why God allows some seeds (divine words) to fall on "rocky soil" (hardened souls). He argues that a quick, superficial conversion can be harmful, and that God's providence manages every soul's development over vast periods of time.</meta>

# OF ORIGEN

...is momentary. Why indeed does a portion of the seeds fall on that shallow and outermost soil—a soul clearly resembling a rock? The answer is that it is better for this soul, which is carried too impulsively toward the good but does not proceed there by way of method and reason, to obtain what it desires <note>Origen suggests that sometimes God lets us succeed in a superficial way so we can realize our own emptiness and eventually seek a deeper, more lasting growth.</note>. This is so that, by condemning itself in that very act, it may thereafter wait more patiently and justly for that cultivation which comes from nature. For our souls are, so to speak, immense to us, and their characters are infinite, with countless movements, plans, desires, and impulses. Of these, there is one best steward <note>original: *dispensator* — a manager or provider who distributes resources where they are needed.</note>, God and the Father of all, who knows the seasons, the appropriate aids, the directions, and the paths. He knows how to lead Pharaoh through so many wonders and even through the drowning where Pharaoh’s administration <note>original: *administratio* — referring to the divine management of Pharaoh's life and role in history.</note> ends. For he did not perish simply because he was drowned; "for in the hand of God are both we and our words, and all practical wisdom and knowledge of works." <note>This quote is from the Wisdom of Solomon 7:16, used here to argue that God's care extends even to those who appear to be destroyed.</note> And these things...

<column-break/>

...to endure. Why then does the portion of the seeds fall upon the ground that is superficial—a soul being as if it were a rock? It must be said in response to this that it is better for such a person, who has too hastily desired the better things and has not traveled toward them by the proper road, to obtain what she desired. This is so that, having found fault with herself for this, she might later wait a long time to receive the natural cultivation. For our souls are, as one might say, infinite, and their dispositions are infinite, and their movements, purposes, applications, and impulses are very many. Of these, there is only one best steward <note>original: οἰκονόμος (*oikonomos*) — one who manages a household or a complex system; the root of our word "economy."</note>, who understands the seasons and the fitting helps, and the directions and the paths: the God and Father of all. He is the one who knows how even to lead Pharaoh through such great trials and the drowning, at which the dispensation <note>original: οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*) — the divine plan or arrangement of events.</note> of Pharaoh concludes. For he was not destroyed because he was drowned; "for in the hand of God are both we and our words, and all prudence and knowledge of crafts." And these things I have said moderately <note>original: μετρίως (*metrios*) — Origen uses this to indicate he has given a sufficient, though perhaps not exhaustive, explanation.</note>.

<summary>Origen explains that God, as the supreme Divine Steward, manages the slow progress of hardened souls, allowing even figures like Pharaoh to undergo "drowning" as part of a longer educational process rather than simple destruction. He argues that spiritual growth must be deep and methodical rather than impulsive and superficial.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen's deep dive into the problem of free will versus divine intervention. Having just discussed why God might allow a soul to fail temporarily for its own long-term benefit, Origen now pivots to address specific "difficult" Bible verses that seem to suggest God controls human morality directly, specifically the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart and the promise in Ezekiel to replace stony hearts with hearts of flesh.</meta>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XX. 289

...moderately as a defense <note>original: *apologia* — Origen is offering a "defense" of God's justice against those who argue that these scriptures prove humans have no free will.</note> regarding the hardening of Pharaoh's heart; and regarding the passage, "He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens." <note>A famous and controversial quote from the Apostle Paul in Romans 9:18.</note> And let us also look at the word from Ezekiel saying: "I will take away their stony hearts, and I will put in hearts of flesh, so that they may walk in my justifications and keep my ordinances." <note>Referencing Ezekiel 11:19. A "stony heart" represents someone stubborn or dead to spiritual truths, while a "heart of flesh" is living and responsive.</note> For if, whenever God wills, He removes the stony hearts and replaces them with hearts of flesh, so that His ordinances are kept and His commandments observed, then the putting away of wickedness is not "up to us." <note>Origen is highlighting the logical problem: if God is the one who changes our hearts, then we are not responsible for being either good or evil.</note> For the removal of stony hearts is nothing else than the removal of the wickedness by which a person is hardened, from whomever God wills; and the implantation of a heart of flesh, so that a person may walk in the ordinances of God and keep His commandments—what else is it but to become obedient and not resistant to the truth, and a practitioner of virtues? But if God promises to do these things, and before He removes their stony...

<column-break/>

...these things have been moderately said, so that the scripture may be defended: *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*; and that saying: *He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens*. <margin>Ezekiel 11</margin> But let us also see this from Ezekiel: *I will take away their stony hearts, and I will send in hearts of flesh, so that they may walk in my decrees and keep my mandates*. For if, when God wills, He takes away stony hearts and sends in hearts of flesh so that His mandates and edicts are kept, it is not within us to cast away malice <note>original: *malitiam* — meaning spiritual or moral wickedness.</note>. For the taking away of stony hearts is nothing other than the removal of malice—through which one is hardened—from whom God wills. And the sending in of a heart of flesh, so that one walks in the mandates of God and guards His mandates—what else is it, but to yield and not resist the truth, but to pursue virtues? But if God promises that He will do these things, and does not do so until He himself takes away the hearts...

<meta>This page continues Origen's argument against a deterministic reading of Scripture. He is specifically addressing the passage in Ezekiel where God promises to replace a "stony heart" with a "heart of flesh." If God does all the work, the skeptic argues, then human free will is an illusion. Origen begins his rebuttal here by using the analogy of a student and a teacher.</meta>

# OF ORIGEN

-> 190 <-

...stony [hearts], and we do not put them away ourselves, it is clearly apparent that it is not "up to us" <note>original: *eph' hēmin* — This is a technical term in Greek philosophy referring to things within our own power or free will.</note> to put away wickedness. And if we do nothing so that a heart of flesh may be within us, but it is instead God's work, then it will not be our own work if we live according to the rule of virtue, but plainly a divine benefit. Such is the argument of one who, by taking these words in their barest sense, would take away our liberty and our powers. But we respond that these things are to be understood by us in this way: it is as if someone who is ignorant and unlearned, being conscious of his own defects, either by the encouragement of a teacher or being moved by some other means, gives himself up of his own accord to someone he believes can lead him by the hand <note>original: *manuductu-rum* / *χειραγωγήσειν* — Literally "to lead by the hand," suggesting a gentle guidance rather than forced control.</note> toward instruction and virtue. When the student gives himself up, the teacher promises that he will remove the student's ignorance and instill learning—not because the person who committed himself to be cared for contributes nothing toward his own education or toward fleeing ignorance, but because the teacher promises to provide the cure to one who is willing. In this same way, the divine Word <note>The *Logos*, or the personified Wisdom of God.</note> promises to those who have come to Him...

<column-break/>

...hearts, and we do not put them away ourselves, it is clear that it is not "up to us" to put away wickedness. And if we do not do anything so that the heart of flesh may be born in us, but it is God's work, it will not be our work to live according to virtue, but rather divine grace. These things will be said by someone who, following the bare words, does away with what is "up to us." But we shall respond, saying that these things should be understood in this way: that just as someone who happens to be in a state of ignorance and lack of education, perceiving his own evils, either from the encouragement of teachers or even otherwise of his own accord, gives himself over to one whom he thinks can lead him by the hand toward education and virtue; and when he gives himself over, the teacher promises to take away the lack of education and to instill education. This is not as if the one presenting himself to be healed contributes nothing toward being educated and fleeing lack of education, but as promising to improve the one who *wills* it. In the same way, the divine Word promises to those who approach Him...

<summary>Origen argues that although God "replaces" our stony hearts with hearts of flesh, this divine intervention requires the individual's willing consent, much like a student must choose to submit to a teacher's instruction.</summary>

...some people turn, so that they might be worthy of the forgiveness of sins, but it is not within their power to hear the clearer teachings; rather, it lies with the teacher. If this is so, we are not free <note>original Latin: *liberum* — "free," referring to the capacity for choice.</note> to be saved or to perish. And indeed, if the phrase, *Lest they should ever turn back and be forgiven*, had not been added, a likely and probable defense could be made: that the Savior did not wish those who would not be good and holy to understand the more hidden things, and for this reason He spoke to them in parables. But since the addition is made, *Lest they should ever turn back and be forgiven*, the defense of this passage is more difficult. First, then, we must note this passage against the heretics, who are accustomed to hunt for certain sayings from the Old Testament, from which—as they dare to say—a certain cruelty of the Creator <note>original Latin: *opificis* — literally "the maker," a common term for the God of the Old Testament in these debates.</note> appears in his plan of vengeance and punishment, or whatever other...

...certain people turn, so that they become worthy of the forgiveness of sins, but it is not in their power to hear the clearer words, but in the power of the teacher. But if this is the case, we do not possess free will <term>autexousioi<gloss>The Greek term for self-determination or the inherent power to choose one's own moral path.</gloss></term> over salvation and destruction. Now, a persuasive apology <note>In this context, a formal legal or logical defense.</note> regarding these things would be possible if there were not added the words: *Lest they should ever turn back and be forgiven*. One could argue that the Savior did not wish those who were not going to be noble and good to understand the more mystical things, and for this reason He spoke to them in parables. But as it stands, with the phrase *Lest they should ever turn back and be forgiven* being present, the defense is more difficult. # ORIGEN

...[similarity], we shall lead them to this point, so that they may believe both testaments belong to one and the same God. But let us bring forward the clearest possible explanation of the proposed question. We were saying, when discussing the case of Pharaoh <note>Origen refers to his famous treatment of Exodus 9:12, where God hardens Pharaoh's heart; Origen argues this was for Pharaoh's ultimate benefit</note>, that it is not always good for the sick to be cured immediately, especially if, as soon as they fall into a difficult disease, they are very easily relieved of it; for, despising the evil as if it were easy to cure, and taking no care lest they relapse into it, they will lie in it for a longer time. Therefore, for such sick persons, the eternal God and Knower of hidden things, who knows all things before they exist, in His goodness delays the swifter cure; and, so to speak, he heals them while not healing them. It was necessary, therefore, that those "outsiders" of whom we speak, whom (as was stated) the Savior saw would not be stable in their conversion if they heard His words more clearly, should be so treated by the Lord, lest they should openly understand the deeper things,

<column-break/>

...[similarities], toward considering all things to be the writings of the one God. Come then, let us also make a defense concerning the matter at hand as far as possible. We said, while examining the case of Pharaoh, that sometimes it is not for the benefit of those being healed to be healed too quickly. For if, having fallen into difficult circumstances, they were easily delivered from those things into which they had fallen—despising the evil as easy to heal and not taking care against falling into it a second time—they would remain in it. Therefore, in the case of such people, the eternal God, the Knower of secrets, who knows all things before their birth, according to His kindness <note>original Greek: *chrestoteta*; this implies a benevolent utility rather than just abstract "niceness"</note> delays the faster help for them; and, so to speak, by helping them He does not help them, as this is more profitable for them. It is likely, therefore, that the "outsiders" of whom we speak, who were seen by the Savior—according to the matter at hand—as not likely to be stable in their conversion if they heard the things spoken more clearly, were dispensed <note>original Greek: *oikonomeisthai*; this term refers to the "divine economy" or the way God manages human history and salvation like a household manager</note> by the Lord not to hear the deeper things more plainly.

Instead, He makes those who have cleansed themselves into vessels of honor, and those who have neglected themselves and remained unpurified into vessels of dishonor. Thus, it is not because of "older" <note>meaning prior or pre-existing</note> causes in the very construction of the vessels that one is made for honor and another for dishonor.

But if we were to admit for a moment that there are certain causes older than the creation of the vessel of honor and the vessel of dishonor, what would be so absurd about extending this inquiry to the topic of the **soul**? We might say that older causes for **Jacob** being loved and **Esau** being hated <note>A reference to Romans 9:13: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." ...for honor; but he who truly neglects his own impurity becomes a vessel for ignominy. For He makes vessels of honor and vessels of ignominy, but not from the start or origin through **foreknowledge** <note>original Latin: "praenotionem"</note>, because He does not pre-judge either side by that knowledge alone. Rather, He makes those who have purged themselves into honorable vessels; conversely, He leaves those who remain impure and unclean as vessels of ignominy. Thus, it is not from the primary causes of creation into vessels of honor and ignominy that one becomes for honor and another for ignominy.

<summary>Origen argues that spiritual status is fluid rather than fixed, asserting that even "outsiders" like Egyptians can become Israelites through faith, while "insiders" can fall through sin. He uses 2 Timothy 2:21 to prove that individuals have the power to "cleanse themselves" to become vessels of honor, placing the responsibility for salvation on human free will.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the argument from the previous page regarding 2 Timothy 2:21 and Romans 9:21. Origen is harmonizing two seemingly contradictory Pauline passages: one that suggests humans must "cleanse themselves" to become vessels of honor, and another that suggests God, like a potter, has total authority to create vessels of honor or dishonor as He pleases.</meta>

->### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XX.<-

...prepared. However, elsewhere he does not even pretend to mention what lies within our power, but appears to attribute everything to God, saying: *Does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?* <note>Original Greek: *skeuos eis timen, ho de eis atimian*. This famous "Potter and Clay" metaphor from Romans 9:21 is often used to argue for predestination, which Origen seeks to qualify here.</note> These statements are not contradictory. We must bring both together and produce one complete, harmonious explanation from them: our own agency does not act without the <term>knowledge of God <note>Greek: *episteme*; Latin: *scientia*. In this theological context, Origen refers to God’s foreknowledge—His ability to see how a person will use their free will before they are even born.</note></term>, nor does God’s knowledge compel us to progress unless we also contribute something toward the good. Our agency, without God’s knowledge and the [proper] use of our inherent worth, does not result in one becoming a vessel for honor or dishonor; nor does God alone fashion someone for honor or dishonor unless He has the "raw material" of our own <term>choice <note>Greek: *proairesis*. A technical term for the moral purpose or the faculty of will that makes a deliberate choice between good and evil.</note></term>—inclining toward the worse or the better—as a basis for the distinction. Let this suffice as our defense of <term>free will <note>Greek: *autexousion*; Latin: *libertas arbitrii*. Literally "self-authority," the core concept Origen is defending against the "nature-based" determinism of Gnostic thinkers.</note></term>.

<column-break/>

...prepared. At times, he does not grant it to us, but seems to ascribe the whole to God when he says, *The potter is able from the same clay to make one vessel for honor, another for dishonor.* Nor are these things at odds with one another; both are to be reconciled, and from them a single, perfect reasoning and conclusion is to be formed. Neither our liberty without the knowledge of God, nor the knowledge of God, forces us to advance, unless we ourselves contribute something to the good. For neither does our liberty, without God's knowledge and the abuse of the dignity of our own choice, cause someone to be for honor or for ignominy; nor does the will of God alone make anyone for honor or ignominy, unless it has our own will as a certain material of difference, which leans toward the worse or the better. And let these things have been sufficiently discussed by us concerning the **freedom of choice**.

<summary>Origen reconciles the paradox of human free will and divine sovereignty by arguing that God's "potter-like" shaping of souls is based on the "raw material" of an individual's own moral choices. He concludes that neither human effort nor divine will acts in isolation to determine a person's spiritual destiny.</summary>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAP. XXI. 317

...the creator of all things. And according to him [Celsus], **holiness** will not exist by nature, but by some decree and law. For instance, among some it is holy not to worship a **crocodile** <note>original: κροκόδειλον. In this way, the same person will be performing holy acts according to one set of laws, but unholy acts according to others—which is the most absurd thing of all. But it is likely they will say in response to this: that the one who guards his **ancestral customs** is holy and in no way unholy, since he does not even observe the laws of others. Again, they might say that a man thought to be unholy is not actually unholy among certain people, so long as he worships his own [gods] according to ancestral tradition, while he makes war against and **consumes** <note>original: καταθοινᾶται. <column-break/>

...the maker of the universe, they forbid to worship. And it will be, according to his own opinion, not by nature but by a certain imposition and judgment. Thus, someone will conduct himself justly and piously according to those laws, but impiously according to others: which certainly is the most absurd of all. But perhaps they might say to this: he is pious who preserves **ancestral rites**, nor is he in any way impious because he does not preserve foreign ones. Then, he who is considered impious is not impious among these people, since he protects ancestral institutions and opposes and fights against contrary laws. But see how much these things bring confusion into the reasoning of the holy, the just, and of **piety**: for if these things are not distinguished, and do not have their own nature which designates with a mark of piety those who [act] according to its norm...

# THE WORKS OF ORIGEN

...they live. If therefore both **piety** and **holiness** and **justice** are of that kind which are relative <note>original: *quæ ad aliud referuntur*. In logic, a "relative" thing is something that has no fixed identity but changes based on what it is compared to.</note>, so that the same thing is pious and impious according to different perspectives, habits, and laws; from that it certainly follows, as you see, that **temperance** <note>original: *temperantiam*. Celsus’s reasoning seems to lead to and conclude all these points: that all men should protect their **ancestral institutions** <note>original: *patria instituta*. The traditional laws and religious rituals handed down by one's forefathers.</note> and cannot be blamed for doing so. He argues that Christians, however, who have abandoned their ancestral rites and are not a single nation (like the Jews), cannot embrace the teaching of Jesus without fault. 

But I ask this of Celsus: when those who study **philosophy** and are commanded to abhor **superstition** <note>original: *superstitione*. <column-break/>

Nothing could be more absurd than this. 

Through these points, Celsus’s argument seems to travel toward the conclusion that all men must live according to their **ancestral ways**, and should not be blamed for it. He suggests that Christians, having left their ancestral ways and not being a single nation like the Jews, are to be accused for having joined the teaching of Jesus. 

Let him tell us then: when those who practice philosophy and are taught not to be **superstitious** <note>original: δεισιδαιμονεῖν. This Greek term can mean "fearing the spirits/demons." # PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXI

...ancestral customs, and should eat things that had been forbidden to them by their fathers, why should not Christians also—since reason <note>original: *logos*. Here referring to both the Divine Word and the power of rational argument.</note> chooses not to linger around images and statues, or even around the works of God’s creation, but rather to transcend them and present the soul to the Creator—be free from blame when they do the same as those who study philosophy? 

But if Celsus, or those who agree with him, says (in order to defend his proposed thesis) that even a philosopher might maintain his ancestral customs, let them consider how ridiculous those philosophers are, for instance, among the Egyptians, who take care not to eat onions <note>original: *krommyou*. Onions were sacred to some Egyptian deities and forbidden to certain initiates.</note> so that they may preserve their ancestral traditions, or refrain from eating certain parts of the body, such as the head or the shoulder, so that they do not transgress the things handed down to them by their fathers. 

In the same way, then, the person who has been led by reason to worship the God of all things, yet remains stuck below with the statues and human-made shrines because of ancestral customs, and is unwilling to ascend...

<column-break/>

...they preserved [their traditions] and ate things forbidden by their ancestors, why should not Christians also, since the divine word <note>original: *diuinus sermo*. The Latin translator's equivalent for Origen's Greek *logos*.</note> forbids them to be affected by images and statues, or by the works of God, or to cling to them, but rather to ascend higher and give their mind to the Craftsman <note>original: *opifici*. The Creator or Architect of the universe.</note>? 

Those who do nothing different from the philosophers should surely be free from blame. But if Celsus and those who feel as he does, in order to cling to their purpose, should respond that there would be some philosopher who nonetheless preserves ancestral customs: let them remember how ridiculous the philosophers among the Egyptians are thought to be, who out of reverence for ancestral rites abstain from onions, or from certain parts of the body of animals, such as the head and shoulder, so that they do not violate the religion handed down to them from their fathers. 

Thus, he who has been led by the divine word to the worship of God, the builder of all things, and yet lingers among the statues and human-made shrines because of ancestral ritual, and [does] not [ascend] to the Creator in mind...

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXII.

It is necessary to distinguish <note>The Greek *dialabein* (διαλαβεῖν) suggests a careful analytical distinction or discussion.</note>: not only how many nations, being strangers to the faith of Christ, go astray concerning the subject of fate <note>original: *heimarmene* (εἱμαρμένη)</note> because of the entanglement of the "wandering stars" <note>the planets</note> with those in the Zodiac, believing that everything on earth happens to them and to each individual human—and perhaps even to irrational animals—but also how many of those who are thought to have believed are being dragged away [to wonder] whether human affairs are perhaps forced by necessity. They wonder if it is impossible for things to happen otherwise than how the stars, according to their various configurations, bring them to pass. It follows for those who hold these dogmas that, in sum, what is in our power <term>what is in our power / to eph’ hēmin (τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν): a technical term for human agency or free will.</term> is destroyed. Consequently, so are praise and blame, and actions that are acceptable or, conversely, those that are blameworthy. If this is the case, the proclaimed judgment of God disappears, as do the threats against those who have sinned, as if they were to be punished, and the honors and blessings for those who have devoted themselves to better things. For none of these things would be happening for a rational cause. And if one examines the consequences...

<column-break/>

...it must be debated, not only because many nations alien to the faith of Christ have thought, regarding this subject of fate, that from the conjunction of wandering stars with the signs of the Zodiac, all things happen on earth and to individual humans—and perhaps also to brute animals; but also because by this error many of those who are held to be faithful are distracted and doubt whether human affairs are contracted into the narrows of necessity. They worry that things cannot happen otherwise than the diverse positions and figures of the stars perform. By these [ideas], it is necessary that freedom of choice, praise and blame, and upright and wicked actions are fundamentally removed. Thus, that terrible judgment of God, celebrated in preaching, the threats of punishment aimed at the wicked, and the rewards of eternal blessedness promised to the good, all vanish. For which of these things could finally be done justly? And these men, if any of their own...

<meta>The Latin text here ends mid-sentence ("si quid ex illâ suâ do-"), corresponding to the Greek ending. The catchword at the bottom "Tt ij" is a printer's signature for the leaf.</meta>

He notes that even some Christians were being tempted by these pagan ideas of "fate" determined by the stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen’s polemic against fatalism. In the preceding text, he argued that if the stars control human destiny, then human agency (to eph’ hēmin) is destroyed. # ORIGEN

...one would see the consequences of this doctrine: that faith is vain, the coming of Christ is useless, the administration of the Law and the Prophets is superfluous, and the labors of the Apostles in establishing the Churches of God through Christ were empty and void. Why would those who dare such things not also say that Christ was born under that same necessity of the motion of the stars, and that He did and suffered all things—as if it were not God, the Father of Him and of all things, who had given Him those wonderful and stupendous powers, but rather the stars? From this wicked and impious recklessness of words, it also follows that the faithful believe only by the force and influence of the stars. But I ask of them: for what purpose did God make such a world? Was it so that those men who inhabit it should suffer womanly things <note>This refers to the ancient Roman and Greek legal and social categories of "passive" sexual roles, which Origen argues would be a matter of cosmic cruelty if forced by fate rather than chosen by vice.</note>, yet fall into such disgrace and obscenity through no fault of their own? Or that others, changed into the habits and manners of wild beasts, should be made so by the motion and revolution of the universe as instituted by God...

<column-break/>

...one would see for himself the nature of what he dogmatizes: whether faith shall be in vain, and the advent of Christ achieve nothing, and the whole economy <term>economy / *oikonomia* (οἰκονομία): in this context, the "divine plan" or the way God manages human history.</term> of the Law and the Prophets, and the labor of the Apostles for the sake of establishing the churches of God through Christ. Unless perhaps, according to those who are so daring, Christ also, having come into being and taken on our natures, was under the necessity of the motion of the stars, and did and suffered all things—not because God and the Father of all granted him miraculous powers, but because the stars did. It follows from these godless and impious arguments that those who believe are said to believe in God because they are led by the stars. We would ask them: what was God's purpose in making such a world? Was it so that some who are men in it should suffer the things of women, being in no way themselves the cause of their own debauchery? Or that others, having taken on the state of wild beasts, should be made so by the revolution of the whole, because God had thus...

<summary>Origen argues that God’s foreknowledge of an event, such as Judas's betrayal, does not cause the event to happen, just as a book describing a crime is not the cause of the crime itself. He emphasizes that human actions proceed from individual malice or choice, even if they are known in advance by divine providence.</summary>

...that it is impossible for **what is in our power** <term>what is in our power: the Greek term "to eph' hēmin" refers to human moral agency or free will</term> to be preserved. To these people it must be said: that when God applied Himself to the beginning of the creation of the world <note>original: "κοσμοποιΐας"</note>—since nothing happens without a cause—He traversed with His mind each of the things that were to be, seeing them. He saw that because this thing has happened, this other thing follows; if this follows, then that occurs next. And once this is established, that will be the result; and so, having traversed through to the end of all matters, He knows what will be. Yet He is not at all the cause <term>cause: "aitios," meaning the responsible agent or source</term> of each event simply because He knows it will happen. For it is just as if someone saw a person who was headstrong through ignorance, and because of that rashness was walking mindlessly; if that observer saw the person taking a slippery road, he would realize that the person will fall and slip. However, the observer does not become the cause of the slip for that man. In this way, we must understand that God has foreseen what each person will be like, and He clearly perceives the causes for why each person will be such. He knows that if a man does this, he will sin, and if he performs that, he will act rightly. And if we must speak truly, foreknowledge <term>foreknowledge: "prognōsis," the act of knowing something before it happens</term> is not the cause of the things that happen; for God does not lay hold of the one He foreknows will sin [to force the sin].

<column-break/>

...destroys the **freedom of the will**. To these people it should be answered in this way: From the beginning of the creation of the world, since nothing happens without a cause, God proceeds through individual things with His mind and foresees all future things. He sees that if this happens, that will follow; if this which follows occurs, that also succeeds it; and when that has been, this next follows. And thus, having proceeded to the very end of things, He knows what the future will be. Yet He is not the cause of any thing, as to why it so happens. For just as if someone, seeing a person who is rash due to ignorance, and because of that rashness walking incautiously, should see him enter a slippery path, he knows he will fall miserably—yet the observer is in no way the cause of the fall. So it must be understood that God, who has foreseen what each person will be like, and sees the causes why he will be such, knows if indeed he will sin, and knows if he will act rightly. Nevertheless, the foreknowledge of those things that have happened is not the cause; for God does not embrace or take up <note>original: "amplectitur ac suscipit"</note> the one whom He foreknew would sin.

</columns>

<summary>Origen argues that God's foreknowledge of the future is like an observer watching someone walk on a slippery path: the observer can predict the fall without being the cause of it. He maintains that while God knows all causes and effects from the beginning of creation, this knowledge does not force human beings to sin or act rightly.</summary>

But the former does not seek the truth because he is inclined toward pleasure; the other examines the truth, led by <term>common notions: "communibus notionibus," the basic moral intuitions shared by all people</term> and by encouragement. One obeys pleasure, not because he was unable to resist it, but because he does not struggle against it; another rejects pleasure when he sees its foulness and disgrace.

This person does not seek the truth because he leans toward <term>pleasure: "ἡδοvήv" (hēdonēn), referring here to physical or base gratifications</term>. <meta>This page continues Origen’s defense of human free will against the concept of divine determinism. Having previously argued that God’s knowledge of an event does not cause that event to happen—much like a doctor’s prediction of a patient’s recovery does not cause the health—Origen now examines the specific language used in Biblical prophecy.</meta>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXII.

<page-num>349</page-num>

<columns>
That the <term>foreknowledge: "prognōsis," the ability to know events before they occur</term> of God, therefore, does not impose necessity upon those things of which He has prior grasp, shall be stated in addition to what has already been said. In many places in the Scriptures, God commands the prophets to preach <term>repentance: "metanoia," a transformative change of mind and heart</term>; He does not do this by pretending that He does not foreknow whether those who hear will turn back or remain in their sins. As it is said in Jeremiah, "Perhaps they will hear and repent" <note>See Jeremiah 26:3</note>. For God does not say "perhaps they will hear and repent" because He is ignorant of whether they will repent or not, but He shows through these words, so to speak, the <term>equality of powers: "to isostasion tōn dynamēōn," the balanced capacity of the human soul to choose either good or evil</term>. This is so that His foreknowledge, if announced in advance, might not cause those who hear to lose heart by presenting an appearance of necessity—as if it were not in their power to turn back—and thus foreknowledge itself might become, as it were, the cause of their sins. Or again, for those to whom it is beneficial to be ignorant of what has been foreknown as good, the lack of foreknowledge allows them to live in virtue through the act of struggling and resisting wickedness...

<column-break/>

Wherefore God’s foreknowledge <note>original Latin: "prænotio"</note> imposes no necessity on those things which He foresees: which, besides the things mentioned above, will also be demonstrated by these. God in the Scriptures often commands the prophets to preach repentance, not because He disguises the fact that He foreknows whether those who hear will return, or will remain in their sins: as is said in Jeremiah, *Perhaps they will hear, and it will repent them.* For God is not ignorant whether they will restore themselves to a better way of life or not when He says, *Perhaps they will hear and they will repent*; but by these words He demonstrates, as it were, an equal capacity for both. And [this is done] so that His foreknowledge, if made public and announced, might not bring ruin to the listeners, and they might think themselves constrained by necessity, as if it were not in their power to be converted; and that opinion would be, as it were, a cause of sins: nor again, for those who are ignorant of the good foreknown concerning them, since they are able to live with virtue by striving and resisting vices...

<sig>Xx iii</sig> <note>This "Xx iij" is a signature mark, used by early modern printers to track the order of the large sheets of paper before they were folded and bound into the book.</note>
</columns>

<summary>Origen explains that when God uses uncertain language like "perhaps" in prophecy, He is not expressing ignorance, but is protecting human free will and preventing fatalism. He argues that knowing a future good or evil might discourage people from the necessary moral struggle of choosing virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen’s discussion on the psychological impact of divine foreknowledge. He moves from the theoretical nature of God's knowledge to the practical reason why God keeps the future hidden from human beings: to preserve the necessary struggle for moral improvement.</meta>

-># THE WORKS OF ORIGEN<-

<page-num>350</page-num>

<columns>
...foreknowledge <note>original Latin: "prænotio"</note> might be the cause of laxity and negligence for those who would no longer rise up bravely against **vices**, because that which has been predicted would entirely come to pass; and thus foreknowledge would, in a certain way, hinder the future good. 

God, therefore, who usefully administers the world, rightly willed us to be blind toward future events. For the foreknowledge of these things would have led us away from the fight and struggle against vice. It would have brought about a state where, thinking we had already comprehended the outcome, we would not resist **sin**, and would more quickly be subjected to it. 

Furthermore, if someone were to know that they would certainly be good, they might become more lax and sluggish in that struggle for **virtue**. For we have need of a vehement and sharp zeal, even beyond our innate powers, so that we may be upright and honest. Truly, the anticipated knowledge of future probity would break our practice and our impulse toward virtue. For this reason, we are usefully ignorant of whether we shall be good or evil in the future. And since, regarding future events...

<column-break/>

...might become a cause of <term>laxity: "eklyseōs," a loosening or weakening of moral resolve</term>; for those no longer standing strenuously against **sin**, as if what was foretold would certainly happen; and so foreknowledge <note>original Greek: "prognōsis"</note> would become an obstacle to the future good. 

Most usefully, therefore, God, in His <term>providential administration: "oikonomia," God's careful management of the universe</term> of the world, reasonably blinded us toward the future. For the foreknowledge of these things would release us from the <term>struggle: "athlein," a term originally used for athletes competing in the games</term> against wickedness. It would increase the <note>original: "δόξα" (doxa), meaning an impression or opinion</note> of having already attained the goal, leading us to not fight against sin and to more quickly become its subjects. 

At the same time, if the foreknowledge were to enter someone's mind that they would certainly be good and virtuous, it would conflict with their current efforts. For there is need of greater intensity and tension to become good and virtuous; but the knowledge, grasped in advance, that one will certainly be good and virtuous, relaxes our <term>discipline: "askēsin," the practice of self-denial or spiritual exercise</term>. Therefore, we advantageously do not know whether we will be good or whether we will be wicked. Since we have said that...

</columns>

Furthermore, let us also admit that while many things are **within our power** <term>within our power: "eph' hēmin," a technical term in Greek philosophy for things subject to human will and choice</term>, many causes of these actions are found in things *not* within our power. If these external things had not occurred—I mean those not within our power—then these specific actions of ours would not have been carried out. These actions of ours are performed as a consequence of those preceding events that were beyond our control, even though it was possible, given those same preceding events, to act differently than we actually do.

For this is not the time to explain that matter of the dull of hearing and the deaf. 

Nor indeed do we doubt that many things which are within us are given cause by many things which are not within us. If those things—I mean those not within us—had not existed, those things which are within us <note>original Latin: "in nobis," referring to internal states or actions</note> would never have been done. Moreover, certain things among those within us are done as a consequence of those which, though not in our power, preceded them; since it was possible that those things which preceded might lead to actions other than those we actually perform.

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXII.

<columns>
"This will happen absolutely, and it is impossible for it to happen otherwise." This kind of claim extends to all foreknowledge of things that are within our power <note>Greek: "ἐφ' ἡμῖν"</note>, whether according to the Divine Scriptures or the histories of the Greeks. Indeed, the so-called "lazy argument" <term>argos logos: a famous sophism used by ancient skeptics to argue that if the future is determined, human effort is useless</term> among the dialecticians happens to be a sophism—though it will not be considered a sophism as far as Celsus is concerned; however, according to sound reason, it is a sophism. To understand this, I will use the prophecies about Judas from Scripture, or our Savior's foreknowledge of him as the one who would betray him. From Greek histories, I will use the oracle given to Laius <note>The father of Oedipus, who was warned by an oracle that any son he fathered would kill him</note>, conceding for the present that the oracle is true, since it does not hinder the logic of our argument. Concerning Judas, then, it is said from the person of the Savior in the one hundred and eighth Psalm <note>In the Septuagint numbering; this is Psalm 109 in modern English Bibles</note>, the beginning of which is: *"O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me."* And if you observe the things said in the Psalm, you will find that it was foreknown he would betray the—

<column-break/>

"This will be altogether so, nor can it happen that it turns out otherwise." And this pertains to all foreknowledge concerning things placed within our own power, both from divine writings and from the histories of the Greeks. And that sophism which the dialecticians call the "idle and lazy argument" <note>Latin: "futilem & ignauam rationem"</note> will not be a sophism in Celsus's judgment, but in truth it is a sophism. That this may be understood, I bring forth the prophecies concerning Judas from Scripture, or I shall declare our Savior's foreknowledge concerning him, as one who would betray him. From Greek histories, I will use the oracle given to Laius, and for now, I will admit it as true, because it does not conflict with our discussion. Concerning Judas, therefore, in the one hundred and eighth Psalm, it is said in the person of the Savior; its beginning is: *"O God, do not keep silence of my praise: Because the mouth of the sinner and the fraudulent is opened against me."* And having observed those things which are said in the Psalm, [it is clear] that Judas was foreknown as the traitor—
</columns>

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXII.
-> Yy ii <-

<columns>
For the oracle did not command him to do something that was impossible; it was possible for him to refrain, and he was not forced into either choice. However, he followed the path of the one who did not guard himself against **sowing the furrow of children** <note>original: "σπεῖραι τέκνων αὔλακα" — a poetic metaphor for procreation, echoing the quote from Euripides on the previous page</note>, and he suffered the consequences of that sowing: the events of the tragedy involving Oedipus, Jocasta, and their sons. Furthermore, there is the so-called **Lazy Argument** <term>Lazy Argument: (Greek: *argos logos*) A famous sophism designed to prove that human effort is futile if everything is already determined by fate.</term>, which is a sophism. It is presented as a hypothetical case to a sick person; as a sophism, its goal is to discourage him from using a doctor to regain his health. The argument goes like this: "If it is fated for you to recover from the disease, you will recover whether you bring in the doctor or do not bring in the doctor. But if it is fated for you not to recover from the disease, you will not recover whether you bring in the doctor or do not bring in the doctor. Now, it is fated either that you recover or that you do not recover; therefore, it is in vain that you bring in the doctor." But this argument will be wittily refuted by a similar logic: "If it is fated for you to father children, whether you have intercourse with a woman or whether you do not..."

<column-break/>

For the oracle did not predict anything to him that he was unable to do; it was entirely within his power to behave differently, for he was compelled toward neither outcome. But truly, after he failed to guard himself against seeking children, it followed that by having sought children he suffered that disaster which is well known from the tragedy of Oedipus, Jocasta, and their sons. Moreover, the "lazy and futile" argument, as they call it, is a sophism directed against a sick person based on a condition: for since it is deceptive and fallacious, it thus forbids him from the use of a doctor: "If it is fate that you be relieved of the illness, whether you employ a physician or do not employ a physician, you will be relieved; on the contrary, if it is by fate that you will not be relieved, whether you employ a physician or do not employ a physician, you will not be relieved; therefore, whether it is in fate that you be relieved of the illness, or in fate that you are not, you employ a physician in vain." Indeed, that reasoning is wittily countered by this: "If it is decreed by fate that you should raise children, whether you take a wife or do not..."
</columns>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXII.

If this is impossible—as it is found that the information regarding older family members is not chronologically consistent with the birth—it is clear that the stars moving in the heavens in such a way did not cause events that had already passed and occurred before the stars were in this position. If this is so, perhaps a person who accepts that their predictions are true will, after considering what is said about the future, say they speak the truth not because the stars *cause* things, but only because they *signify* <note>Origen is making a crucial philosophical distinction: the stars might be "omens" or "signs" that can be read, but they do not have the power to "force" or "cause" human destiny.</note> them. <column-break/>

...greater, in wealthy or meager circumstances, and whether he performs this or that work. They inquire the same regarding the mother, and regarding older brothers, if there happen to be any. But for the present, let us admit that they have discovered the system of that **place**; nevertheless, we will later demonstrate that it is otherwise. Let us therefore ask of those who think human affairs are driven by the stars, how today’s position could have caused things that are older than it. If this cannot be done—since what was predicted concerning the past is found not to be true in terms of timing—it is evident that the stars, moved in the heavens in this way, did not cause those things which had happened before that positioning of the stars existed. If this is the case, perhaps he who thinks that truths are predicted by them, having weighed those things which are said concerning the future, will respond that they are spoken truly not because the stars *effect* them, but only because they *signify* them. But if anyone should affirm that the stars do not cause the past, but other...

<summary>Origen argues that astrology cannot be causal because a birth chart cannot "cause" the status of parents or siblings who existed before the birth; instead, he suggests stars might act as signs rather than causes.</summary>

For from the <term>birth-charts: Origen uses the terms "ortu" and "genesis" to refer to the astrological configuration of the stars at the moment of a person's birth.</term> of many people, the events pertaining to a single individual can be gathered. We might grant this for the sake of argument, assuming that it is possible for such things to be grasped by human knowledge. For example, if a certain man is destined to suffer this or that—say, to be killed by robbers—astrologers claim they can discover this from his own birth-chart. However, if he happens to have several brothers, they also believe they can discover the same thing from the birth-charts of each of those brothers. For they believe that each individual's <term>horoscope: a forecast of a person's future based on the relative positions of the stars and planets at the time of their birth.</term> contains the fact that their brother will be killed by bandits. Similarly, they think this is contained in the charts of the father and the mother, the wife, the sons, the servants, and his closest friends—and perhaps even the <term>genesis: the Greek term "γένεσιν," meaning origin or birth-calculation.</term> of the killers themselves. If an event is thus entangled in so many different birth-charts (even if we grant their premise for a moment), how is it possible for the event to occur because of the configuration of the stars in *this* particular birth-chart rather than *that* one? For it is implausible to claim that the configuration in one person’s particular birth-chart produced these effects, while the configuration in the charts of the others did not,

<column-break/>

For from very many birth-charts it is possible to take the things concerning one man. We say this by way of hypothesis, conceding that it is possible for human knowledge to take this up. For they think that the birth-chart of each brother contains the fact that a brother will be killed by robbers. For from the birth <note>The Latin *ortus* and Greek *genesis* here refer to the astrological configuration or "horoscope" at the moment of birth.</note> of many people, those things which pertain to a single man can be gathered. But the astrologers, to whom that mystery is unknown, pronouncing immediately on every counsel, having often slipped, invented "steps" <term>climacterics; critical periods in a person's life, such as every seventh or ninth year, which astrologers used to explain away unexpected turns of fate</term>, leading man's free will into ignorance, as we demonstrated yesterday. <header>PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXII.</header>

---

## On matter: that it is not uncreated, nor the cause of evils.

<column-break/>

## On matter: that it is not uncreated, nor the cause of evils.

---

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->From the seventh book of Eusebius Pamphilus’s *Preparation for the Gospel*<-

I think you are not unaware that it is impossible for two uncreated <term>ingenita; things that have no beginning, cause, or creator</term> things to exist at the same time. This is true even if you especially seem to have introduced this premise into the argument—that one must of necessity say either that God is separate from matter, or on the other hand, that He happens to be indivisible from it. If, then, someone should wish to say that He is united with it, he will be speaking of one uncreated thing; for each of these will be a part of the other. But being parts of one another, they will not be two uncreated things, just as different parts fragmented into many created things are not many separate beings; rather, as reason requires, we say that man—a single created thing consisting of many parts—was made by God. Furthermore, we sometimes call a man "evil" because he kills, and at other times "good" because he acts well; and these names are attached to the substance from the **accidents** <note>original: "accidentibus" / "συμβεβηκότων" (symbebekoton); in ancient logic, an "accident" is a property or quality that a person has (like being a doctor) that isn't part of their essential nature as a human.</note> themselves, which are not the substance itself. For murder is not a substance, nor likewise is adultery, nor any other similar evils. But just as a grammarian is named from grammar, a rhetorician from rhetoric, and a physician from medicine—even though the substance is neither medicine, nor rhetoric, nor grammar, but rather receives its name from the things which happen to it, from which...

<column-break/>

...receive [existence] to be, **evils** will not be **substances**. But if evils are substances, and murder is evil, murder will be a substance. However, murder is clearly an **activity** <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia); an action or a working out of potential.</note> of someone; therefore murder will not be a substance. If you want the things that act to be substances, I also agree; for example, the man who is the murderer. For by the definition of being a man, he is a substance. But the murder he commits is not a substance, but a certain work of the substance. And we call the man sometimes evil because of the act of murdering, and then again good because of acting well. And these names are woven together with the substance from its **accidents**, which are not the substance itself. For murder is not a substance, nor again is adultery, nor any of the similar evils. But just as from grammar, one is called a grammarian; and from rhetoric, a rhetorician; and from medicine, a doctor—the substance being neither medicine, nor rhetoric, nor grammar, but receiving its title from the accidents belonging to it; from which...

<summary>This page argues that evil acts like murder or adultery are not physical "substances" or entities in themselves, but are instead actions or "accidents" performed by a human substance. ### ORIGEN

...[to be contrary]? <note>original: *contrarium* / *antikeitai*</note> It seems so.
Is water indeed contrary to fire? It seems to be contrary.
Also darkness to light, cold to heat, and likewise moist to dry? I think so.
Therefore, if nothing that exists is contrary to itself, these things will not be a single matter <note>original: *materia una*; the underlying substance of the universe.</note>; nor indeed will they be made from a single matter.
But I would like to inquire into something related to this.
Does it seem to you that parts do not destroy <note>original: *tollere*; to lift away, remove, or cancel out.</note> one another? It seems so.
And do fire and water, and likewise the rest, seem to be parts of matter? Entirely.
What then? Does it not seem to you that water removes and destroys fire, light destroys darkness, and other similar things? It seems so.
If, therefore, parts do not destroy each other, but the parts of matter do destroy each other, they will not be mutual parts. Therefore, if nothing that exists is contrary to itself, they will not be one matter <note>original: *hylē mia* (ὕλη μία)</note>, nor will they be from one matter.

Does it seem to you that parts happen to not be destructive of one another? It seems so.

Therefore, if parts are not to be destructive of one another, but the parts of matter are destructive of one another, they will not be parts of each other. ### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXIII.

...reason of parts; for nothing is contrary to itself. For things that are contrary are naturally contrary to *other* things; for example, white is not contrary to itself, but is said to be contrary to black. And light similarly is shown not to be contrary to itself, but appears to be so in relation to darkness; and so it is with many other things. If, therefore, matter <note>original: *hylē* (ὕλη); referring to the underlying substance of the universe.</note> were also a single thing, it would not be contrary to itself; but since opposites are as they are, it is shown that matter does not exist <note>The argument concludes that "matter" cannot be a single, eternal substance if it contains inherently conflicting properties.</note>.

## Being set apart based on foreknowledge does not destroy our free agency.

*From the 1st volume of the explanations on the Epistle to the Romans; on the phrase, "Set apart for the Gospel of God."*

...let them respond; let us suppose, as a condition, that some things are <term>within our power</term> <note>Latin: "in nostrâ esse potestate." Origen is using a standard philosophical premise to test his opponents' logic.</note>: and let this be said against those who take away the freedom of the will, until by this condition their own opinion is proven false. Let there be, therefore, free will within us: will God then, looking upon the sequence of future events, foreknow those things which each of us, being possessed of liberty, will do out of that liberty? Or will He not foreknow? 

He who responds that He will not foreknow would be ignorant of the infinite mind and the greatness of God. But if they acknowledge that He will foreknow, we shall ask them again: is His knowledge the cause of why these future things will happen—given that it is granted that something is within our power—or does He foreknow it because it is going to happen? 

In no way is foreknowledge the cause of those things which will come to pass for each of us from the freedom of our choice. It was possible, then, that if certain obstacles were encountered, he who was created free might not do this, but rather do that. If these and similar things are said, this too is preserved:

<column-break/>

...let them answer us regarding these things: let it be assumed for the sake of the argument that there is something <term>within our power</term> <note>Greek: "ἐφ' ἡμῖν" (eph' hēmin). This is the core technical term for human agency or "that which depends on us."</note>, and we shall say this to those who would destroy <term>that which is in our power</term>, until by means of this hypothesis their argument is shown to be unsound. 

Now, since there is "that which is in our power," will God, by observing the sequence of things to come, foreknow those things that will be performed by "that which is in our power" by each of those who possess such power, or will He not foreknow? He who says He will not foreknow is ignorant of the Mind that is over all and the majesty of God. 

But if they grant that He will foreknow, let us ask them again: is His having known it the cause of the existence of those things which will happen—granted that there is something <term>within our power</term>—or did He foreknow them because they will happen? Foreknowledge <note>original: "πρόγνωσις" (prognosis).</note> is in no way the cause of those things which will happen from the power within each person. It was possible, then—certain things having occurred in this way—for the one created to be <term>self-governing</term> <note>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion). This refers to a being that has the power of self-determination or "free will."</note> to have acted not in this way, but in that. If these and similar things are said, then that [saying] is also preserved: "It is well...

"...good and faithful servant, you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your lord" <note>original Greek: δούλε ἀγαθὲ καὶ πιστέ... (Matthew 25:21). Origen argues that praise only makes sense if the servant chose to be faithful.</note>; and all such praise [is preserved]. And the fairness of this is also preserved: "Wicked and lazy servant, you should have put my money in the bank" <note>original: τράπεζαν (trapezan), meaning a money-changer's table or bank.</note>. In this way only can the words spoken to those on the right be preserved as just: "Come to me, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat," and what follows; and to those on the left: "Depart from me, you cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry and you did not give me food to eat," and what follows. Furthermore, if the phrase "set apart for the gospel of God" <note>original: ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ (Romans 1:1)</note>, and the phrase, "He who set me apart from my mother’s womb" <note>original: ὁ ἀφορίσας με (Galatians 1:15)</note>, implied some kind of necessity, how could Paul reasonably say, "I discipline my body and make it my slave, lest after preaching to others I myself should be <term>disqualified</term>" <note>original: ἀδόκιμος (adokimos). This term refers to a contestant who fails a test or is rejected from a competition.</note>?

<column-break/>

"...*good and faithful servant, you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many: enter into the joy of your Lord.*" This, and all praise which is granted to the good; and finally, it is shown to be justly said, "*Wicked and lazy servant, you ought to have committed my money to the <term>money-changers</term>*" <note>Latin: trapezitæ. In the ancient world, these were bankers who sat at tables in public squares.</note>. Thus also will those things stand which are justly said to those who stand at the right: "*Come to me, blessed of my father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, because I was hungry, and you gave me something to eat*," and those things which follow. To those indeed who are at the left: "*Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels, because I was hungry and you did not give me something to eat*," and so forth. And indeed that phrase, "*destined for the Gospel of God*": and, "*he who destined me from my mother's womb*," if they contained any necessity, would Paul rightly say, "*I <term>buffet</term> my body* <note>Latin: suggillo. This is a vivid term meaning to strike or bruise, used here to describe Paul's strict self-discipline.</note> *and bring it into servitude, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself [become] a castaway*"?

...disqualified; and also that saying, *Woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel.* <note>original Latin: "Vae mihi nisi Euangeliū enunciaue- ro" (1 Corinthians 9:16).</note> For by these words he clearly declares that unless he buffeted <note>original: "suggillaret," referring to Paul’s "striking" or "bruising" his body in self-discipline.</note> his body and brought it into servitude, it was possible for him—even after preaching to others—to become **disqualified**, and that a "woe" would be upon him unless he preached the Gospel. And He who set him apart for His own Gospel saw these things: that he would be in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes exceedingly, in deaths often; that from the Jews five times he would receive forty stripes save one; <note>original: "πεντάκις τεσσαράκοντα παρὰ μίαν."</note>

### CHAPTER XXV.

*From the volume on the fourth Psalm, regarding those words: "Many say, who will show us good things?"* <note>original Latin: "Multi dicunt, quis ostendet nobis bona?" Quoting Psalm 4:6.</note>

### CHAPTER 25.

*From the volume on the 4th Psalm; on the verse: "Many say, who will show us the good things?"* <note>original: "πολλοὶ λέγουσι, τίς δείξει ἡμῖν τὰ ἀγαθὰ;"</note>

While there is much inquiry among men concerning what things are good and what things are evil, some say that good and evil are things **outside our choice** <term>outside our choice: Greek "ἀπροαίρετα" (aproaireta). These are things that happen to us, like health or wealth, rather than things we decide to do.</term>—as they pronounce pleasure to be good and pain to be evil—while others confine good and evil only to things **within our choice**, calling the virtues and the actions according to them alone "good," but vices and the activities according to vice "evil." There are also a third group who mix these, saying that good things are found both in things within our choice and things outside our choice... <note>This "third group" refers to the Peripatetics (followers of Aristotle), who believed that while virtue is the highest good, external goods like health and prosperity are also necessary for a truly "happy" life.</note>

# ORIGEN'S PHILOCALIA

## CHAPTER XXV (CONTINUED)

<columns>

...who possess a bare and simple faith have been deceived; but even some of those who profess the wisdom that is in Christ have been led astray, thinking that these are the promises of the Creator <term>Creator: "opificis" in Latin, "dēmiourgou" in Greek. From all those, therefore, who suppose that such things are established by the Scriptures, we must ask: did the prophets observe the Law? We ask this because their sins are not condemned in the text. Consider **Elijah**, who was so destitute <note>original: "aktemonestatos," meaning possessing absolutely no property</note> that he did not even have bread of his own to eat, and for this reason was sent to a woman in **Zarephtha** of Sidonia. Consider **Jeremiah**, who was cast into a pit of mud <note>original: "lacum coeni" / "lakkon borborou," referring to the cistern where Jeremiah was imprisoned</note> and was always held in derision, so much so that he even prayed to live in the wilderness. Consider **John**, who dwelt in the deserts and, besides locusts...

<column-break/>

...as is admitted, those of the believers who are simple have been deceived; but even some of those who profess the wisdom according to Christ, supposing that such are the promises of the Creator; and they think that nothing else is signified beyond the literal meaning of the words in the threats. To all those, then, who take such things from the Scriptures, the question must be put: did the prophets keep the Law? For their sins are not brought as an accusation against them. For example, **Elijah** was so penniless that he did not even have bread with him to eat, and because of this he was sent to a woman in **Zarephtha** of Sidonia. And **Elisha**, who at the house of the **Shunammite** woman received the tiniest of quarters, and a small couch, and a cheap lamp-stand; who also died after falling ill. And **Isaiah**, who journeyed naked and barefoot for three years. And **Jeremiah**, who was thrown into a pit of mire; and was always mocked, so that he even prayed to inhabit the wilderness. # PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXV.

<columns>

...and partaking of no wild honey; girded with a leather skin about his loins, and clothed in camel’s hair <note>original: "δέρματι περιεζωσμένος τὴν ὀσφὺν, καὶ ἀπὸ τριχῶν καμήλου ἠμφιεσμένος." This description usually identifies John the Baptist, whom Origen links here to the succession of ascetic prophets who kept the Law yet lacked physical "goods."</note>. For they will admit that these men kept the Law. And we will ask them if the things they consider to be "good" were present for these men who kept the Law. 

And since they are unable to show this, they will be forced into a corner: either the promises said to be given to the godly are false, or, if they are true, they must require a spiritual interpretation <term>anagogēs: A Greek term meaning "leading upward." It refers to a method of interpretation that seeks a higher, spiritual meaning beyond the literal text.</term>. 

If they are forced by necessity to turn to allegory, their assumption will be overturned—namely, their belief that the Law threatens the ungodly with physical sickness and what are considered external evils, or that it promises healthy bodies and an abundance of wealth to those who have followed God. 

How, indeed, is it not foolish to take great pride in "evils" and to boast while being in the midst of them? For if tribulations are "evils," yet the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul, likely citing Romans 5:3: "we also glory in our sufferings."</note> says that he boasts in "evils"—this would be foolish, and the Apostle is not foolish. Therefore, such things are not truly "evils."

<column-break/>

...and he took nothing of wild honey for food, girded about the loins with a skin and clothed in the hair of a camel. For they will confess that these men kept the Law. We will ask, therefore, if those things they think are "good" were present for those who kept the Law.

Since they cannot demonstrate this, they will be reduced to saying either that the promises made to the pious and religious are false; or if they are true, they must be interpreted in a higher sense <note>original: "altiori sensu," the Latin equivalent of the Greek "anagoge."</note>. 

If they come to this hidden sense by necessity, their opinion will be destroyed—the opinion that the Law threatens the ungodly with bodily disease and what are thought to be external "evils," or that it promises health of body and riches to those who have cleaved to God. 

But how would it not be foolish to glory and rejoice in "evils" for those who are held by them? For if distresses <note>original: "angustiae," referring to the Greek "thlipseis" or tribulations.</note> are "evils," and the Apostle says he glories in "evils," that indeed is foolish; yet the Apostle is not foolish. Certainly, then, those things are not "evils."

### ORIGEN

<columns>

...no one, unless they are remarkably unrefined and ignorant <note>original Latin: "rudis & ignarus." This refers to someone lacking both basic education and spiritual training.</note>, should think so, since the causes of such a disease are often obvious: for they arise either because of the surrounding air, or because of the quality of the water, or because of the nature of one's food. Furthermore, if health and riches were offered as the specific rewards for the righteous, then it would follow that no wicked person should be healthy or wealthy. True "wealth," on the other hand, is that which—according to the sentiment of Solomon—is the ransom for a man's soul. As he says, *A man’s own wealth is the ransom for his soul* <note>Proverbs 13:8.</note>. Conversely, we must flee from that "poverty" about which it is written: <margin>Psalm 48 <note>Though the margin cites Psalm 48, the text is quoting Proverbs 13:8.</note></margin> *But the poor man does not endure threats.* Likewise, we should understand "wounds," "welts," and "diseases" as those things which happen to neglected souls because of vice. For this reason, the Prophet <note>Isaiah.</note> rebukes those who find themselves in such a state: *From the feet,* he says, *all the way to the head, there is neither wound, nor welt, nor inflamed sore; there is no medicine to apply, nor oil, nor bandage* <note>Isaiah 1:6.</note>. These points should be sufficient for those who are not entirely negligent, so that from these examples they might...

<column-break/>

...is a doctrine held only by those who are excessively uneducated; for the causes of such a disease are often manifest: for they are either due to the environment, or due to such waters, or due to such foods. And if health and wealth were the prizes for the righteous, then it would be necessary that none of the impious be healthy or wealthy. But one must seek health as this specific state of the soul, and wealth as that which, according to Solomon, happens to be the ransom of the soul, when he says: *A man's own wealth is the ransom of his soul.* One must flee from the poverty according to which it is written: *The poor man does not withstand a threat.* Furthermore, "wounds," "welts," and "diseases" must be understood as the things that happen through wickedness to inattentive souls. Regarding these, the Prophet also blames those who are found in such conditions, saying: *From feet to head there is neither wound, nor welt, nor inflamed sore; it is not possible to apply a soothing ointment, nor oil, nor bandages.* These things, then, are sufficient for those who are not altogether careless, so that from these they might [provide] for themselves...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s argument that spiritual rewards and punishments in Scripture should not be understood as literal, physical conditions. He uses a philosophical argument regarding "means" versus "ends" to demonstrate that virtuous actions are far more valuable than the material wealth or health that some mistakenly believe are the "prizes" for those actions.</meta>

### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXV.

<columns>

...so that they might attain a worthy understanding of the activity of the Holy Spirit, beyond the incomparable literal words of the Scriptures. Furthermore, this is to silence those who believe that *these* [physical things] are the rewards to be given to the saints, and *those* [physical pains] are the evils for sinners. One must also add this point: everything that exists for the sake of something else is lesser than that for which it exists. For example, surgery <note>original Greek: "τομαὶ," literally "cuttings."</note>, cautery <note>original Greek: "καυσῆρες," or burnings.</note>, and plasters applied for the sake of health are inferior to health itself. Even if these are called "goods" among medical treatments, one must understand that they are not "final goods" <term>final goods: "τελικά," the ultimate goal or "telos" of an action.</term> of medicine, but "productive goods" <term>productive goods: "ποιητικά," the tools or means used to achieve a result.</term>. The final good in medicine is the health of the body. So, if these commandments are kept to obtain these [physical] rewards, and the prizes are bodily and external, then good deeds would not be good as ends in themselves, but only as means to produce other goods. Wealth and physical health—which they think the Scripture promises—would then be superior [to the spiritual life].

<column-break/>

...having collected for themselves the sayings of Scripture that seem to conflict, they should strive to attain a worthy understanding of the action of the Holy Spirit. Everything that exists for the sake of something else is lesser than that for which it exists; just as surgery, cautery, and plasters, which are taken for the sake of health, are lesser than health. Even if these are called "goods" among medical aids, it is to be understood that they are not the "final" <note>original Latin: "finis."</note> or ultimate goods of medicine, but "efficient" <note>original Latin: "efficientia."</note> goods. The final good in medicine is the health of the body. Thus, if these commandments must be kept so that we may obtain these "goods," and if the prizes are bodily and external goods, then good actions will not be good as ultimate and perfecting things, but as the means for producing goods; and wealth and bodily health, which they think the Scripture promises, will stand out as superior.

<summary>Origen uses a medical analogy to argue that if physical health and wealth were the "prizes" for virtue, then those material things would be superior to the virtues themselves—a conclusion he finds absurd. He distinguishes between "means" (like painful medical treatments) and "ends" (like health) to show that spiritual life is the true goal, not material reward.</summary>

<columns>

I also observe this regarding specific passages: whether, just as <unclear>doctors</unclear> <note>original Greek: *ἰατροὶ* / Latin: *medici*</note> when treating those bitten by rabid dogs <note>original: *λυσσοδήκτων* / *rabido cane morsi*</note> draw the venom <note>original: *ἰὸν* / *virus*</note> to the surface so that it does not consume the person from within and destroy them—even though this causes more painful conditions and inflammations—in the same way, God draws out the wickedness hidden and nesting in the depths of the soul through His own medicinal art. I also consider this point: whether, just as doctors treat those who have been bitten by a rabid dog by drawing the venom out into the open—lest by feeding on the man from within it should kill him—and in doing so cause a sharper sense of pain and inflammation; so too does God, by His own medicine, draw out to the surface the depravity hidden and shut up in the very marrow of the soul, as it were. He does this so that it might become open and evident, allowing Him then to apply the appropriate healing. To this purpose, I believe, these words were written in Deuteronomy:
