### PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXVI.

...explaining <note>original: παραμυθούμενος (*paramythoumenos*), which carries the sense of encouraging or offering a persuasive explanation.</note> the matter: that often kind masters, showing patience toward their servants who go astray, are accustomed to say, "I have ruined you" and "I have made you wicked"—indicating by their tone that their own kindness and patience <note>original: μακροθυμία (*makrothymia*), literally "long-suffering."</note> seems to have become the pretext for the servant's increased wickedness. Just as when these things are said, someone might say in a slanderous way that the master admitted to having made the servant wicked; so too the things that proceeded from the goodness <note>original: χρηστότης (*chrestotes*), meaning moral goodness or kindness.</note> of God, becoming a pretext for Pharaoh's hardness, are recorded as God having **hardened the heart of Pharaoh.** He will explain what he meant to say using the words of the Apostle: *Or do you despise the riches of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But because of your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation and the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his deeds.* The same Apostle in...

<column-break/>

...softening <note>original Latin: *molliens*. This is the conclusion of a word begun on the previous page, likely *punctus* (point) or a similar term describing the "softening" of a difficult theological point.</note> the point: often good masters, being patient with the faults of their servants, are accustomed to say: "I have ruined you: I have made you wicked"; showing in this way, with a certain emotion, that their own goodness and patience seem to have provided the cause for why the servants' wickedness increased. Therefore, just as when these things are said, someone could make a false accusation that the master has confessed to making the servant wicked; so too the things which have proceeded from the kindness of God, as if they were the cause of the hardening in Pharaoh, are said to have **hardened the heart of Pharaoh.** But they are softened by the words of the Apostle in this way: <margin>Romans 2</margin> *Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and forbearance and patience? Not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But because of your hardness and a heart that does not know how to repent, you heap up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath, and of the declaration, and of the justice of God, who will repay each one according to his works.* The same Apostle in...

<summary>Origen argues that God "hardening" Pharaoh's heart is a figure of speech; it means God's patience and kindness inadvertently gave Pharaoh the opportunity to become more stubborn, much like a kind master's leniency might be blamed for a servant's bad behavior.</summary>

--- Page 506 ---
<meta>This page continues Origen's explanation of divine "hardening." He argues that God’s patience (makrothymia) is the catalyst: just as a kind master's refusal to punish might make a rebellious servant even bolder in their defiance, God's mercy allows the "vessels of wrath" to grow more hardened in their own choice to resist. This is a central theme in Origen’s defense of free will.</meta>

# ORIGEN

...says in the Epistle to the Romans:
> *If, however, God, wishing to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction.* <note>Romans 9:22. The "vessels of wrath" are individuals who have set themselves against God.</note>

<margin><image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand) points toward the start of the following paragraph.</image-desc></margin>
It is as if His patience itself sustained the vessels of wrath and, in a sense, brought them forth. For if—because He was gentle and patient, not punishing sinners but showing mercy—those vessels abounded in their wickedness, then He Himself made all the vessels of wrath, and to that extent, He Himself "hardened" their hearts. <note>original Latin: *indurauit cor eorum*. Origen is arguing that "hardening" is a figure of speech: God's kindness provides the opportunity for a person to either repent or become more stubborn.</note>
For when Pharaoh does not obey despite so many signs and wonders being performed, but resists after such great and numerous miracles, how can he not be proven even harder and more unfaithful? It seems that his hardness and unbelief actually arose *because* of the miracles. A similar point is made in the Gospel: *I came into this world for judgment* <note>John 9:39.</note>. It was not the Savior’s primary purpose to come for judgment, but as a result of His coming, it followed that He [came] for judgment—

<column-break/>

...says in the Epistle to the Romans:
> *If, however, God, wishing to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with great patience <note>original Greek: μακροθυμίᾳ (*makrothymia*), meaning long-suffering or forbearance.</note> the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction.*

...as if His patience had made the vessels of wrath liable, and as it were, begotten them. For if, by His being patient, He does not punish those who sin, but they are shown mercy, the abundance <note>original Greek: χύσει (*chysei*), literally a "pouring out" or "overflowing."</note> of their sin overflowed; in a way, He Himself sustained the vessels of wrath by His own patience, and—to put it this way—He Himself made everything into vessels of wrath. In this sense, He Himself hardened their hearts. For when Pharaoh is not persuaded despite so many signs and wonders, but resists after such great events, how is he not shown to be even harder and more unfaithful? His hardness and unbelief seem to have been able to arise from the very miracles themselves. There is a similar passage in the Gospel: *I came into this world for judgment.* For the Savior did not set out with the purpose of coming for judgment, but it followed from His having come, that He [came] for judgment...

<summary>Origen interprets the "hardening of Pharaoh's heart" not as a divine act of malice, but as a result of Pharaoh's negative reaction to God's patience and miracles. He compares this to Jesus's coming, which resulted in judgment even though His primary purpose was salvation.</summary>

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XXVI.

Once they are now forced to examine these things under pressure, they will reach the point of no longer accusing the Creator <term>Creator: the Greek word used is *demiourgos*, referring to the God who fashions the material world. Origen's opponents, the Gnostics, often argued that this Creator was distinct from the "Good God" of the New Testament.</term>, but of asserting that He is good. Therefore, we must ask those who think they have understood the passage, *the Lord God hardened Pharaoh’s heart* <note>Exodus 9:12</note>, whether they believe these words were spoken truly by God through Moses while he was divinely inspired, or whether they were spoken falsely. For if they were spoken falsely, then according to their own opinion, God is neither just nor truthful—and insofar as these qualities are missing, He is not even God. But if they were spoken truly, let them consider whether He does not blame him <note>i.e., Pharaoh</note> as one possessing free will <term>free will: the Greek *autexousion* literally means "having power over oneself" or self-governance.</term>, when He says: "But if you are not willing to let him go" <note>Exodus 4:23</note>; and elsewhere: "How long will you refuse to show respect to me?" <note>Exodus 10:3</note> This is said to shame Pharaoh because he did not show respect—not because he *could* not, but because he *would* not. And what is said by Moses to Pharaoh—"So that you may know that the earth is the Lord's, and you and your servants; I know that you have never yet feared the Lord"—indicates that they *will* fear Him. This argument is fitting for use against the heterodox <note>original: "heterodoxous"—those who hold "different opinions" or beliefs contrary to the established church teachings.</note>,

<column-break/>

Finally, if they are now compelled to weigh these things, they will arrive at the point where they no longer disparage the Creator <term>Creator: the Latin *opifex* means "craftsman" or "maker."</term>, but affirm that He Himself is good. Therefore, those who think they understand the phrase *The Lord God hardened Pharaoh’s heart* must be questioned: do they think these words were spoken truly by God through Moses, who was breathed upon by the divine spirit, or were they spoken falsely? For if falsely, then in their opinion God will be neither just nor true; and indeed, He would not even be God. But if truly, let them consider whether He does not rebuke him as one who has freedom of choice <term>freedom of choice: the Latin *arbitrij liberum* is the standard term for free will.</term>, saying: *But if you are not willing to let him go.* And elsewhere: *How long will you refuse to show respect to me?* This is said to Pharaoh to cover him with shame because he would not show respect—not because he was unable to, but because he was unwilling. And that which is said by Moses to Pharaoh: *So that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord, and you and your servants; I know that you have never feared the Lord*, signifies that it shall come to pass that they will fear Him. This indeed has force against those who wander away from the correct view,

<summary>Origen argues that the biblical statement "God hardened Pharaoh's heart" does not negate free will, as God simultaneously rebukes Pharaoh for his refusal to obey. He maintains that Pharaoh's stubbornness was a result of his own will, not a lack of capacity given by the Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 26 of the Philocalia, where Origen addresses the problem of divine justice in the Old Testament. ->OF ORIGEN<-

### on the goodness of God, and that nature is not perishable.

*Again from the second volume of the Commentary on the Song of Songs <note>original: "Canticum Canticorum"</note>.*

Pay attention also to this: the sun, although it is clear and bright, appears to be the cause of darkening <note>The Latin text uses *denigrandi* (turning black/tanning), referring to the bride's "darkness" in the Song of Songs</note>, not of itself, but because of the one who, as we have said, is darkened. In the same way, the Lord never hardens Pharaoh's heart on His own; rather, the cause of this hardening is in the one who exhausted the life of the Hebrews with hard labors—with mud, the baking of bricks, and all kinds of work, not only those in the mountains and hills, but also those in the fields. For by his own vice he became, in a sense, "materialized" <term>materialized: Origen uses the term *materiatus* (Latin) / *hylikos* (Greek) to describe someone so focused on physical, "muddy" desires that they lose their spiritual lightness</term> and lived entirely according to the flesh. Being a friend to the mud, he even wished to make the Hebrews soak in mud, for he did not keep the ruling part of his mind <term>ruling part: the *hegemonikon*, the highest faculty of the soul that should be directed toward God</term> pure from the "mud" of sin. Indeed, just as mud is hardened by the sun, so was he hardened by the rays of God looking upon Israel. These matters are specific to that place, and the history <note>Latin: *historia*</note> in it is not bare—

<meta>catchword: history,</meta>

<column-break/>

### on the goodness of God, and that nature is not perishable.

*And again from the second volume of those [writings] on the Song of Songs <note>original: "Asma Asmaton"</note>.*

Pay attention to these things as well: that the sun, being white and bright, seems to hold the cause of blackening <note>Greek: *melanoun*</note>, not because of itself, but because of the one being blackened, as we have explained. In this way, perhaps, the Lord does not harden the heart of Pharaoh, since the cause of this exists within the man himself. He was one who oppressed the life of the Hebrews with hard works—with mud and brick-making and all the tasks; not only those in the mountains and hills, but those in the plains. For having become a "material" person <term>material: *hylikos*, a person governed by the lower, physical elements of the world rather than the Spirit</term> by his own wickedness, and living according to the flesh in all things, he happened to be a friend to the mud. He wished to make even the Hebrews into "mud-makers," for he possessed a ruling faculty <term>ruling faculty: *hegemonikon*, the "command center" of the human soul</term> that was not clean of mud. Just as mud is hardened by the sun, so he was hardened by the rays of God as they watched over Israel. Because these things are such in their specific context, and not [merely] history—

# PHILOCALIA, CHAP. XXVI.

...account as bare [history] <note>original Greek: "ψιλὴν [ἱστορίαν]... ἀναγράφειν". The text completes the thought that the Bible is not merely a literal record of past events.</note>, it will be clear to anyone who investigates it that when the sons of Israel groaned, they did not groan because of the **brick-making**, nor because of the **mud**, nor because of the **straw**, but because of their **labors** <term>labors: Origen uses the Greek "erga," implying spiritual works or the internal struggle of the soul, rather than just physical toil</term>; and their cry rose up to God, not from the **mud**, but again by reason of their **labors**. Therefore He also listened to their groaning. He does not listen to the groaning of those who cry out to Him not from their **labors**, but from the "mud" and from **earthly activities**.

->T H E  E N D .<-

<column-break/>

...history being set forth <note>original Latin: "[histo]riā proponi"</note>, it will be plain if anyone observes that when the sons of Israel were distressed and groaned, they groaned neither because of the **brick-factory**, nor because of the **mud**, nor because of the **straw**, but because of their **works**; and their cry ascended to God, not from the **mud**, but again from their **works**. Wherefore the Lord heard their groans—not hearing the groans of those who were crying out to Him not from **works**, but from the **mud** and from **earthly actions**.

...in his epistle to the Romans, he says:
<margin>a</margin>
*But what if God, wanting to show His wrath and make His power known, bore with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction?* <note>original Latin: "Si autem Deus volens ostendere iram..." Quoting Romans 9:22. The "vessels of wrath" are a famous metaphor for people who set themselves against God’s will.</note> It is as if His very patience "carried" the vessels of wrath and, as it were, gave birth to them. For if, because He was lenient and patient—not punishing sinners immediately, but showing mercy—those vessels increased in abundance, then He Himself produced all those vessels of wrath through His patience, and thus He Himself "hardened" their hearts. For when Pharaoh does not obey despite so many signs and wonders being performed, but resists after such great and numerous miracles, how is he not proven to be even harder and more unfaithful? ...in the epistle to the Romans, he says:
*But what if God, wanting to show His wrath and make His power known, bore with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction?* <note>original Greek: "Εἰ δὲ θέλων ὁ θεὸς..." Quoting Romans 9:22. The Greek text here mirrors the Latin column precisely.</note> It is as if His patience supported the vessels of wrath and, in a sense, generated them. For if, on account of His patience—by not punishing those who sin, but showing mercy—the outpouring of sin increased, then in a way He Himself "bore" the vessels of wrath through His own patience. And so to speak, He Himself made everything into vessels of wrath. In this sense, He "hardened" their hearts. For when Pharaoh is not persuaded even when so many signs and wonders occur, but resists after such great events, how is he not shown to be harder and more unfaithful? Hardness and unbelief seem to have been made possible by the very miracles themselves. It is similar to the passage in the Gospel: *I have come into this world for judgment.* For the Savior did not set out with the goal of coming for judgment, but it followed from His having come, that He had come for judgment...

<meta>catchword: ...judgment (θέναι).</meta>

<summary>Origen interprets the "hardening of Pharaoh's heart" and the "vessels of wrath" not as God forcing people to be evil, but as a side effect of God’s patience and miracles, which the wicked choose to resist. He compares this to Jesus coming for "judgment"—a result of his arrival rather than his primary merciful intent.</summary>

# PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER 26.

Once they are now forced to examine these matters rigorously, they will reach the point of no longer accusing the Creator <note>original: "dēmiourgou." This refers to God as the "maker" or "craftsman" of the world.</note>, but will instead affirm that He is good. Therefore, we must question those who think they have understood the passage, *"The Lord God hardened Pharaoh's heart,"* whether they believe these things were truly spoken by God through Moses while he was under divine inspiration <note>original: "enthousiōntos," meaning to be filled with the divine spirit.</note>, or whether they were spoken falsely. For if they were spoken falsely, then according to them God is neither just nor truthful; and in that case, He is not even God. But if they were spoken truly, let them consider whether He does not hold Pharaoh responsible as someone who possesses free will <note>original: "autexousion." This is the technical term for the power of self-determination or "free choice."</note>, when He says, *"But if you are not willing to send him away,"* and elsewhere, *"How long will you refuse to respect me?"* These words are spoken as a reproach to Pharaoh because he would not show respect—not because he *could* not, but because he *would* not. Furthermore, what Moses said to Pharaoh—*"So that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord; but as for you and your servants, I know that you have not yet feared the Lord"*—indicates that they eventually *will* fear Him. This argument is well-suited for use against the heterodox <note>original: "heterodoxous," referring to those who hold "other" or "wrong" opinions, specifically those who argued that the God of the Old Testament was different from the God of the New Testament.</note>,

<column-break/>

Finally, if they are now compelled to weigh these things, they will reach the point where they no longer disparage the Creator <note>original: "opificem." The Latin translation of the Greek term for "craftsman" or "maker."</note>, but affirm that He Himself is good. Therefore, those who think they understand the phrase, *"The Lord God hardened the heart of Pharaoh,"* must be asked whether they think these things were said truly by God through Moses, who was inspired by the divine spirit, or falsely. For if falsely, God would be neither just nor true in their opinion; nor would He truly be God. But if truly, let them reflect whether He reproves him as one who possesses free choice <note>original: "arbitrij liberum."</note>, saying: *"But if you are not willing to let him go."* And elsewhere: *"How long will you not wish to revere me?"* This is said to Pharaoh to fill him with shame for not showing reverence—not because he was unable to do so, but because he was unwilling. And what is said by Moses to Pharaoh—*"That you may know that the earth is the Lord's, and you, and your servants; I know that you have never feared the Lord"*—signifies that they will come to fear Him. This indeed has force against those who wander from the right opinion <note>original: "à rectâ sententiâ aberrant," a Latin rendering of "heterodox."</note>,

### On the goodness of God, and that nature is not perishable.

*Again, from the second volume of the Commentaries on the Song of Songs.*

Pay attention also to this: that the sun, although it is clear and bright, seems to be the cause of darkening <note>original: "denigrandi" (Latin) / "melanoun" (Greek). For by his own vice, he has become, in a sense, materialistic <note>original: "materiatus" (Latin) / "hylikos" (Greek). Being a "friend of mud," he wishes also to make the Hebrews into "mud-kneaders," for he does not keep the governing part of his mind <term>principale animi partem</term> <note>original: "hēgemonikon." This is a Stoic term for the highest, rational part of the soul that makes decisions.</note> pure from the mud. ### On the goodness of God, and that nature is not perishable.

*And again from the second volume of the [Commentaries] on the Song of Songs.*

Pay attention to these things as well: that the sun, being white and bright, seems to hold the cause of blackening—not because of itself, but because of the one being blackened, as we have explained. In this way, the Lord does not at any time harden the heart of Pharaoh, for the cause of this is within the man himself. He is the one who causes the life of the Hebrews to suffer in hard works—in the mud and the brick-making and all the tasks—not only those in the mountains and hills, but those in the plains. For having become a sort of "materialistic man" from his own wickedness, and living according to the flesh in all things, and happening to be a friend of mud, he wishes also to make the Hebrews into makers of mud, since he possesses a governing part of the soul <term>hēgemonikon</term> that is not clean of mud. Just as mud is hardened by the sun, in this way he was hardened by the rays of God as they watched over Israel. Because such things are relevant to the specific context, and not merely—

# THE DIALOGUE OF ZACHARIAS THE CHRISTIAN SCHOLASTIC,
### WHO LATER BECAME BISHOP OF MITYLENE.
<note>Mitylene was the capital city of the island of Lesbos and an important ecclesiastical center in the Byzantine Empire.</note>

That the world is not co-eternal <note>original Greek: "synaidios." A philosophical term meaning "existing together for eternity," a concept Zacharias argues against.</note> with God, but is instead His handiwork <note>original Greek: "demiourgema." This implies something fashioned by a craftsman or "Demiurge."</note>. Having begun at a starting point in time, it will also pass away whenever it pleases the Creator to transform it. Furthermore, the reasoning regarding the goodness of God is in no way harmed by this. From these points, it is concluded that the world is not God, but God’s creation.

# THE DISPUTATION OF ZACHARIAS THE CHRISTIAN SCHOLASTIC,
### LATER BISHOP OF MITYLENE, ON THE CREATION OF THE WORLD AGAINST THE PHILOSOPHERS.
<note>original Latin: "De Mundi Opificio." This refers to the divine "crafting" or "workmanship" of the universe. The "philosophers" referenced are likely the Neoplatonists of the 6th century, such as Ammonius, who argued the world was eternal.</note>

Nothing is taken away from God's goodness by this opinion. From these things, it is gathered that the world is not God, but God’s work.*

<meta>This page transitions from the preceding theological works of Origen to the specific philosophical dialogues of Zacharias Scholasticus. # ZACHARIAS

->The Premise of the Dialogue.<-
<note>original Greek: "Hypothesis tes dialexeos." In classical literature, a hypothesis is a summary of the plot or the situational background of a work.</note>

A certain student of Ammonius—the so-called philosopher—having gently inclined toward Hellenism <note>meaning the student began to favor pagan Greek philosophy over Christian doctrine</note>, arrived in Berytus <note>modern-day Beirut, then famous for its prestigious law school</note> to study the law. When he began to present his teacher's Greek doubts concerning the world to his companions, they reported these matters to Zacharias the Scholastic <note>term: "Scholasticus," referring to a professional lawyer or a highly educated scholar-official</note>. Zacharias happened to have already conducted many discussions on these topics in Alexandria with Ammonius and Gesius the iatrosophist <note>term: "iatrosophistes," a professor of medicine who also taught philosophy</note>; therefore, his companions asked that these debates be committed to writing. These, then, are the characters of the dialogue: the one marked with the letter **A** represents Zacharias; the one marked with the letter **B** represents the person who provided the premise for the dialogue. Furthermore, there is the character of Ammonius, and then Gesius the iatrosophist. In the specific discussions against Ammonius, the character of Zacharias is labeled as "the Christian." At the conclusion of the dialogue, the first characters—those designated by the aforementioned letters—resume their conversation. The entire arrangement is Platonic, both in its phrasing and in the "meadow-like" flow <note>original: "leimonon," a metaphor for a lush, ornate, and varied literary style</note> of the prose.

---

->THE ARGUMENT OF THE DISPUTATION.<-
<note>original Latin: "Disputationis Argumentum." This section provides a Latin summary that mirrors the Greek text above.</note>

**A** certain disciple of *Ammonius* the philosopher, having gradually slipped into the error of the *Greeks* or *Pagans*, came to *Berytus* to apply himself to the study of the law. He began to propose to his comrades certain *Greek* controversies of his master concerning the world. When they had reported these to *Zacharias the Scholastic*—who had formerly disputed much on that matter at *Alexandria* with *Ammonius* and *Gesius*, a Doctor of Medicine—they requested that he refute them in writing. These are the characters of the Dialogue: *A.* indicates *Zacharias*. *B.* indicates the one who provided the occasion for the disputation. The remaining parts belong to *Ammonius* and *Gesius*, the Doctor of Medicine. Where they speak and dispute among themselves, the character of *Zacharias* is labeled as the *Christian*. Again, at the very end of the Disputation, the earlier characters designated by those letters speak together. The entire apparatus is *Platonic*, both in its style and in the manner of a blooming meadow, with the little flowers of its oratory.

<summary>This page provides the introductory background (the "Hypothesis") for a dialogue by Zacharias Scholasticus, explaining how a law student's pagan leanings prompted Zacharias to record his previous philosophical debates against the Neoplatonist Ammonius.</summary>
<keywords>Zacharias Scholasticus, Ammonius, Berytus, Alexandria, iatrosophist, Neoplatonism, Christian philosophy, creation of the world, legal studies</keywords>

# THE DISPUTATION.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial letter T at the start of the Greek text, featuring a human figure entwined with foliage and vines. Parallel to it in the Latin column is a decorative historiated initial letter N depicting a figure within ornate scrollwork.</image-desc>

**A.** What news is there, my dear companion? Why have you left your studies in Egypt and the Nile—where the great city of the Macedonian <note>original: "mega tou Makedonos asty," referring to Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great</note> is located—to spend your time here?

| ...be placed? For it is surely necessary that you, by telling myths about God and the sun and acting like the Giants of old <note>The Greek term *gigantiontes* refers to the myth of the Giants who rebelled against the heavens—here used to describe the audacity of the opposing philosophers.</note>, are making a god. Instead, they imagine a <term>Democracy|δημοκρατίαν / populare imperium</term> in divine matters—a system that is disordered, the most shameful of all forms of government, and always full of confusion and seditions. But those people were unable to behold the beauty and dignity of Monarchy, nor did they seek after its pure and blessed light. For they suffer as if from vertigo regarding the truth of their opinions; they acknowledge the "Good" and the <term>Craftsman|opificem / δημιουργὸν</term> in word only, but they strip the craftsmanship of this universe away from Him. They assign the whole, or parts of it, to whomever they please. They refuse to understand what a "Craftsman" and "Maker" truly is, or what the works and effects of God are. They do not see how the sun, placed by God like a small lamp in this vast hall of the world, illuminates the whole, yet is least of all able to "make" or "act" on its own, except where it has been appointed...

<column-break/>

...they invent; just as they have also enrolled certain wicked and violent demons into the ranks of the gods. Being unable to gaze upon the beauty of Monarchy, they do not even reach for its immaterial and blessed light. For, reeling with dizziness concerning the truth of their doctrines, they confess the "Good" and the "Craftsman" with their voice alone, but they plunder from Him the craftsmanship of all things here. They attribute the whole or its parts to anyone they wish. And they do not want to understand what a "Craftsman" and "Maker" is, nor what the "works" and "creations" of God are—and how the sun, placed by God like a lamp in this great courtyard, shines upon this whole world, being least able to "do" or "effect" anything, except when it is commanded...

[The sun was appointed] by the <term>Commander|Ταξιάρχου (Taxiarchos) / imperatore</term> and sole <term>Craftsman|δημιουργοῦ (demiourgou) / opifice</term>. Its purpose, I say, is to illuminate living creatures and to warm the plants; and to consume and remove the excess moisture and the areas and parts prone to rot. For these actions alone, and others like them, the Creator instilled in it, and this is the nature He has granted it. Therefore, obeying His law, it revolves around this universe like a wheel, possessing a uniform motion that is involuntary—much like a slave. It is soulless, and not in any way a rational being, despite the suspicions of those who treat it as a god or who gape at their own wretched and miserable little dogmas. Instead, it maintains a rhythmic and harmonious motion, never overstepping the boundaries set by the Creator or the rank it was assigned. Rather, through its friendship, harmony, and accord with the universe, it proclaims the Creator. Just as a well-constructed house, adorned with beauty, often points to the builder who is absent and unseen, and to the admirable skill of the craftsman—

<column-break/>

[The sun] was established by the Commander and sole Craftsman. I mean that it shines for living beings and nourishes plants with heat, and absorbs and dries out overflowing moisture and rotten places and parts. For the Craftsman gave it these powers of action alone, and granted it this nature. Thus, obeying His law, it is rolled around the world like a wheel, endowed with a single kind of motion, and that not by its own choice, but like a servant. It lacks a soul and is by no means a creature sharing in reason, as is suspected by those who proclaim it to be God, or who hanker after the wretched and unhappy opinions of such men. ...simplicity and the One itself, and composition is nowhere to be found, nor is it caused by anyone; for nothing is accidental to the King of all. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Christian (labeled "Chr." or "Christ.") and the Physician (labeled "Me. D." or "Iat."). On the previous page, the Christian began refuting the Neoplatonic idea that God must create eternally by necessity. He is now using Plato's own logic from the "Timaeus" to show that if God is currently "perfecting" the world, it implies the world was initially imperfect, which contradicts the idea of a perfect Creator.</meta>

### 486 ZACHARIAS

...this world according to Plato's opinion? **MEDIC.** He is fashioning the world even now. **CHRIST.** Listen then, I say, so that you may see how this proposition and response of yours is inconsistent with your own opinions. **MEDIC.** Speak. **CHRIST.** Did God perfect and complete the things that exist, or did he leave certain things imperfect from the beginning? If he perfected them, then any work or occupation in perfecting things already perfect and finished would be vain and superfluous. If he left them imperfect, he did not perfect them from the start either out of envy <note>original Latin: *inuidiâ*; Greek: *phthonō*. This refers to the famous passage in Plato's *Timaeus* stating that the Creator is "without envy."</note>, or out of ignorance of perfection. This is a direct reference to Plato's *Timaeus* (37d), where time is described as the "moving image of eternity."</note> Therefore, it is not necessary for time to be created within a pre-existing time; otherwise, we would be searching, in a ridiculous and circular fashion, for a "timeless time" just so that time itself could exist. 
**PHYSICIAN.** You speak well. But tell me this: how can you—who confess that God is good, and say that He made this universe out of His goodness, and claim that this goodness is the sole cause for the ordering of all beings—now affirm that this world will perish? For it was made by a Good Being, and it is beautiful and good; and since He is good, He creates all things beautiful. Will the Good one change? Will He become—though it is forbidden to say such a thing—someone who wishes to destroy what was rightly made and harmoniously fitted together?
**CHRISTIAN.** Not at all! Let such a thought about the Good not even enter the mind. For let us contemplate the Spirit <note>original: "ψυχήν" (psyche) / "animus." While literally "soul," in this Neoplatonic dialogue it refers to the divine essence or the animating principle of the One.</note> of the Only and One, who truly is forever and has no beginning, but remains always fixed and unswerving, never admitting any change.

<column-break/>

...and the heaven shall be, if not in time?
**CHRISTIAN.** In eternity, oh good man: for of this, time is the image; therefore it is not necessary for time to be made in time; or else, ridiculously and perplexingly, time would be sought within time, so that time might exist.
**PHYSICIAN.** That is beautifully said: but tell me, he said, how you, who confess God to be good, and that He founded this universe because of His goodness, and that this is the one cause for the ornament of things, yet you affirm that the world here—which was made by a good Being—is going to be destroyed? It is both good and beautiful, because He who is good makes all things good. Shall the Good one be changed, and—which is an unspeakable thing—become such that He wishes those things which were rightly made and fitly established to be corrupted?
**CHRISTIAN.** By no means, indeed, I say: far be it from us to even entertain such a thought about the Supreme Good in our minds, since He alone is One, and always is, and truly has no beginning, but remains always fixed and constant, nor will He ever admit any change:

# DISPUTATION

### 503

->### DISPUTATION ###<-

Let him try to frighten us like children <note>original: "μορμολυττέτω," referring to a 'Mormo' or bogeyman used to scare children.</note> by saying that a dissolution of these things might occur, and yet you shall not meet the fate of death. For he said that "everything that has been bound can be dissolved," and that you shall not be entirely free from dissolution. He even says that the heaven is nourished by its own decay <note>original: "φθορᾶς / corruptione." This refers to the ancient idea of a self-sustaining cosmological cycle.</note>, as he discusses with **Timaeus** <note>The main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name, which deals with the creation of the world.</note>, and he recognizes that all these things are by nature perishable materials. He knows they are capable of being dissolved since they were brought into being. But if he says these things are immortal by the will of the **Demiurge** <note>The "craftsman" or creator of the world in Platonic philosophy.</note>, I believe he would say so in distress, contradicting himself and fighting with himself as if in a <term>night-battle</term> <note>original: "νυκτομαχίᾳ / nocturnâ pugnâ," a metaphor for a confused struggle where one cannot distinguish friend from foe, or in this case, a philosopher's self-contradiction.</note>. For human wisdom is worth little or nothing; yet has it not already testified to their nature—that they are able to perish because they were created?

**PHYSICIAN:** So it seems.

**CHRESTOS:** If, then, these things are perishable by nature, should we be slow to suspect that these "gods" are also perishable by nature? Or if this world is thought to be a god, being created and perishable by nature—as the argument has shown and as Plato himself posits?

<meta>This page continues the Christian’s argument against the "Physician" (a Neoplatonist philosopher). # OF ZACHARIAS

### 512

...wishing <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page: "wishing to avoid a small absurdity..."</note> to avoid it, you stumble into a massive evil. For in your desire to say that God has never sat in idleness, but has been a benefactor from all eternity, you are actually saying that He is a cause of things that is not free, nor prudent, nor knowing. You raise up a creation that is a **fellow-servant** <term>conservam / homodoulon: literally "slave alongside," implying the world is on the same level as its creator</term> to its Maker, and you imagine works that are co-eternal with the Creator. You elevate these things among the gods, and you distribute that great name and office as if it were some common and trivial thing to whomever you please. You do not grant the first place in all things and among all things to God alone—who is the **One** and the **Good** <note>original: "ipsum unum ac bonū / αὐτὸ τὸ ἕν, καὶ τἀγαθόν". These are the highest principles in Neoplatonic philosophy, which Zacharias is here reclaiming for the Christian God.</note>—nor do you allow Him to be One, and Alone, and in a singular way. For if this world is co-eternal with God, in what way is God better than this world? If that superiority consists in being eternal, how shall we say that God is altogether superior to all things? And if God and the world exist together, and God is always, and the created works must exist together with the Maker <term>sumpephykenai: to be grown together or naturally joined</term>, where then is that unity of the blessed God? **PHYSICIAN:** Certainly.

**CHRISTIAN:** And if something is incorruptible, is it uncreated?

**PHYSICIAN:** Entirely so.

**CHRISTIAN:** And conversely, if something is created, is it perishable? And if something is perishable, is it certainly created?

**PHYSICIAN:** Excellently put.

**CHRISTIAN:** But the world is perishable, as its own parts demonstrate; therefore, it clearly appears to be created as well. Furthermore, if we said that the incorruptible is uncreated, and the uncreated is incorruptible—and the world is created because every body <note>In this context, "body" refers to any material or physical substance.</note> is created—then surely the world must be perishable. And again, if no writings speak of the incorruptible, and if it is said that a ship was first built in Libya...

<column-break/>

...it might have, whenever it should seem good to the Craftsman to place a conclusion upon its nature. In this way, that long and far-reaching silliness of yours would seem to be nothing, having been detected and cross-examined by the word and by proof. For that this world is created and perishable, be eager to follow the argument, and this doctrine of truth will become clearer to you.

**PHYSICIAN:** I follow you.

**CHRISTIAN:** Is that which is unbegotten also incorruptible, or not?

**PHYSICIAN:** It appears so.

**CHRISTIAN:** And if something is incorruptible, is it unbegotten?

**PHYSICIAN:** Necessarily.

**CHRISTIAN:** And yet, on the other hand, if something is created, is that also perishable? And if something is perishable, is that created?

**PHYSICIAN:** You speak well.

**CHRISTIAN:** But the world is perishable, as its parts show; does it not then also appear to be created? Moreover, if we said the incorruptible is unbegotten, and the unbegotten is incorruptible, and this world is created—since every body is created—the world is therefore also perishable. And again, if no writings are spoken concerning the incorruptible, and if a ship was first built in Libya...

...[thought], for it was made. However, we say that it is corrupted not fundamentally or for eternity—and this on account of the goodness of the Craftsman <term>Craftsman: Latin *opifex*. ...[thought], for it has come to be. ### 547

At the same time, the abundance of God’s power and wisdom is clearly revealed, as He makes mortal things immortal. He allows us neither to be ignorant of our mortality, nor to remain within it forever—as one of the wise men among us has said <note>original: *τις τῶν καθ’ ἡμᾶς σοφῶν*. Therefore, the dissolution of those things which are perceived by the senses does not introduce a permanent corruption to the whole universe. For if it did, that which happened would be alien to God and not for the sake of good. Instead, the great and manifold wisdom of God devised a plan, through the dissolution of human bodies, to destroy the corruption which wickedness had introduced. By sharing immortality with mortals, He ensured that after humans had experienced corruption and dissolution, they might hate the cause of that dissolution—and we say that wickedness is that cause. Furthermore, we are able to learn through the dissolution and reshaping of this universe, and through its abundant transformation, that He Himself is the one who created the magnitudes and beauties of visible things from the beginning. He neither permits us to be ignorant of our mortality, nor to remain in it: as one of our wise men has excellently declared. Therefore, the dissolution of those things which fall under the senses does not bring a perpetual destruction upon the universe; and certainly, that would be alien to God, nor would it come from the Good. But that great and varied wisdom of God, through the dissolution of human bodies, found a way <note>Latin: *rationem invenit*. ...ain the Spirit accomplishes anything without the Son and the Father. Return, then, from the archetypes and first forms to the form of our own soul, which was made according to the image and likeness of God; you will see a single and similar action within us. For the soul does nothing without **reason** <note>original Latin: *ratio*</note>, nor does reason act without the soul; nor indeed does the **mind** <note>original Latin: *mens*</note> by itself effect anything without the soul and reason. Nevertheless, when it is separated from the body, the soul—which by its nature is a pure **substance** <term>substance: Greek *ousia*; the fundamental "stuff" or essence of a thing that exists in itself.</term>—then becomes even more perceptive, and more spiritual, and simple, and undisturbed, and more illustrious—

<column-break/>

—gain the Spirit accomplishes anything without the Son and Father. Of the powers of the soul, some are irrational, while others are rational. Of the rational powers, some are vital and appetitive <note>Related to the 'appetite' or the faculty of desire and drive.</note>, while others are cognitive. And through this reason, I say, our soul is led up to the contemplation of those things grasped by the mind, which is the perfection of the soul. For since our soul is nurtured with and shares a kinship with the things of the senses, it is unable—due to its habituation to the senses—to raise itself to the contemplation of things that are immaterial and grasped only by the mind. *...common* **notions**, and mental **shadows** and **likenesses**. For whatever we know better than through demonstration, we know according to a **common notion** <term>common notion</term> <note>original Latin: "communes notiones" / Greek: "κοινὴν ἔννοιαν". These, then, are the rational powers that strive toward knowledge. The active powers, however, are **will** and **choice**. And will is indeed directed toward the good alone; choice, however, inclines toward both <note>meaning both good and evil</note>. And will itself, truly by itself, belongs to the rational soul; but choice belongs to that which is connected with a lack of reason. For when the soul is first outside of **generation** <term>generation</term> <note>original Latin: "generatio" / Greek: "γενέσεως". But when it enters into generation, because powers void of reason are connected to it (for the reasons we shall state), then by the connection of that part which lacks reason, it has as much power as choice: wherefore it happens sometimes before the lack of reason, and sometimes before reason; and this is preferred by it.

But I respond that "desire" is understood in two ways: one broader, and the other stricter and more specific. Just as a "disposition" <note>original: "dispositio" / "διάθεσις". I say, therefore, that this is because "desire" is spoken of both more generally and more specifically. This refers to the concept that while individuals die, the species lives on forever through offspring.</note> as far as they are able. Therefore, all things seek the eternity of the First Cause as their own origin, and each participates in this according to its own measure and capacity. 

And this is the most purposeful work of nature: that every being endowed with a **soul** <term>soul</term> <note>original: *anima* / *ψυχή* (psyche)</note> should produce another like itself. And because generation is necessary, and the power of this reproduction only manifests at a certain and defined stage of maturity...

<column-break/>

...the mole. Whatever things have touch, these do not necessarily have the others; for example, sponges participate in touch, but in none of the other senses. And it is clear that it is not possible to participate in the better sense without participating in the lesser. And this is not because the better senses need the inferior ones in order to exist, but on the contrary, the body is not able to participate in the better ones without first having attained the lower ones. Because it was necessary that none of the species should be destroyed, so that the universe might not be incomplete—for the world is a fullness of the species—and since it was impossible for the same individuals to remain in number, being both generated and perishable, these also participate in eternity as they are able. Therefore, all things also strive for the eternity of the First, as their own proper origin, and each participates in this according to its own measures. # ON THE SOUL

<columns>

...as **Aristotle** established. 
And that this was **Aristotle's** intent—that he recognized one kind of soul as **separable** and another as **inseparable**—he himself declares sufficiently at the end of his treatise *On the Parts of Animals* <note>Aristotle's *De Partibus Animalium*, a foundational text in biology and physiology.</note>. There, he states that every part of an animal is shaped according to some **vital activity**, such as the heart, the liver, the brain, and others. 
Next, he says: "***Whether this activity should be called the soul, or a part of the soul, or something that cannot exist without the soul, is a question that must be asked***" <note>original Latin: *Hæc actio, utrum animæ, vel pars animæ, vel non sine animâ vocanda sit, quærendum*.</note>. 
By this, he shows that he recognized the great range, or rather the **depth**, of souls. 
He also asks: "***Whether it is the job of the Physicist*** <term>Physicist: in the ancient sense, a 'Physicus' was a natural philosopher who studied the 'physis' (nature) of material things.</term> ***to discuss every kind of soul, or whether there is not another kind of soul that exists without matter.***" 
Thus, he acknowledges a soul that is **separable from matter**. 
And in that same commentary *On the Parts of Animals*, he says: "***The mind seems to come from the outside*** <note>original Latin: *extrinsecus aduenire*. This refers to Aristotle's famous concept of the 'nous thyrathen'—the mind entering from 'outside' the biological process.</note> ***and to be divine; for its activity has nothing in common with the activities of the body.***" 
And again in the second book, he says: "***Concerning the mind and the faculty of contemplation, it is not yet...***"

<column-break/>

...as **Aristotle** maintained. 
That **Aristotle** also holds this opinion, and knows that one soul is **separable** and another **inseparable**, he made clear even at the end of the treatise *On the Parts of Animals*. 
For he said that each of the parts of animals is characterized by some **vital activity**, such as the heart, and the liver, and the brain, and the rest. 
Then, he says: "***whether this activity should be called soul-like, or a part of the soul, or not without the soul, must be investigated***" <note>original Greek: *poteron psychikēn dei kalein, ē morion psychēs, ē ouk aneu psychēs, zētēteon*.</note>. 
So he knows the great breadth, or rather the **depth**, of souls. 
And he asks: "***whether it is for the physicist to speak of every soul, or not of every soul but only that which is not without the material***" <note>original Greek: *hōsē mē aneu tēs hylikēs*.</note>. 
So he knows a soul **separable from matter**. 
And again in the same treatise *On the Parts of Animals* he says: "***The mind seems to enter from the outside and to be divine. For no activity of it communicates with the activities of the body.***" 
And again in the second book, he says: "***Concerning the mind and the contemplative power, it is not yet...***"

</columns>

It cites Aristotle's own works to prove he distinguished between "material" souls and a "divine" mind that comes from the outside.</summary>

But one can similarly conclude from his other writings that **Aristotle** also recognized the **rational soul** as **immortal** and **separable** from every body. Furthermore, it is unnecessary to prove that **Plato** also considered the rational soul to be immortal; but that he also knew the **irrational** part was **mortal**, the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue by Plato that describes the creation of the world and the human body.</note> teaches most powerfully. For it says that the irrational soul, which is joined to the rational, is clearly **mortal**. But it is clear from this that no soul can be a **body**, whether **simple** <note>Consisting of a single element like pure fire or air.</note> or **composite** <note>A mixture of different elements.</note>. For every body, by its own nature, is dispersible and divided into infinite...

But also from other books of **Aristotle**, it is easily understood that the **rational soul** seemed **immortal** to Aristotle and **separable** from every body. Moreover, there is no reason why we should prove that **Plato** judged the soul endowed with reason to be immortal; indeed, that he thought the part **devoid of reason** was **mortal**, his *Timaeus* sufficiently shows. 

For he clearly affirms that the part lacking reason, which is connected and woven into the rational part, is **mortal**. But that part which is possessed of reason—the **principle** part, as it were, in mortals and living beings—is **divine** and **immortal**. But that no soul can be a **body**, neither **simple** nor **composite**, can be understood from this: for every body by its own nature is distracted into infinite parts...

### ON THE SOUL

<columns>

...might be [divided], wherefore it requires a **container** <note>original Latin: *continente*; refers to the force that holds a physical object together so it does not dissipate or fall apart.</note>. Therefore, is the container a **body**, or **incorporeal**? If it is a body, then that too will need a container, and so on to **infinity**. It is therefore necessary that the **virtue** and **power** which holds bodies together be **incorporeal**. Now, in **living beings**, the **soul** holds the bodies together; therefore, the soul is incorporeal. Furthermore, the lowest of the soul's **cognitive faculties**—I mean **sense perception**—is incorporeal; therefore the **nobler faculties** <note>The author refers to higher functions like reason and intellect, which are considered superior to basic physical senses.</note> are much more so. Aristotle shows that sense perception exists without a body in this way: "No body," he says, "can receive **opposites** <term>Opposites: In Aristotelian logic, these are "contraries" (like hot and cold) which cannot exist in the same physical space at the same time.</term> in the same part." For a **finger** cannot be entirely white and entirely black at the same time; nor can it be heated and cooled at once in the same part. But sense perception receives opposites at the same time and knows that this is the first and that is the second, judging **black** from **white**, and then **white** from **black**...

<column-break/>

...divisible <note>original Greek: *diaireton*. This word completes the sentence from the previous page.</note>. Because of this, it requires a **container**. Is the container, then, a **body** or **incorporeal**? If it were a body, that too would again require a container, and this would go on to **infinity**. It is necessary, then, for the **power** that holds bodies together to be **incorporeal**. Among **living things**, the **soul** is that which holds the bodies together; the soul, therefore, is incorporeal. Furthermore, even the lowest of the soul's **perceptive powers**—I mean **sensation**—is incorporeal, so the **superior** powers are much more so. Aristotle demonstrates that sensation is incorporeal as follows: he says that "no body is capable of perceiving **opposites** <note>original: *enantia*</note> at the same time and in the same part." For the **finger** cannot partake of both **white** and **black** as a whole at the same time; nor is it heated and cooled at once in the same place. <meta>This page continues the logical proof that the rational soul is distinct from the body. Following the previous argument that the soul must be incorporeal because it can reflect upon itself—a feat impossible for physical matter—this page explores the relationship between the body's decline and the soul's vigor.</meta>

### ON THE SOUL
638

<columns>

...powers that are in the body as their **underlying subject** <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "subject" is the underlying material or vessel that a quality depends on to exist, like the wax that holds the shape of a seal.</note>, they grow strong and waste away together with the body. Such, therefore, are the **senses**; and also **anger** and **desire**. On the contrary, however, the **rational soul** <note>original Latin: *rationabilis anima*</note> flourishes and thrives while the body itself is withering. Therefore, it is not in the body as in a subject. 

Furthermore, no thing strives to destroy its own subject; for all things desire to exist. But the rational soul looks down upon the body, and taming it through the **exercises of virtue**, it often casts it away entirely. Therefore, it does not have its existence in the body as a subject. 

Furthermore, it must be demonstrated that the soul possessing **reason** has a substance separated from every body; whereas the remaining powers are in the body: specifically, the **irrational power** is in the *spirit* <note>original: *spiritali*. This refers to the 'pneuma', a refined substance ancient thinkers believed acted as a bridge between the physical body and the mind.</note>, while the **vegetative power** <note>The 'vegetative' or 'nutritive' soul is the lowest level of life, responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> is in this [physical body]. **Aristotle** provides a norm and rule concerning the soul and all other things—one that even those who think the soul is mortal agree with—which is as follows: judgment must be made, he says, about substances based on their **actions**.

<column-break/>

The powers that exist in the body as an **underlying subject** reach their peak and wither away together with the body. Such are the **senses**, **anger**, and **desire**. But the **rational soul** <note>original Greek: *logikē psychē*</note> does the opposite: while the body wastes away, it reaches its peak. It is therefore not in the body as an underlying subject. 

Furthermore, nothing is eager to destroy its own subject, for all things desire to **be**. Yet the rational soul despises the body, subduing it through the labors of **virtue**, and often casting it away entirely. Therefore, it does not have its being in the body as a subject. 

In addition to these points, one must show that the rational soul has its **essence** <term>Essence: translating the Greek *ousia*, meaning the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</term> separate from every body, while the rest have their being in a body. The **irrational soul** is in the *spirit* <note>original: *pneumati*</note>, and the **vegetative soul** is in the physical body. 

Aristotle passes down a rule in his work *On the Soul* which is acceptable to everyone, even to those who believe the soul is mortal. The rule is this: "We must," he says, "judge **essences** by their **activities** <note>original: *energeiōn*</note>."

</columns>

**Vocabulary:** Soul, Aristotle, substance, virtue, reason, rational soul, body.

<summary>This page argues that the rational soul is independent of the body because it can flourish during physical decline and often acts against bodily desires. It concludes by citing Aristotle’s rule that the nature of a thing (its essence) is revealed through its actions.</summary>

<columns>

...in whatever way each **substance** <note>original Greek: *ousia*. In Aristotelian philosophy, the 'substance' is the fundamental essence or 'thing-ness' of an object that exists in its own right.</note> exists, it possesses a corresponding **activity** <note>original Greek: *energeia*. This refers to the actualization or functional operation of a substance.</note>. How then, he asks, can a substance that possesses no activity separable from the body, not also necessarily lack a substance separable from the body? For if it possessed a separable substance but had no activity apart from the body, then whenever it was separated from the body, it would have nothing upon which to act; thus, it would exist in vain. It is therefore impossible for a separable substance to have no activity apart from the body. Again, there is another rule: every substance that possesses an activity separable from the body must itself necessarily be separable from the body. If it were not separable, it would follow that the **effect** <note>original Greek: *aitiaton*</note> is superior to the **cause** <note>original Greek: *aition*</note>, and that which is inferior would be superior to the more excellent. Which is absurd. For the cause must always be superior to the effect, just as that which is prior by nature must be superior. It is therefore impossible for an activity separable from the body not to proceed from a substance that is also itself separable. Of the aforementioned rules, one will be useful to you...

<column-break/>

...whenever any **substance** <note>original Latin: *substantia*</note> has an action related to itself and of the same kind. How then, he says, can a substance which has no action separable from the body, not also necessarily have no substance separable from the body? For if, while possessing a separable substance, it were to have no action without the body, after it has been separated from the body, it will have nothing to act upon; thus, it will be in vain. It is therefore impossible that a separable substance should have no action without the body. The other rule is this: every substance that has an action separable from the body must itself also be separable from the body. But if it were not separable, it would follow that the **effect** <note>original Latin: *effectus*</note> is more noble than its **cause** <note>original Latin: *causa*</note>, and that which is worse is more excellent than the more distinguished. But that is absurd; for the cause must always be more distinguished than the thing effected, as must that which is prior by nature. It is therefore impossible that an action separable from the body should not flow from a substance that is itself separable. And regarding the latter...

<summary>This page outlines two logical rules: first, that a substance capable of existing without a body must have a purpose or function outside of the body; and second, that if an action is independent of the body, the substance performing that action must also be independent.</summary>

However, if those things which can be separated from matter are not immaterial, it is not because they can exist in reality, but they shall always exist in reality. Even if the soul is eternally unmoved <note>original: *akinētos*; referring to the soul's stable, unchanging essence</note>, it must still act; therefore, it must have some body eternally bound to it. But these are merely **Greek and Platonic myths**.

They say that **anger** and **desire** are inseparable from the **spiritual body**. It is also clear that just as the **vital** and **nutritive** powers of the **irrational faculty** <note>The part of the soul responsible for basic biological life, shared with animals and plants</note> are established in the spirit, so too are the **cognitive** powers. For if the lesser powers are separable from this **thick body** <note>The physical, material body</note>, then much more so are the superior ones. And the cognitive powers—by which I mean **imagination** <note>original: *phantasia*</note> and **sensation**—are indeed superior. But even if the irrational powers of the soul have their being in that spiritual vehicle, nonetheless some traces...

<column-break/>

...determined: then therefore it <note>the soul</note> casts away both **anger** and **desire** with this vehicle—the **breathing** <note>original Latin: *spiranti*; a translation of the Greek "pneuma"</note> body, I say—so that there is thereafter another somewhat eternal **heavenly body** depending from the soul itself. This is thus eternal and, as they say, **transparent** <note>original Latin: *pellucidum*</note> and **starry**. Since it is part of the nature of things, it is necessary that the soul has some lot and condition which it may administer as a part of the world. And if the soul is always unmoved, yet it must act, it is necessary that it also has some eternal body bound to itself. But these are **Greek and Platonic fables**.

Some affirm that **anger** and **desire** cannot be separated from the **spiritual body**; but it is certain that just as the **vital** and **growth-producing** <note>original Latin: *auctrices*; powers of nutrition and development</note> powers of the irrational faculty are situated in the spirit, so too are the **cognitive** ones. For if those which are inferior to them are separable from this **thick** <note>original Latin: *crasso*; heavy or material</note> body, much more so are the more excellent ones; and the cognitive powers are more noble—**imagination**, I say, and **sense**. <insert>Physiology</insert> is more certain than Medicine; likewise Geometry is more certain than Mechanics. Arithmetic is more certain than Music, and for that reason is more thoroughly explored. ...by genus, or not. For those things that differ in **species** do not necessarily differ in **genus**; for example, a man and a horse <note>Both are species within the same genus: "Animal."</note>. For among bodies, some exist in potentiality in terms of generation and corruption, both according to substance and according to quality, and according to change from place to place. ...it sets potentially; and in the rest of its movements, and those of the other stars, change of place is observed potentially. But why, when he had used the term "potentially" <note>original Latin: *potestate*; Greek: *δυνάμει* (dynamei)</note> in relation to the body, did he not say "in actuality" in the sixth case <note>The "sixth case" refers to the Latin ablative, used here to translate the Greek dative case. It implies a state of being rather than a naming of the thing itself.</note> for the incorporeal, but instead used "Actuality" <term>Entelechy: The full realization or complete expression of a thing's potential.</term> in the direct case <note>The nominative or naming case.</note>?

Because, clearly, power <note>The capacity to do something.</note> is one thing, and being "potentially" <note>The state of having that capacity.</note> is another; likewise, Actuality is one thing, and being "in actuality" is another. For matter alone is all things potentially, but in act, it is nothing; but form is actuality only. However, that which is composed of matter and form is also potentially that which it is in actuality. For all these things concur as one, and whatever exists in potentiality, that also exists in actuality. For all forms are by virtue in matter, which becomes now this, now that, in act. For now, while a human is such potentially <note>For example, as an embryo or a child with the potential for reason.</note>, at another time they will become a human in act; or rather, a human possesses both being potentially and in act at the same time. This is because matter is never stripped of form; when it has received this specific form, it is indeed in act...

<column-break/>

...potentially, it sets. And regarding its other movements and those of the other stars, likewise in change according to place, one must observe what is in potentiality. But why then, having assigned "in potentiality" <note>original: *δυνάμει* (dynamei), in the dative case</note> to the body, did he not say "in actuality" <note>original: *ἐντελεχείᾳ* (entelecheia), also in the dative</note> in the dative case for the incorporeal, but instead "Actuality" <note>original: *ἐντελέχειαν* (entelecheian), in the accusative/nominative form</note> in the direct case? 

We say, therefore, that power <note>original: *dynamis*</note> is one thing, and "in potentiality" is another; and Actuality is one thing, and "in actuality" is another. For matter, on the one hand, is only all things in potentiality, and it exists potentially, but in activity <note>original: *energeia*</note> it is nothing. But form, on the other hand, is only Actuality. That which consists of matter and form is also "in potentiality," and this same thing is also "in actuality." For all these things run together at once; and that which is "in potentiality" is also "in actuality." For indeed all forms are potentially in the matter, which at one time becomes this, and at another time becomes that in activity. For now, being a human potentially, it later becomes a human in activity. Or rather, it possesses the "potentiality" and the "activity" together. Since matter is never stripped of form, when it possesses that form, it is in activity...

...it is this specific thing, already in potentiality. Since, therefore, in those things where potentiality exists, actuality also exists—as has been said regarding material bodies—but in divine and incorporeal things, potentiality does not exist, because there is no matter. And for this reason, there is not even "being in actuality" <note>original Greek: *ἐνεργείᾳ* (energeia)</note>; for they are not a specific thing *in act*, but are already truly **self-actualities** <note>original Greek: *αὐτοενέργειαί* (autoenergeiai)</note> pure of material substance. For this reason, in distinguishing the immaterial and incorporeal nature from matter and composite nature, he signified the latter through "potentiality" and the former through **Entelechy** <term>Entelechy: The state of a thing when its essence is fully realized; the opposite of mere potential.</term>.

He says that it is possible to speak of the soul in a human as both **one and many**. Many, because they differ from one another in kind—the **vegetative**, the **irrational**, and the **rational**—and they are separated from one another. But one, because of their harmony and mutual sympathy. For the activities of reason pass down even to the vegetative part, and their movements and lives, as it were, dispose the reason within them. Therefore, the soul is also one.

Those who say the soul is one in kind across all living beings believe it to be a **mixture** <term>Krasis (Greek: κρᾶσιν): A blending or temperament of physical elements or "humors" in the body.</term>. They change—

<column-break/>

...this is, in potentiality, another thing. Because therefore in those things it [potentiality] exists, it is also there in act, just as was said concerning material bodies; but in divine and incorporeal things, nothing exists in potentiality, because in them there is no matter; and for that reason, neither is there anything in act, for they are not in act some such thing. But they are themselves **acts**, pure from all matter. Therefore, when he distinguishes the immaterial and bodiless from matter and composite nature: he signified that [material] one by "power," and this [immaterial] one by the word **Entelechy**.

One can say there is one soul in man, and many: many indeed, because they differ among themselves in kind—the **vegetative**, the **animal**, and the **human**—and they are separated from one another. But one, because of their mutual harmony and agreement. For from reason, actions proceed to the vegetative part, and their motions and lives, in a certain way, constitute and adorn the reason within themselves. Therefore, the soul of man is also one.

In the same way, the mind remains the same in its underlying nature. When it corresponds to a straight line, it acts by itself and knows immaterial things. But at other times it is like a **bent line** <note>original Greek: *keklasmenē eutheia*. This beautiful metaphor suggests that when the mind "bends" down toward the physical world of the senses, it does not stop being the mind, but simply changes its orientation.</note>, inclining toward sensation and using it as a tool; it is then that it knows material things. This, then, is the first difficulty and its solution. 

A second difficulty, which is taken as a starting premise, is this: that which moves from **potentiality** to **actuality** <term>Potentiality and Actuality: A core concept in ancient philosophy where something has the "potential" to be something (like a seed) and then becomes "actual" (a tree).</term> is undergoing a complete change. And change is a form of **being acted upon** <note>original Greek: *pathos*; original Latin: *affectio*. In this context, it means the mind is "receiving" an impression from the outside world, like wax being stamped.</note>. ...things, and those things are **material**. But it can be answered to this that the mind is one in its subject, but diverse in its reason. For just as a straight line is the same in its subject, yet diverse in its reason; for that which is now straight can be curved and bent: so also the mind is the same in its subject. Likewise, a straight line represents the mind when it acts by itself and knows immaterial things: occasionally the straight line is bent; and the mind is "bent" toward sensation, and uses it as an instrument when it knows material things. <columns>
...knows material things, it **suffers** <note>original Latin: *patitur*. In this context, "suffering" refers to the philosophical concept of being "passive" or "acted upon" by an external object.</note> something from them, being led from **potential knowledge** <term>Potentiality: The capacity to know something before actually thinking about it.</term> to **actual knowledge** <term>Actuality: The state of actively thinking about or realizing a piece of knowledge (*actus*).</term>. Now, that which is led from potentiality to act is **changed**. And that which is changed is "suffering" (acted upon). Therefore, the mind is acted upon by material things. And because nothing can be acted upon by that which is of a different matter, it is clear then that the mind is of the same matter as material things, and is itself both material and **incorruptible**. <note>This presents a contradiction: if the mind is material, it should be subject to decay; yet the author argues it is incorruptible.</note> This is the difficulty which we, in resolving it, say was wrongly assumed: that wherever there is an agent, there is also a sufferer. For that is false. An agent only suffers in return when it is of the same matter as the sufferer. Since the mind is not of the same matter as material things, it is not necessary that it be acted upon by material things when it knows them. For the **Creator God** <note>original Latin: *opifex*. This refers to the divine craftsman or architect of the world.</note> acts when He does us good, yet He suffers nothing from us in return. Therefore, only those agents suffer in return which share the same matter as the things they act upon. It is also characteristic of the Mind that it acts by its very **substance** <term>Substance: The fundamental essence or nature of a thing (*substantia*).</term>; for one who knows is neither by knowledge alone...

<column-break/>

...the mind knows material things <note>original Greek: *enyla*. Things existing within matter.</note>, it is clear that it is acted upon by them, moving from potential knowledge to actual knowledge. But that which is led from potentiality to actuality is **altered**. And that which is altered is acted upon. Therefore, the mind is acted upon by material things. Since nothing is acted upon by that which is dissimilar, it is clear then that the mind is **of the same matter** <note>original Greek: *homoylos*. Sharing the same physical or essential material.</note> as material things. Thus, it is itself both material and incorruptible. This is the puzzle, which we solve by saying it was wrongly taken as a rule that where there is a "maker" there is also a "sufferer." This argument is false. For the maker only suffers in return when it is of the same matter as the thing it acts upon. Since, then, the mind is not of the same matter as material things, there is no necessity for it to be acted upon by them when it knows them. For the **Creator** <note>original Greek: *demiourgos*. The "Demiurge" or Craftsman who shapes the universe.</note> also acts, doing us good; and yet he does not suffer in return from us. So only those agents suffer in return which are of the same matter as the sufferers. It is not unique to the mind to act by its substance. For the one who knows is neither knowledge alone...

When Aristotle asserts that everything which moves is in a place, he admits that the heaven of the fixed stars moves; yet he denies it is in a place, either because it is not in a place as a whole, but because its parts are in a place—not because they are born to be uncontained, but because there is no body above them, so that the whole is enclosed within itself. Therefore, the soul can be said to move itself only through incidental movement from place to place, and in no other way. For it is not altered when the body is altered, nor does it grow or shrink.

...the distinction and lack of confusion between things. For just as weaving, perhaps, is an action of the living being <note>original: ζώου (*zoou*)</note> according to the body, so also thinking is an action of the living being according to the soul. Therefore, when the living being perishes, the soul retains none of those things which were added to it from its entanglement with the body. Consequently, it does not even remember. For in this life, its knowledge is fleeting <note>original: παραῤῥέουσα (*pararrheousa*) — literally "flowing past."</note>, and it requires **memory** <term>memory: defined here as a physical or semi-physical faculty needed only when knowledge is not constant.</term> to hold onto what has been learned. But after it is separated from the body, because it possesses stable knowledge and encounters the things themselves directly, it has no need for memory. For memory is only for things known in the past.

Aristotle says that when the **mind** <term>mind: the Greek *nous*, the highest part of the soul capable of rational thought.</term> does not rule, but the human being exists in an unnatural state, then the natural order is reversed; the powers of the soul follow the **temperaments** <term>temperaments: the physical balance of hot, cold, wet, and dry in the body.</term> of the body. However, when the mind rules, the human being then being in a natural state, the powers of the soul no longer follow the physical temperaments of the body; rather, the body follows the soul.

<column-break/>

...to be mixed by a similarity of things, because it is distinct and not confused. For just as weaving, for instance, belongs to the living being according to the body, so understanding <note>original: *intelligere*</note> belongs to the living being through the soul. Therefore, once the living being is destroyed, the soul will possess none of those things which it had from its union with the body. Indeed, it does not even remember. For in this life, its knowledge flows away and it requires memory to retain what it has learned; but once released from the body, as it possesses stable knowledge and reaches the things themselves, it needs nothing from memory. For memory belongs to things known previously.

When the mind does not command, Aristotle says, but the human being is in an unnatural state, then, with the order perverted, the powers of the soul follow the **temperament** <note>original: *temperaturam*</note> of the body. But when the mind commands, the human being then being in a natural state, the faculties of the soul no longer follow the temperament of the body, but the body itself follows the soul.
