<header>->ON THE SOUL<-</header>
<meta>catchword: just as (καθάπερ)</meta>

Aristotle overturns the opinion of
Thales of Miletus concerning the soul;
Thales devised that the soul is 
mixed into every body, 
so that the body is alive <note>original: *vivens*</note>. 
For first, he asks why, 
since the soul is in every body, 
are these things animals, 
and those are not? Then, why 
is no element an animal? 
Even though it would be more 
fitting for them to be animals. 
For if the soul were in fire and in air, 
it would be better off in these, 
as they are primary and subtler 
bodies, than in composite ones; 
from which its actions would 
have shone forth more clearly. 
He then connects other 
absurdities to these, quite 
a many, which follow from 
Thales' opinion.

Since there are many and 
different actions of the soul, 
Aristotle asks whether, 
since the soul is one and 
indivisible according to its 
substance <term>substance: the essential nature or "being" of a thing</term>, those 
different powers and actions 
proceed from it, so that 
it is the same in substance 
and one in number: 
the nourishing, the growing, 
the generative, the rational, the 
spirited, and the desiring:

<column-break/>

He is overturning Thales' opinion 
concerning the soul—the one who 
said that the soul is mixed in 
every body, so that the body is 
besouled <note>original: ἔμψυχον (*empsychon*)</note>. 
First, for what reason 
does he say that, while the soul 
exists in every body, some things 
are animals <note>original: ζῶα (*zoa*)</note>, while others 
are not? Next, why is none of 
the simple elements an animal? 
And yet these especially ought 
to be. For being in fire and 
in air, since these are purer and 
finer-parted bodies, the soul 
would be better in these 
than in the composite ones, 
from which its activities 
ought to have been more 
transparently visible. He also 
brings up several other 
absurdities following 
this assumption.

Because the activities of the 
soul are many and various, 
Aristotle seeks to know whether, 
the soul being one and 
indivisible in essence, these 
different powers and activities 
come from it: so that it is the 
same in essence, and one 
in number—namely the 
nutritive, the augmentative, 
the generative, the rational, the 
spirited, and the appetitive. And 
just as

<summary>This page presents Aristotle's critique of Thales of Miletus, arguing against the idea that the soul is a substance mixed into all physical elements. It also introduces the fundamental question of whether the soul's various functions (like reason and growth) stem from a single, unified essence.</summary>

# ## FAMOUS OPINIONS ##

<page-num>673</page-num>
<header>### FAMOUS OPINIONS ###</header>

...just as the substance <term>substance: the fundamental "being" or essence of a thing</term> of fire is one and the same, from which the power and activity of burning, drying, and illuminating proceed; so either the power of the soul is another kind, or the soul is divisible, and each of these activities occurs according to a different part of it. Aristotle says this, not because he is satisfied with the doctrine, but because he is bringing a charge against Timaeus <note>Timaeus is the main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the soul</note> for dividing the soul according to the parts of the body. For Aristotle himself does not wish for the soul to be one single substance, but rather for it to be composed of different substances; yet these are united and continuous with one another in such a way that they share a single "sympathy" <note>original: συμπάθειαν (*sympatheian*), meaning a shared feeling or interconnectedness</note>. For something passes from reason into the passions, and from the passions back into reason. For when it is necessary for the passions to be subordinate and yield to reason, this command reaches them from above, from the mental grasp of reason. Conversely, when reason is hindered in its own proper activities, this occurs because of its relationship to the passions. Thus, the soul is one substance in the same way that we say a whole human being <insert>is</insert> one.

<column-break/>

Just as the substance of fire is one and the same, from which the force and action of burning, drying, and illuminating flow; so too is there either another power of the soul, or the soul can be divided, and any of these operations occurs according to different parts of it. Aristotle says this further, in no way agreeing with that doctrine, but rather rebuking Timaeus, who divided the soul according to the parts of the body. For he himself does not want the soul’s substance to be one, but rather that it be composed of different substances—yet these are joined together and so coherent that their "affection" <note>original: *affectio*, here meaning the way they are influenced or moved together</note> is one. Indeed, something passes from reason into those passions <note>original: *affectiones* / *perturbationibus*</note>, and from them into reason. For sometimes it happens that the disturbances are subjected to and obey reason because of reason’s understanding; at other times, it happens that reason is hindered in its works due to its habit and connection with these disturbances. Thus, the soul is one substance, just as we say the whole man is of one substan-

the body, insofar as it is an

...to lead to the measure which, when animals and plants have reached it, they arrive at the most excellent end of nature, that is, at the power of reproduction <note>original Latin: *generandi potestatem*</note>. For this is the ultimate and most perfect goal of nature, because of the desire for eternity and immortality in generated living things, which is attained through succession <note>since individual living things die, they achieve "immortality" as a species by having offspring</note>. Thus, the power of growth <note>augmentative power</note> serves as the material for the power of reproduction, and the power of nutrition serves as the material for the power of growth.

According to the mind of Aristotle, the intellect <note>original Latin: *mens*</note> can be called the entelechy <term>entelechy: a term from Aristotle meaning the full realization or functional "perfection" of a thing</term> of the body; and therefore it cannot be separated from it—not in its substance, nor in all its actions, but only in those which it possesses through its disposition and relationship to the body. The most significant of these are the active functions; these actions, however, cannot be separated from the body. For as soon as the body is destroyed, those actions of the intellect which it possessed through its union with the body also perish. It is just like a pilot <note>original Latin: *gubernator*</note>, who is the movement of the ship; because he is not only a pilot, but also a man—

<column-break/>

...to lead to the midpoint, which when animals and plants have reached it, they arrive at the most purposeful end of nature—I mean the reproductive power <note>original Greek: *γεννητικὴν δύναμιν*</note>. For this is the most final goal of nature, because of the longing for eternity and immortality in generated living things, which is provided for by the occurrence of succession. Thus, the power of growth holds the place of matter for the reproductive power; and for the power of growth, the nutritive power.

The intellect <note>original Greek: *νοῦς*</note>, according to Aristotle, could be said to be the entelechy of the body in potential, and in this respect, it is inseparable from the body—not in its essence, nor in all its activities, but in those which it has from its relationship to the body, of which the practical ones are the most prominent. These activities are inseparable from the body. For simultaneously with the destruction of the body, such activities of the intellect as it possessed from its relationship to the body are destroyed as well. And just like a pilot <note>original Greek: *κυβερνήτης*</note>, who is the entelechy of the ship, since indeed he is not only a pilot, but also a man—

But since the soul also possesses certain actions that are separable from the body—I mean those regarding things understood by the mind <note>original Greek: *νοητῶν* (noēton), objects of pure thought</note>, in which the body not only fails to contribute, but actually acts as a hindrance—it is manifest that the mind <note>original Greek: *νοῦς* (nous)</note> also possesses a separable substance. When it exists in this state, it is called "mind," and is no longer called "soul" except potentially. He says that animals share in the nutritive and sensitive powers; and because of the sensitive power, they also share in the appetitive power. He establishes that wherever there is even a single sense, there must necessarily be desire and appetite <note>original Greek: *ὄρεξιν* (orexin)</note>. For this reason, all animals possess sensation; for in all of them there is certainly the sense of touch, even if no other sense is present. Sensation perceives both the pleasant and the painful. And where there is pleasure, there is certainly also desire and appetite. For—

So also our mind, which is the motion of the soul, cannot be without the body in this way. But because it has some actions separable from the body—I mean concerning intelligible things, to which the body does not contribute but even hinders them—it is clear that the substance of the mind will be separable. It is then both "mind" and is called "mind," but it is not "soul" except by potential: just as when it is in the body, it is not "mind" only by potential.

Animals, he says, have the power of nourishing and sensing, and through the power of sensing, also of desiring. This he proves thus: because where even one sense exists, there must be craving and appetite. <page-num>678</page-num>
<header>ON THE SOUL</header>

—desire <note>original: "cupiditas"; completing the word from the previous page</note> is the appetite for what is pleasant. Even those animals that possess only the sense of touch are seen to expand themselves if pleasant things approach, and conversely to contract if something painful draws near. He defines "appetite" <note>original Latin: *appetentia*; Greek: *orexis*</note> through three things: desire, anger <note>original: *ira*; often translated as "spirit" or "passion"</note>, and will. For any of these is a form of appetite. It appears that simple appetite exists entirely within the instrument of sensation. However, not every kind of appetite exists in every sense. For in those animals that have only the sense of touch, appetite exists according to desire. But in those endowed with all the senses, there is also a propensity for anger. For these latter animals appear equipped for seeking vengeance <note>the author links the higher senses to the ability to react defensively or aggressively</note>. Yet will <note>original: *voluntas*</note> belongs to reason alone; thus, the term "appetite" is used equivocally <note>meaning the word has different meanings depending on the context</note>, as is "desire" in a general sense. Appetite is likewise spoken of regarding anger, concupiscence <note>bodily longing</note>, and reason; for we are said to "appetite" after divine things and even after knowledge. But in a more proper and strict sense, "appetite" is used for natural motions that are opposed to reason. Likewise, one kind of desire is common, while another is opposed to the spirited part of the soul and to reason.

<column-break/>

—desire <note>original Greek: *epithymia*</note> is a reaching for the pleasant. Hence, even those creatures participating only in touch are seen to be diffused <note>expanding or relaxing</note> when pleasant things approach, but they shrink back when something painful draws near. He defines appetite <note>original: *orexis*</note> by desire, spirit <note>original: *thymos*</note>, and will <note>original: *boulesis*</note>. For each of these is a certain kind of appetite. It is clear that simple appetite appears to belong simply to the sensitive faculty. However, not every appetite belongs to every sensitive being. For in those having touch alone, appetite exists according to desire. But in those with all the senses, it also exists according to spirit. For such animals are seen to be capable of self-defense. But will belongs to the rational faculty alone. Thus, the term appetite is used equivocally, and desire likewise. For appetite is spoken of generally in relation to spirit, desire, and reason. Indeed, we say we "appetite" for divine things, and we "appetite" for knowledge. But there is also a more specifically named "appetite" used for natural movements, which is distinguished in opposition to reason. And desire is the same: one kind is general, while the other is distinguished in opposition to spirit and reason.

<page-num>679</page-num>
->### FAMOUS DOCTRINES.<-

<meta>The text is presented in two columns: the left is translated from the original Greek and the right from the parallel Latin translation. Both discuss the same philosophical argument regarding the nature of light.</meta>

**That they do not call light a body.**
Since some say that light is a **body** <note>In ancient physics, a "body" refers to a three-dimensional physical substance that occupies space.</note>, they say that a certain sphere of light proceeds from the sun. Since the sun is spherical, and the air is also spherical, it is absolutely necessary for the sphere of light, in traveling toward us, either to push the sphere of air aside and thus, by occupying its place, illuminate the space around us. If it occupies the place, the illuminated hemisphere will be a **vacuum** <note>original Greek: κενόν; meaning a void or space empty of matter</note> of air, which is impossible. But if it does not push the air, it also does not illuminate, as it would not arrive to us. But if it should pass through the air, it will be a body having passed through another body, which is an impossibility. But if some should say that one body can pass through another body, the argument is especially impossible. For in this way, the **heaven** could be said to be contained in a **millet seed** <note>original Greek: κέγχρῳ; a common ancient analogy for something infinitesimally small</note>. Furthermore, if light can pass through a body because it is **immaterial** <note>original: ἄϋλον; literally "without matter"</note>, it would have passed not only through air, but through any other thing whatsoever. For what would be the logical restriction that an immaterial body, passing through a body, would not pass through every body?

<column-break/>

**They do not call light a body:**
Because some say light is a body, they assert that a certain sphere of light arises from the sun. Since indeed both the sun is round and also the air, it is entirely necessary that the sphere of light which comes to us either expels the sphere of air; and thus, having occupied its place, it illuminates the place surrounding us. If it occupies it, the half-sphere which is illuminated will be **empty** <note>original Latin: vacua</note> of air, which is absurd; but if it does not expel the air, it likewise does not illuminate, as it is not about to reach us. But if it will penetrate the air, a body will be penetrated by another body, which cannot happen. But if some will say that a body can be penetrated by a body, that is certainly most absurd. For thus the heaven could be contained in a **grain of millet** <note>original Latin: milij grano</note>. Then, if because light is **devoid of matter** <note>original Latin: materiæ sit expers</note> it can penetrate a body, it would have penetrated not only air, but any other body whatever: for what would that condition be, that an immaterial body should penetrate a body, and yet not every body?

<note>This argument relies on the Aristotelian principle that two physical bodies cannot occupy the same space simultaneously. If light were a "body," it would have to either displace the air (creating a vacuum) or coexist in the same space as the air (which was considered logically impossible).</note>

<summary>This page presents a logical refutation of the theory that light is a material substance or "body." It argues that if light were physical, it would either create a vacuum by displacing air or perform the impossible feat of occupying the same space as another substance.</summary>
<keywords>light, body, physics, vacuum, immateriality, Aristotelian logic, optics, sphere, millet seed analogy</keywords>

Therefore, it would be necessary
for light to penetrate solid

<column-break/>

Thus it would be necessary for
light to pass even through solid
bodies; I mean through the earth,
and similar things. Why then,
when the sun is under the earth,
do we not see it above the earth,
since light would be passing
through the earth? Furthermore,
if light, being a body, passes
through the body of the air,
it would follow that the whole
becomes more compact and thicker.
But now the opposite is true.
For the air becomes thinner <note>original Greek: λεπτομερέστερος (*leptomeresteros*); referring to a substance with smaller or more widely spaced parts</note>
when it is illuminated, just as if
water were to pass into earth;
and the space occupied by both
becomes greater. It is absolutely
necessary for the body made from
both to become thicker. In this
way, it would be necessary for
the air also to become thicker
when light is present; but now
the opposite occurs, as it
becomes thinner.

-> THE END. <-

<meta>catchword: IN</meta>

<summary>This page concludes a philosophical proof that light cannot be a physical "body." The author argues that if light were material, it would pass through the earth (making the sun visible at night) and increase the air's density, whereas observation shows illuminated air actually becomes thinner.</summary>

# ON THE PHILOCALIA
# OF ORIGEN

## NOTES BY JEAN TARIN.

In these matters, which we briefly note here, Friendly Reader, brevity itself will sufficiently excuse me; for besides the variety of readings and several errors that are corrected here, there seemed no reason at all to insert myself into your studies, especially with the presses rushing and the daily diligence of my laborious duty demanding their daily task from me. If I seem to have kept to this limit less than I should, I would wish you to be persuaded that it is a matter of necessity rather than will. For what I had chiefly undertaken was to compare the Royal manuscript—provided by the most learned man Nicolas Rigault <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654) was a French classical scholar and librarian of the King’s Library.</note>, who guards that most exquisite treasury of books with equal faithfulness and authority—with the books published *Against Celsus*, and likewise with two other manuscripts. These were brought forth by Pierre Dupuy, a man of singular kindness and elegant learning, from the most select library of the late <term>of blessed memory</term> <note>original Greek: τῷ μακαρίτῃ (*tō makaritē*)</note> great hero Jacques Auguste de Thou <note>A famous French statesman and book collector.</note>. I have done this as accurately as I could, and I have made a selection upon which I would prefer you to judge after knowing these facts. Effort also had to be given at times to comparing passages of Scripture. I have not been afraid to touch upon the interpretation of Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia, known for translating Greek Church fathers into Latin, often with significant alterations.</note>—if indeed he is a translator and not an <term>independent</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτόνομος (*autonomos*)</note> writer—nor the interpretations of others when I encountered them. Why should I constantly point out how far he deviates from Origen, since I have always thought that in writing one should seek appropriateness rather than abundance? Truly, I should least of all allow these notes, however small they are, to grow by criticizing the industry of others.

<margin>Origen.</margin>
In both of de Thou's manuscripts, the name is constantly written as Origen <note>original Greek: Ωριγενης (*Ōrigenēs*)</note>. And immediately after the index of chapters, there is prefixed: "Origen: Preliminary Observation. Of Selections," etc. Perhaps to someone he will be called <term>Born at the right time</term> <note>original Greek: ὡριγενὴς (*ōrigenēs*), suggesting a pun on the Greek word for "seasonable" or "timely."</note>, as if "timely" or "born in season." Jerome more justly, in my opinion, gives him the fourth name of "Chalcenterus" <note>original Latin: *Chalcenteri*; a nickname meaning "brazen-guts," applied to scholars with tireless industry.</note> than his own age gave to Didymus, who had written three thousand five hundred books; for they commonly attribute six thousand to Origen, and Epiphanius does not disagree.

<margin>Philocalia.</margin>
And Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> in his letters calls Origen a <term>lover of beauty</term> <note>original Greek: φιλόκαλον (*philokalon*)</note>. So says Photius. This title, however, belongs no more to Origen than to Basil and Gregory, the <term>greatest lovers of beauty</term> <note>original Greek: φιλοκαλωτάτων (*philokalōtatōn*)</note>.

<summary>Jean Tarin introduces his critical notes on Origen's Philocalia, identifying the prestigious manuscript sources he used and explaining his editorial philosophy of brevity and restraint. He also discusses the etymology and nicknames associated with Origen, and the origin of the title "Philocalia" (Love of Beauty).</summary>

# ON THE WORKS OF ORIGEN

I would say it is. You see the use of this word among the Latins in the time of Augustine in the second book of *Against the Academics* and Chapter 1 of the *Retractations* <note>original: *Retractationum*</note>. What the *Philocalia* <note>A title meaning "Love of the Beautiful," used for an anthology of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen.</note> represents here is demonstrated by Gregory’s letter, which is numbered 87. In that letter, one should read <unclear>k.</unclear> where, instead of our current reading, "the greater things, which we might have, let us give in return," that hindered version was "of which we have the greater, let us give in return." And where it is read here, "may you have that of its own," there it is "may you have that itself." Here it says "useful things" <note>original Greek: χρησίμοις (*chrēsimois*)</note>, while there it says "of the useful things" <note>original Greek: τῶν χρησίμων (*tōn chrēsimōn*)</note>.

**Page 2, verse 24. Philosophers.** Both of the De Thou manuscripts read "to practice philosophy" <note>original Greek: φιλοσοφεῖν (*philosophein*)</note>; this is correct. Furthermore, Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), known for his Latin translations of Origen which often took liberties with the text.</note> distorted this entire preface and, as is his habit, went off into something else entirely. These remarks of Origen are taken from his teacher Clement at the end of the 6th book of the *Stromata*.

**Verse 29. to implant.** Rufinus uses "to grow in" <note>original Latin: *inolescere*</note>. Aulus Gellius uses it similarly in book 12.

**Page 3, verse 18. those considered.** Rufinus has "those whom they thought were gods." This is clear enough; but that Greek word <note>original: νομιζομένοις (*nomizomenois*)</note> actually implies something even more significant.

**Verse 26. for the [purpose of],** perhaps instead "at the [thing]."

**Verse 27. of the words,** restore "the word" <note>original Greek: τὸν λόγον (*ton logon*), referring to the Logos or a specific argument</note>.

**Page 4, verse 12.** I read this as "more justly" <note>original Greek: δικαιότερον (*dikaioteron*)</note>.

**Verse 17. such as that,** for example in the De Thou manuscript. "Such a thing" <note>original Greek: οἷόν τι (*oion ti*)</note> is an error. The common edition reads: "you shall be brought before governors and kings."

**Verse 26. to have said.** Rufinus substituted his own ideas here.

**Page 5, verse 10.** Common edition: "or that their offspring." This is found in both the Greek and Latin Church Fathers.

**Verse 17.** The word "for" <note>original Greek: γὰρ (*gar*)</note> is redundant.

**Page 6, verse 1. in the,** and so forth. Rufinus did not touch this part.

**Verse 2. from,** perhaps it should be "by."

**Verse 4. governors.** The Jews call such men "Heads of the Exile" <note>original Hebrew: ראשׁים הגלה (*Reshim HaGolah*), referring to the Exilarchs who led Jewish communities in Babylon</note> or princes of the exiles. Rufinus added many things to this, being eager—as he says himself—for the sake of explanation.

**Page 7, verse 8.** The article "the" <note>original Greek: ἡ (*hē*)</note> is missing in the common edition.

**Page 8, verse 26. virgin.** Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion <note>Three 2nd-century translators of the Old Testament into Greek</note> had corrupted "virgin" <note>original: παρθένον (*parthenon*)</note> into "young woman" <note>original: νεᾶνις (*neanis*)</note>.

**Page 9, verse 5. having been captured.** Rufinus adds this from his own mind, I believe, as if we exist as some spoils of his victory.

**Verse 21. for the wronged.** Rufinus translates "nothing for those to be harmed by him," a way of speaking familiar to that century.

**Page 10, verse 21. to confirm,** read instead "to have completed."

**Verse 25. clear.** Rufinus inserts many things here.

**Page 11, verse 8.** Rufinus wanders very far afield into his own thoughts, I think, and not Origen’s; hereafter, I shall sail past them so that I do not always run aground on these rocks.

**Page 12, verse 9. concerning <unclear>k.</unclear>** I would read it, if permitted, as "the rational principle of the craftsmanship of a provident God"; I could not translate it more correctly. Rufinus has: *“since the reason is hidden from them, through which all things are dispensed by a certain ineffable art.”*

**Page 13, verse 4. treasure in.** Both De Thou manuscripts read "treasure of."

**Page 14, verse 5. the [destruction].** The common edition has "of those being destroyed," and likewise below on page 21. But Origen referred this to "wisdom."

### NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA

**page 15, verse 15. after the.** This is the beginning of chapter 2 in Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), who translated Origen's works from Greek into Latin, often adapting the text freely.</note>.
**P. 15. v. 13.** read "to rest together" <note>original Greek: συναναπαύσασθαι (*synanapausasthai*)</note>.
**v. 27. [from] the heresies.** These are the Marcionists <note>Followers of Marcion, an early Christian leader who taught that the God of the Old Testament was different from the God of the New Testament</note>. See Origen in various places, as well as Tertullian, Epiphanius, Augustine, etc.
**P. 16. v. 2.** add, "and a fourth."
**P. 17. v. 23. uncreated** <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητος (*agennētos*)</note> or "increatus." Rufinus reads: "who is the God of all." I read: "that they were described by the will of God the Father of all things, through Jesus Christ."
**P. 18. v. 10. mysteries** <note>original Greek: μυστήρια (*mystēria*)</note> translated as "sacraments" <note>original Latin: *sacramenta*</note> by Rufinus; and in that era, everyone [did so].
**P. 19. v. 15.** these are held separately. **v. 16. 12. & 13.**
**v. 25. mystery** <note>original Greek: μυστήριον (*mystērion*)</note> of the sacraments. Hence Jerome, writing to Paulinus, says: "The Apocalypse of John has as many sacraments <note>In this context, 'sacraments' refers to sacred mysteries or hidden meanings</note> as it has words," etc.
**P. 20. v. 13. someone** <note>original Greek: τις (*tis*)</note>; I would read "type" <note>original Greek: τύπος (*typos*)</note> or "but someone."
**v. 29. to have received back** <note>original Greek: ἀπειληφέναι (*apeilēphenai*)</note>; read, if you prefer, "detected" <note>original Latin: *deprehensa*</note>.
**P. 21. write down.** The common edition reads: "you to them?" and "into counsel [and intent] and knowledge."
**v. 8. to you.** The common edition reads "you" (as an object).
**v. 20.** insert if you please, "nor of the rulers," and so forth.
**last verse. for just as.** See Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 9. Clement, in the 6th book of the *Stromata* <note>Clement of Alexandria's 'Miscellanies'</note>, calls the words and the names "the body of the scriptures" <note>original Greek: τὸ σῶμα τῶν γραφῶν (*to sōma tōn graphōn*)</note>.
**P. 22. v. 5. let us be looked down upon.** And not without cause, if that [text] was the one we have.
**v. 11. we describe.** Origen had written commentaries on *The Shepherd* <note>A popular early Christian work by Hermas</note>. See book 1, chapter 2.
**v. 21. to all the souls.** Rufinus reads: "childlike souls," which he also calls "orphaned": clearly!
**v. 29. bridal chamber.** Rufinus reads "heavenly." Perhaps "heaven" <note>original Greek: οὐρανός (*ouranos*)</note> should be added.
**P. 23. he might say.** Rufinus reads: "if he were to say." He was reading "on the one hand he might say." He changed this sentence.
**v. 18. for purification** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ καθαρισμόν (*epi καθαρισμόν*)</note>; the common edition reads "and the drinking vessel" <note>original Greek: κὶ τὸν κώθωνα (*kai ton kōthōna*)</note>. Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and bishop</note> points out this custom more than others in Letter 121: "lustral water from the city will be hung in sprinkling vessels." I omit the profane rite.
**P. 24. v. 16. the muzzler.** Rufinus translates "you shall not muzzle" <note>original Latin: *non infrenabis*</note>; correctly.
**P. 25. v. 20. and.** The common edition reads: "not spiritually" and instead of "having been bitten," "having been taught." **v. 25.**
**P. 26. v. 10. you have become.** The common edition reads "you have been."
**v. 12. The De Thou manuscripts** read: "to touch them; for two testaments are proclaimed." This is faulty.
**v. 21. but** is missing in both.
**v. 24. us, you.** And after "let him judge," both [manuscripts read]: "or in food."
**P. 27. v. 2. by examples.** Rufinus and the common edition read: "by an example." Hebrews 8.
**v. 9. and that (feminine).** The other De Thou manuscript reads "and that (neuter)." Another reads "and those things."
**P. 28. v. 7. of the mind.** You may understand this as "of the senses."
**v. 28. into the words, etc.** That is, to be recalled to the logic of divine doctrine.
**P. 30. v. 5. of the scripture.** As in the De Thou manuscript, "of the scripture," which is not out of place, and Rufinus reads "of the legal scripture."
**v. 22. to shut in.** As in the De Thou manuscript, "to shut in good things."
**P. 31. v. 18. not.** The De Thou manuscript reads "which." And at **v. 23**, with the help of both, I restored "more" <note>original Greek: πλείους (*pleious*)</note> from "more."
**v. 24. the proportion.** It will be rendered more clearly as: "the same is to be understood regarding the law."

# 684 NOTES ON ORIGEN

...that a great understanding must be sought from God.
**verse 10.** **near to.** <note>original Greek: πρὸς τῆς (*pros tēs*)</note>. Rufinus reads "until the advent" <note>original Latin: *usque ad aduentum*</note>; he was likely reading "near the presence" <note>original Greek: πρὸς τῇ παρουσίᾳ (*pros tē parousia*)</note>. Either reading is correct.
**v. 16.** **of types** <note>original Greek: τύπων (*typōn*)</note>, etc. Here and in what follows, I rely on the faithfulness of the Manuscripts.
**Page 33. v. 2.** **to have existed before. Just like a root.** <note>original Greek: προυπικέναι. ὥσπερ ῥίζα (*proupikenai. hōsper rhiza*)</note> However, the greatest Theologians <note>A reference to Saints Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus, who compiled the *Philocalia* from Origen's works</note> selected these passages.
**v. 13.** Alternative De Thou manuscript: **under the wood.** <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ τὰ ξύλα (*hypo ta xyla*)</note>
**v. 21.** **to seek the face.** <note>original Greek: ζητεῖν πρόσωπον (*zētein prosōpon*)</note> Read: "the face." And soon after, **in the.** <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ (*en tō*)</note> Read: "in the [feminine]." <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ (*en tē*)</note>
**P. 34. v. 10.** **height having been soaked.** <note>original Greek: δευθέντι ὕψος (*deuthenti hypsos*)</note> Examine this.
**v. 19.** **to be woven together.** <note>original Greek: συνυδαίνεσθαι (*synydainesthai*)</note> Perhaps a small word is missing.
**P. 35. v. 9.** **be traversed.** <note>original Greek: περιοδευθῇ (*periodeuthē*)</note> See if it suits your stomach—what Rufinus devises—that parents should be ordered to be punished if they did not circumcise their sons, as well as those who nourish little ones. Who could bear it?
**v. 11.** The common edition has it thus: **In an uncircumcised male, whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised, that soul shall be destroyed from its race.** <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀπεριτμήτῳ ἄρσενι, ὃ οὐ περιτμηθήσεται τὴν σάρκα τῆς ἀκροβυστίας αὐτοῦ, ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἡ ψυχὴ ἐκείνη ἐκ τοῦ γένους αὐτῆς. This is a Greek rendering of Genesis 17:14</note>
**v. 19.** **to be offered.** <note>original Greek: προσφέρεσθαι (*prospheresthai*)</note> Rufinus reads: "to be worshipped." I read: "to offer."
**v. 21.** **of men.** <note>original Greek: ἀνθρώπων (*anthrōpōn*)</note> As in De Thou: **to a man.** <note>original Greek: ἀνθρώπῳ (*anthrōpō*)</note>
**v. 23.** **few—these.** <note>original Greek: ὀλιγ- οὗτοι (*olig- houtoi*)</note> Rufinus uses a most opinionated observation.
**v. 25.** **to sit.** <note>original Greek: καθῆσθαι (*kathēsthai*)</note> Common edition: **to sit yet by himself.** <note>original Greek: καθῆσθαι ἔτ. παρ' ἑαυτῷ (*kathēsthai et. par' heautō*)</note>
**P. 36. v. 8.** **false.** <note>original Greek: ψευδής (*pseudēs*)</note> Rufinus calls this a "grypho" <note>From the Greek *griphos*, meaning a riddle or enigma</note>. This concerns Dositheus the Samaritan, who falsely claimed to be the Christ; see Origen's 27th commentary on Matthew, Irenaeus Book 1, and Epiphanius, Jerome against Lucifer, and Philastrius’s Catalog.
**v. 23.** **saying.** <note>original Greek: λέγοντες (*legontes*)</note> Common edition and De Thou: **affirming.** <note>original Greek: φάσκοντες (*phaskontes*)</note>
**P. 37. v. 5.** Rufinus interjects about "two tunics," as well as in the following lines, regarding the "struck cheek."
**v. 20. [Greek initials]** Rufinus adds: "or who will be held free from the greatest crime who lays hands upon himself?" <note>A reference to the moral status of suicide</note> He skips over the rest.
**P. 38. v. 10.** **the [neuter]** read **the [dative].** Alternative De Thou: **by being on the surface.** <note>original Greek: τῷ ἐπιπολάζειν (*tō epipolazein*)</note> Indeed, Rufinus thinks this is impossible in every sense, as does Jerome in Book 1 against Jovinian and on Isaiah chapter 52. But this is not the case for one who knows the term and custom of "re-skinning" <note>original Latin: *recutiendi*, referring to epispasm, a medical procedure to undo circumcision</note>, as seen in Cornelius Celsus Book 7, chapter 25; 1 Maccabees 1; and Josephus Book 12, chapter 6 regarding the Jews: **they covered over the circumcision of their private parts so as to be Greeks in their outward appearance.** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τὴν αἰδοίων περιτομὴν ἐπεκάλυψαν ὡς εἶναι τὰ περὶ τὴν ἀπόδοσιν Ἕλληνες</note> Epiphanius, in *On Weights and Measures*, names the **spathistherem** <note>original Greek: σπαθιστήρ (*spathistēr*), a surgical tool</note> as the instrument for recalling the **foreskin.** <note>original Greek: ἀκροβυστίας (*akrobystias*)</note> Theophylact.
**P. 40. v. 10.** **of those despairing.** <note>original Greek: ἀπονούντων (*aponountōn*)</note> Common edition: **one despairing.** <note>original Greek: ἀπονῶν (*aponōn*)</note>
**P. 42. v. 23.** **it might obtain by lot.** <note>original Greek: ἐπιλάχοι (*epilachoi*)</note> These are missing in Rufinus, as are those at **page 45, verse 8**: **but if [they are] mutilated,** <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ πεπηρωμένα (*ei de pepērōmena*)</note> which are also read in a distorted manner.
**P. 44. v. 28.** **it has been thickened.** <note>original Greek: ἐπιπέπυκται (*epipepyktai*)</note> Alternative De Thou: **it has been enjoined/spread.** <note>original Greek: ἐπιπέτακται (*epipetaktai*)</note>
**P. 46. v. 2.** **fixed things.** <note>original Greek: πεπηγότα (*pēpēgota*)</note> Common edition: **from which.** <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐ (*ex ou*)</note>
**P. 47. v. 11.** **to suit.** <note>original Greek: ἁρμόζειν (*harmozein*)</note> As in De Thou: **it suits.** <note>original Greek: ἁρμόζει (*harmozei*)</note>
**v. 18.** **is able.** <note>original Greek: δυνάται (*dynatai*)</note> As in: **ruler/mighty one.** <note>original Greek: δυνάστη (*dynastē*)</note>
**P. 48. v. 9.** The Theologians, being **lovers of beauty** <note>original Greek: φιλοκαλοῦντες (*philokalountes*), a play on the title of the book, *Philocalia*</note>, passed over a few things here.
**v. 10.** **into Hades.** <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸν ᾅδην (*eis ton hadēn*)</note> Here he treats Origen humanely and cautiously.
**P. 50. v. 6.** **to the multitude.** <note>original Greek: τῷ πλήθει (*tō plēthei*)</note> As in De Thou: **the multitudes.** <note>original Greek: τὰ πλήθη (*ta plēthē*)</note>

### 685 NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA.

**Page 51. verse 8.** Alternate: **to suggest/subject** <note>original Greek: ὑποβάλλειν (*hypoballein*)</note>. Alternate: **to suggest/subject** <note>original Greek: ὑποβαλεῖν (*hypobalein*)</note>. Royal Codex: **should suggest** <note>original Greek: ὑποβαλῇ (*hypobalē*)</note>.

**P. 53. v. 7.** For "that" <note>original Latin: *quòd*</note>, read "with" <note>original Latin: *cum*</note>.
**P. 54. v. 6.** **from the.** etc. <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς (*apo tēs*)</note> You will not find these in the common Homilies on Leviticus, from which it appears, from so great a shipwreck of literature, how many mangled fragments we retain.
**v. 23.** **having understood** <note>original Greek: νοήσαντες (*noēsantes*)</note>; read as in the De Thou manuscript: **having supposed** <note>original Greek: νομίσαντες (*nomisantes*)</note>.
**v. 27.** **those from [the sect]**; these are the **unsubmissive** <note>original Greek: ἀνυπότακτοι (*anypotaktoi*)</note>, so called because of their **rebellion against the Creator** <note>original Greek: ἀπόταξιν τὴν πρὸς τὸν δημιουργὸν (*apotaxin tēn pros ton dēmiourgon*)</note>: of whom the giant Marcion, the fighter against God <note>original Greek: θεομάχος (*theomachos*)</note>, was the leader. See *Stromata* <note>A work by Clement of Alexandria, often called the *Stromateis* or "Miscellanies"</note>, book 3.
**P. 56. v. 14.** **from the.** etc. <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ (*apo tou*)</note> Neither does this book exist [any longer], but Epiphanius reports these things up to page 59 in his work *On Heresies*, section 64.
**v. last.** **in the angel** <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ ἀγγέλῳ (*en tō angelō*)</note>. This and the following passage are read variously in the Complutensian, Royal, and common editions.
**P. 57. v. 20.** **to see him** <note>original Greek: βλέπειν αὐτὸν (*blepein auton*)</note>; read as in the De Thou manuscript: **to befit him** <note>original Greek: πρέπειν αὐτὸν (*prepein auton*)</note>.
**P. 58. v. 8.** **farewell** <note>original Greek: ἔρῥωσο (*errhōso*)</note>. Common edition: **Save** <note>original Greek: Sῶ (*Sō*), likely an abbreviation for *Sōson*</note>.
**v. 14.** **confessedly/by agreement** <note>original Greek: ὁμολογουμένως (*homologoumenōs*)</note>; read as in the De Thou manuscript: **to those agreed upon** <note>original Greek: ὁμολογουμένοις (*homologoumenois*)</note>.
**v. 23.** For "not to be grasped" <note>original Latin: *capi non*</note>, read: "scarcely to be perceived" <note>original Latin: *percipi vix*</note>.
**P. 59. v. 4.** **under the** etc. <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ τῷ (*hypo tō*)</note> See Hilary in the prologue to his *Explanation of the Psalms*, who either received it from some Hebrew or transferred it from this passage of Origen.
**v. 12.** **obscurity** <note>original Greek: ἀσάφειαν (*asapheian*)</note>. The Royal Codex had **certainty/safety** <note>original Greek: ἀσφάλειαν (*asphaleian*)</note>.
**v. 12. (second entry).** **to be exhorted/comforted** <note>original Greek: παρακαλεῖσθαι (*parakaleisthai*)</note>; read as in the De Thou manuscript: **to have been exhorted/comforted** <note>original Greek: παρακεκλῆσθαι (*parakeklēsthai*)</note>.
**P. 60. v. 19.** I have restored **he said** <note>original Greek: ἔφη (*ephē*)</note> from the De Thou manuscript.
**P. 61. v. 3.** We have made **a certain peculiarity** <note>original Greek: ἰδιωμά τι (*idiōma ti*)</note> from **peculiarity** <note>original Greek: ἰδιώματι (*idiōmati*)</note>; the De Thou manuscript has **peculiarities** <note>original Greek: ἰδιώματα (*idiōmata*)</note>.
**P. 62. v. 2.** **of the whole** <note>original Greek: τῶν ὅλων (*tōn holōn*)</note>; read, for example, **of the saints** <note>original Greek: ἁγίων (*hagiōn*)</note>.
**v. 20.** **to whom** <note>original Greek: ᾧ (*hō*)</note>; read **whom** <note>original Greek: ὅν (*hon*)</note>.
**P. 63. v. 13.** **and not** etc. <note>original Greek: οὐκ τε (*ouk te*)</note> Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> says: "Explaining the first Psalm, he makes an exposition of the sacred scriptures of the catalog of the Old Testament, saying word for word as follows: 'It must not be ignored that the canonical books <note>original Greek: ἐνδιαθήκους βίβλους (*endiathēkous biblous*)</note>, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, which is the number of the letters among them.'" But for **canonical**, the De Thou manuscript in verse 14 has **in the testament** <note>original Greek: ἐν διαθήκῃ (*en diathēkē*)</note>.
**v. last.** **they are** <note>original Greek: εἰσὶ (*eisi*)</note>; read **it is** <note>original Greek: ἐστὶν (*estin*)</note>.
**P. 64. v. 13.** We require these words.
**P. 65. v. 1.** These things were read continuously. **gospel** <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελίῳ (*euangeliō*)</note>; De Thou manuscripts: **of the gospel** <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελικοῦ (*euangelikou*)</note>.
**v. 10.** **to be said** <note>original Greek: λέγεσθαι (*legesthai*)</note>; read **to say that** <note>original Greek: λέγ. ὅτι (*leg. hoti*)</note>. In verse 12, the [article] **the** <note>original Greek: ἡ (*hē*)</note> is missing in both.
**P. 66. v. 10.** **of God** <note>original Greek: θεοῦ (*theou*)</note>; read **to the** <note>original Greek: τῷ (*tō*)</note>.
**P. 67. v. 6.** This preface has been lost.
**v. 8.** **not upon** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ μὴ (*epi mē*)</note>. In the Royal Codex, it was written in the margin: "He asks for **Ambrose** <note>Origen's patron who funded his transcriptions</note>, to whom nearly all his commentaries were written as letters." See Epiphanius, Jerome's *On Illustrious Men*, and Suidas. But Photius attributes it to Hippolytus. See Jerome on Hippolytus, Eusebius book 6, and Nicephorus Callistus book 4.
**v. 10.** **he was driven out** <note>original Greek: ἐξεδιώκθη (*exediōkhthē*)</note>; a clear letter of Origen declares this.

<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s scholarly commentary on Origen's *Philocalia*. ### 686 ON ORIGEN

**Page 68, verse 21.** **my hand** <note>original Greek: χέι μου (*chei mou*)</note>. They later hurled this weapon against Origen. <note>This refers to a specific theological argument or "weapon" used by Origen's critics based on this passage.</note>
**v. 26.** **the phrase.** <note>original Greek: ἡ λέξις ἡ (*hē lexis hē*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **the phrase set before us.** <note>original Greek: ἡ προκειμένη λέξις (*hē prokeimenē lexis*)</note>
**Page 68, verse 14.** **we shall seem.** <note>original Greek: δόξομεν (*doxomen*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **we shall show.** <note>original Greek: δείξομεν (*deixomen*)</note>
**v. 25.** **to suggest.** <note>original Greek: ὑπαγορεύειν (*hypagoreuein*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **to forbid** <note>original Greek: ἀπαγορεύειν (*apagoreuein*)</note>, which is incorrect.
**Page 69, verse 1.** **of the scriptures.** <note>original Greek: τῶν γραφῶν (*tōn graphōn*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **of the scriptures.**
**Page 70, verse 11.** **it is to be talkative.** <note>original Greek: πολυλογεῖν ἐστίν (*polylogein estin*)</note>. This was missing in the Royal Codex; I have restored it from the De Thou manuscripts, from which also should be substituted: **even if one often says things that are worthy and bring salvation.** <note>original Greek: κἂν ἄξιά τις & σωτήρια λέγῃ πολλάκις (*kan axia tis kai sōtēria legē pollakis*)</note>
**v. 20.** **of a wall.** <note>original Greek: τείχου (*teichou*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **of the wall.** <note>original Greek: τοῦ τείχου (*tou teichou*)</note> See 3 Kings 4. <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 4.</note>
**Penultimate verse.** **I stretched out words.** <note>original Greek: ἐξέτεινον λόγους (*exeteinon logous*)</note>. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion read: **my hand** <note>original Greek: χεῖρά μου (*cheira mou*)</note> from the Hebrew; so also the Latin Vulgate. However, they were expressing the custom of orators commanding silence with the right hand. Thus Paul in Acts 13: **having motioned with his hand** <note>original Greek: κατασείσας τῇ χειρί (*kataseisas tē cheiri*)</note>, and also in chapters 19 and 21. See also Persius, *Satire 4*:

> My mind is moved to have brought silence to the heated crowd,
> By the majesty of the hand ———— and Caesar, according to Lucan,
> Calmed the tumult with his expression, and commanded silence with his right hand.

---

**Page 71, verse 14.** **indeed.** <note>original Greek: δή (*dē*)</note>. Read as: **but/and.** <note>original Greek: δέ (*de*)</note> In the same place, **the word**, etc. <note>original Greek: λόγος ὁ (*logos ho*)</note> It was annotated in the margin: <margin>Understand the "word of God" here not as the essential Word <note>The "Logos" or second person of the Trinity</note>, for that was indivisible God; but rather the word *about* Him, composed of various contemplations, which itself, being essentially named, is said to be "in the beginning with God" in a shared sense.</margin> This caution is certainly our own caution. <note>Tarin agrees with this marginal distinction between the eternal Word and the spoken/written word about God.</note>
**Page 74, verse 20.** **stripped.** <note>original Greek: ψιλόμενοι (*psilomenoi*)</note>. Read as: **made naked/uncovered.** <note>original Greek: γεγυμνωμένοι (*gegymnōmenoi*)</note>
**Page 78, verse 4.** **Jesus.** <note>original Greek: Ἰησοῦς (*Iēsous*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **Lord.** <note>original Greek: κύριον (*kyrion*)</note> **v. 19.** **the divine.** <note>original Greek: ἡ θ. (*hē th.*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **all the divine.** <note>original Greek: πᾶσα ἡ θεία (*pasa hē theia*)</note>
**v. 21.** **was not.** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἦν (*ouk ēn*)</note>. And we lack this one moreover.
**Page 78, verse 18.** **goads/prods.** <note>original Greek: βύκιντρα (*bykintra*)</note>. The printed editions read: **the goads.** <note>original Greek: τὰ βύκ. (*ta byk.*)</note>
**v. 19.** **fixed/fastened.** <note>original Greek: πεπυτευμένοι (*pepyteumenoi*)</note>. Thus Aquila translates from the Hebrew. The printed editions read: **ignited** <note>original Greek: πυρώμενοι (*pyromenoi*)</note>, others **having been ignited** <note>original Greek: πεπυρωμένοι (*pepyrōmenoi*)</note>, for "ignited things are more easily fixed in," as Gregory of Nazianzus observes. Theodotion reads: **fastened.** <note>original Greek: πεπηγότες (*pepēgotes*)</note>
**v. 20.** **of the compositions.** <note>original Greek: σωτημάτων (*sōtēmatōn* - likely a scribal error)</note>. Printed editions read: **of the preservations.** <note>original Greek: σωσθημ. (*sōsthem.*)</note> Others read: **of the arrangements.** <note>original Greek: συνταγμάτων (*syntagmatōn*)</note>. Gregory explains the matter in *Oration 55*: **I know that the precepts of the wise prick the soul no less than... [a goad or a nail driven in].** <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:11.</note>
**Page 80, verse 16.** **of the.** <note>original Greek: τῶν (*tōn*)</note>. Read as: **of the places.** <note>original Greek: τόπων (*topōn*)</note>
**v. 18.** **of music.** <note>original Greek: μουσικῆς (*mousikēs*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **of musicians.** <note>original Greek: μουσικῶν (*musikōn*)</note>
**v. 17. David.** Meaning "beloved," "desirable," "strong," or "capable of hand." So says Jerome on Psalm 33, and Elias of Crete on the first Oration of Gregory of Nazianzus.
**Page 81, verse 16.** **out of the.** <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν (*ek tōn*)</note>. This does not exist. **v. 30.** Where the text reads, "wherefore," read "why/how."
**Last verse.** Observe: read **let it be reserved**, and let it speak other things with her, etc.
**Page 82, verse 21.** **and again.** <note>original Greek: καὶ πάλιν (*kai palin*)</note>. Neither are the rest found here.
**Last verse.** **they are the words.** <note>original Greek: εἰσὶν οἱ λόγοι (*eisin hoi logoi*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **it is the word.** <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ὁ λόγος (*estin ho logos*)</note>
**Page 83, verse 9.** **Holy Spirit.** <note>original Greek: πν. ἅγ. (*pn. hag.*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **the Holy Spirit.** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα (*to hagion pneuma*)</note>
**Page 84, verse 3.** **of grace.** <note>original Greek: τῆς χα. (*tēs cha.*)</note>. As in the De Thou manuscript: **of divine grace.** <note>original Greek: τῆς θείας χα. (*tēs theias cha.*)</note>
**v. 8. was not.** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἦν (*ouk ēn*)</note>. These words have been lost.
**v. 26. they found.** <note>original Greek: εὗρον (*euron*)</note>. Many copies have **they found** <note>original Greek: εὗροσαν (*eurosant*)</note>. Those who distorted these things read: **he wept and pleaded with him, and in Bethel he found him.** <note>A reference to the prophet Hosea 12:4.</note>
**Page 85, verse 1. him.** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸν (*auton*)</note>. The printed editions read: **them** <note>original Greek: αὐτοῖς (*autois*)</note>, but Origen should be followed.
**v. 17. you shall eat.** <note>original Greek: φάγητε (*phagēte*)</note>. Symmachus corrupted these into: **if you eat from the tree, you shall be mortal.** <note>original Greek: φάγητε ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου, θνητὸς ἔσῃ (*phagēte apo tou xylou, thnētos esē*)</note>

<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s scholarly commentary on Origen’s *Philocalia*. Tarin continues to cross-reference Origen’s text with biblical translations (like Aquila's), classical authors (Cicero, Xenophon), and early Church Fathers (Jerome, Gregory of Nyssa), while noting discrepancies between various Greek manuscripts.</meta>

# 687 NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA.

**Page 87, verse 22.** **To the Shepherd.** <note>original Greek: Ποιμένι (*Poimeni*)</note> [From the work *The Shepherd of Hermas*], book 3, similitude 9.
**Page 88, verse 6.** **From the [book].** <note>original Greek: Ex τῆς (*Ex tēs*)</note> A significant number of the fifteen volumes Origen wrote on this Epistle of Paul were already missing from all libraries by the time of Jerome; see Jerome's preface.
**Page 89, verse 17.** **the** <note>original Greek: ὁ (*ho*)</note>. Codex C, chapter 7.
**Page 90, verse 17.** Aquila transferred Paul's words into his own interpretation; for in Isaiah [chapter 28], verse 11, [it says]: **through the mocking of lips, through another tongue.** <note>original Greek: διὰ φαυλισμὸν χειλέων, διὰ γλώσσης ἑτέρας (*dia phaulismon cheileōn, dia glōssēs heteras*)</note>
**v. penultimate.** **inscribed.** <note>original Greek: ἐγγεγραμμένος (*engegrammenos*)</note> soon after: **written in the hearts.** <note>original Greek: γραφεὶς ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις (*grapheis en tais kardiais*)</note> Derived from Plato, or rather from truth itself, as Cicero says: reason is implanted by nature, which commands those things which ought to be done, and forbids the opposite, **the things one must do, and the things one must not.** <note>original Greek: ἅτε δεῖ ποιεῖν, ἅτε μή (*hate dei poiein, hate mē*)</note> [See] Xenophon.
**Page 92, verse 28.** **itself.** <note>original Latin: *ipsa*</note> Read: **the same.** <note>original Latin: *eadem*</note>
**Page 93, verse 12.** **the [way].** <note>original Greek: ἡ ὁ. (*hē ho.*)</note> The other manuscript, the De Thou, says: **into,** <note>original Greek: εἰς (*eis*)</note> etc., in the plural number.
**Page 95, verse 6.** **From the 39th [volume].** Only 14 of these have escaped destruction to reach us.
**v. 11.** **well,** <note>original Greek: καλῶς (*kalōs*)</note> I distrust this reading.
**v. 12.** **stumbling blocks,** <note>original Greek: σκανδὰ (*skanda*)</note> **stumbling block.** <note>original Greek: σκάνδαλον (*skandalon*)</note> Well defined by the Etymologist as: **that which causes limping regarding the narrative.** <note>original Greek: τὸ σκάζον περὶ τὴν διήγησιν (*to skazon peri tēn diēgēsin*)</note> [Also]: **a cause of stumbling.** <note>original Greek: προσκόμμα (*proskomma*)</note> The ancient lexicon calls it an 'offense' <note>original Latin: *offendiculum*</note>.
**Page 96, verse 15.** **of plants.** <note>original Greek: βοτανῶν (*botanōn*)</note> There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by the power of herbs, yet the powers of most are unknown; and Herophilus says that some are perhaps beneficial even when stepped upon. [See] Pliny [Natural History] book 24, verse 27. **Botanical,** <note>original Greek: βοτανικὸς (*botanikos*)</note> [see] Dioscorides book 1.
**Page 98, verse 14.** **From the 33rd [volume].** Only 14 now survive.
**v. 16.** **I distinguish between.** <note>original Greek: διακρίνω ἀνάμεσον (*diakrinō anameson*)</note> Codex C [says]: **separately in the middle.** <note>original Greek: διακριτῶ ἀνὰ μέσον (*diakritō ana meson*)</note>
**v. 20.** **down.** <note>original Greek: κατω (*katō*)</note> Codex C [says]: **you were trampling down.** <note>original Greek: κατεπατεῖτε (*katepateite*)</note> You were treading underfoot.
**Page 100, verse 4.** **thrown away.** <note>original Greek: ῥιπτά (*ripta*)</note> I have translated this as 'rejected things' following Cato and Varro. Origen is noting the Marcionites <note>A group of early Christians labeled as heretics for rejecting the Old Testament God.</note> here. To see what the 'petulant goats' trampled upon, see Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 42.
**Page 101, verse 26.** **From the 20th [homily].** The aged Adamantius <note>A common nickname for Origen, meaning 'man of steel' or 'unbreakable'.</note> delivered these 26 short speeches extemporaneously in the Church.
**Page 102, verse 4.** **the [epistle].** <note>original Greek: ἡ ἐ. (*hē e.*)</note> Jerome makes this the beginning of chapter 12; he not only translates these things most abundantly but also explains them, as was the custom of his age.
**Page 103, verse 3.** **perceiving.** <note>original Greek: νοουν. (*nooun.*)</note> The other Codex says: **of those perceiving, so that.** <note>original Greek: νοούντων ὥστε (*noountōn hōste*)</note>
**Page 104, verse 4.** **by.** <note>original Greek: ὑπό (*hypo*)</note> As in the De Thou manuscript: **from.** <note>original Greek: ἀπό (*apo*)</note>
**v. 11.** **of incantations.** <note>original Greek: ἐπῳδῶν (*epōdōn*)</note> Jerome calls them 'pre-chantings' <note>original Latin: *praecantationes*</note>.
**Page 105, verse 11.** **the** <note>original Greek: ἡ (*hē*)</note> is missing in both manuscripts.
**Page 106, verse 9.** **the [nature] into.** <note>original Greek: ἡ εἰς (*hē eis*)</note> Do you want the meaning that the words themselves demand? *That nature which is prepared for intelligence, as you yourself know, if practice is added, can produce a work which,* etc. And when Origen saw the excellent nature of our Theodore (also known as Gregory) and his brother Athenodorus, Jerome says he exhorted them toward Philosophy. Indeed, [Gregory of] Nyssa commends his **love of learning and love of labor.** <note>original Greek: φιλομαθὲς καὶ φιλόπονον (*philomathes kai philoponon*)</note> But having pursued **education in outside wisdom,** <note>original Greek: παίδευσιν τῆς ἔξω σοφίας (*paideusin tēs exō sophias*)</note> he went to Origen—not elsewhere but in Alexandria—along with a certain Firmilian; at that time Origen was the leader of the Christian philosophy.
**v. 15.** **legal / a lawyer.** <note>original Greek: νομικὸν (*nomikon*)</note> See Gregory’s Panegyric to Origen.

<meta>This page continues Jean Tarin’s philological commentary on Origen’s works, specifically the *Philocalia* (a collection of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus). Tarin focuses here on reconciling differences between various manuscript traditions, most notably the "Thuanus" manuscript (abbreviated as Th.) and the editions produced by scholars like David Hoeschel and Sigismund Gelenius.</meta>

# 688 ON ORIGEN’S [WORKS]

**verse 20. plikōs.** <note>original: πλικῶς (*plikōs*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **plikōn.** <note>original: πλικῶν (*plikōn*)</note> Likewise, it is written for **poetically** <note>original: ποιητικῶς (*poiētikōs*)</note> and **of the poetic.** <note>original: ποιητικῶν (*poiētikōn*)</note> Both are in error. But it should be read correctly and without punctuation as: **"and poetically because of this,"** etc.

**verse 25. general studies.** <note>original: ἐγκύκλια (*enkyklia*); this refers to the "liberal arts" or preliminary education</note> This is taken from the master <note>Clement of Alexandria</note> in the first book of the *Stromata*: **"But just as general studies contribute to philosophy, which is their mistress, so philosophy herself works toward the acquisition of wisdom. For philosophy is a pursuit, but wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, and of their causes."** <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ὡς τὰ ἐγκύκλια μαθήματα συμβάλλεται πρὸς φιλοσοφίαν... (*all' hōs ta enkyklia mathēmata symballetai pros philosophian...*)</note> See also Aristotle in the third book of the *Nicomachean Ethics* and Quintilian, book 1.

**verse 26. preliminary training.** <note>original: προπαιδεύματα (*propaideumata*)</note> **"Most of the philosophers from the outside world, when visiting her, reaped the greatest benefit. For he was considered great even among them, who handed down geometry, arithmetic, and other preliminary subjects."** <note>original Greek: Πλεῖστοι δὲ τῶν ἔξωθεν φιλοσόφων... (*Pleistoi de tōn exōthen philosophōn...*)</note>

**Page 108, verse 19. airr.** Read: **kurr.** <note>likely manuscript corrections for Exodus 27</note>
**verse 22. courtyards.** <note>original: αὐλαί (*aulai*)</note> Read: **curtains.** <note>original: αὐλαῖαι (*aulaiai*)</note> [See] Exodus 26. Hesychius calls them **tents.** <note>original Latin: *tentoria*</note>
**verse 23. inside.** <note>original: ἔσω (*esō*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **more inward** and **to the more inward parts.** <note>original: ἐσωτέραν καὶ ἐσωτέραι (*esōteran kai esōterai*)</note>

**Page 109, verse 25. to say to them.** <note>original: αὐτοῖς εἰπεῖν (*autois eipein*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **to speak into them.** <note>original: αὐτοῖς ἐνειπεῖν (*autois eneipein*)</note>

**Page 110, verse 8. knowing.** <note>original: γινώσκοντες (*ginōskontes*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **having understood.** <note>original: νοήσαντες (*noēsantes*)</note>
**verse 15. Bethel,** house of God, Genesis 28.

**Page 111, verse 5. knock.** <note>original: κρούε (*kroue*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **knock.** <note>original: κροῦε (variation in accentuation)</note> **verse 16. on which.** <note>original: ἐφ' ᾗ (*eph' hē*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **upon which.** <note>original: ἐφ' ἧς (*eph' hēs*)</note> **verse 25. from you,** etc. <note>original: ἐκ σοῦ (*ek sou*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **forever and may you grow.** <note>original: ἐξ αἰεὶ καὶ αὔξοις (*ex aiei kai auxois*)</note>

**Page 112, verse 3. arriving.** <note>original: ἀφικνομένας (*aphiknomenas*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **it is arriving,** which is not bad. <note>original: ἀφικνουμένας ἔστι (*aphiknoumenas esti*)</note>
**verse 11. from the.** <note>original: ἐκ τῶ (*ek tō*)</note> Besides the homilies on Genesis, Origen had dictated thirteen tomes or volumes of continuous explanation on the first four chapters of Genesis.
**verse 14. the** <note>original: τὰς (*tas*)</note> is redundant. **verse 15.** Read: **the sacred troupe.** <note>original: τὸν θίασον (*ton thiason*)</note>
**verse 21. indeed.** <note>original: δὴ (*dē*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **but.** <note>original: δέ (*de*)</note>

**Page 113, verse 1. they say.** <note>original: φασί (*phasi*)</note> See Diogenes Laertius, book seven: **"A predicate is that which is predicated of something,"** <note>original: κατηγόρημα τὸ κατ' τινὸς κατηγορούμενον (*katēgorēma to kat' tinos katēgoroumenon*)</note> etc. Whence Suidas discusses **accusation** and **predicate.** <note>original: κατηγορίαν & κατηγόρημα (*katēgorian & katēgorēma*)</note>

**Page 114, verse 3. ne** read as **num.** <note> Latin interrogative particles</note>

**Page 115, verse 12. ordered things.** <note>original: τεταγμένα (*tetagmena*)</note> As in the Thuanus manuscript: **in an orderly fashion.** <note>original: τεταγμένως (*tetagmenōs*)</note>
**verse 26. to reconcile.** <note>original: καταλλάσσειν (*katallassein*)</note> In the Royal Codex: **to arrange.** <note>original: κατατάσσειν (*katatassein*)</note> Here the Thuanus Codices fail, in place of which the books of *Against Celsus* edited by the illustrious David Hoeschel conveniently follow.

**Page 117, verse 24. of the report.** <note>original: ἀπαγγελίας (*apangelias*)</note> In the book *Against Celsus*: **of the promise.** <note>original: ἐπαγγελίας (*epangelias*)</note>
**verse 25. of that which is under.** <note>original: τῆς ὑπὸ (*tēs hypo*)</note> [Read:] **of that which is as if from.** <note>original: τῆς ὡς ἀπὸ (*tēs hōs apo*)</note>
**verse 27. the things of guidance.** <note>original: τὰ τῆς ὁδηγίας (*ta tēs hodēgias*)</note> Hoeschel reads: **the truth.** <note>original: τὴν ἀλήθειαν (*tēn alētheian*)</note> But this is the true reading, which the manuscripts of his *Philocalia* also maintain.

**Page 118, verse 1. the same** <note>original: αὐτῆ (*autē*)</note> is missing in Hoeschel's edition of the *Philocalia*.
**verse 6. our.** <note>original: ἡμέτερον (*hēmeteron*)</note> [Read:] **ours.** <note>original: ἡμεῖον (*hēmeion*)</note> This is also used by Gelenius, although in a complicated way; but I do not yet regret my choice. Read **if**, read also **and how.** <note>original: εἰ (*ei*), καὶ πῶς (*kai pōs*)</note>
**verse 8. and** <note>original: καὶ (*kai*)</note> is missing in the published editions of *Against Celsus*, though it is found in the *Philocalia*. You will be able to better judge this **discrepancy** <note>original: διλογίαν (*dilogian*)</note> between the codices yourself after inspecting Hoeschel’s notes. **verse 17.** others read **of those perverting** <note>original: διαστρεφόντων (*diastrephontōn*)</note> incorrectly. **verse 20. indeed.** <note>original: δή (*dē*)</note> In the cited place: **but.** <note>original: δέ (*de*)</note>
**verse 25. of words.** <note>original: λέξεων (*lexeōn*)</note> [Read:] **of the word.** <note>original: λέξεως (*lexeōs*)</note> **verse 28. for pleasure.** <note>original: ἐπὶ ἡδονῇ (*epi hēdonē*)</note> [Read:] **beheld.** <note>original: ἐνεῖδον (*eneidon*)</note>

**Page 119, verse 4.** In the cited place: **they might take up.** <note>original: ἀναλάβωσιν (*analabōsin*)</note> Gelenius translates this as **they perceive**; but the *Philocalia* sides with us.

# 689 NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA

**Hoeschel, verse 19. of those perceiving.** <note>original: αἰσθανομένων (*aisthanomenōn*)</note> Hoeschel’s edition: **of those perceiving.** **verse 25. same reading: but also.** <note>original: ἀλλὰ κὴ (*alla kē*)</note> **verse 26. same reading: having said.** <note>original: εἰπόντα (*eiponta*) followed by the letter p.</note> **verse 27. persuasive** <note>original: πιθοῖς (*pithois*)</note> is the true reading over the others: others read **persuasive words of wisdom**; <note>original: πιθοῖς σοφίας λόγοις (*pithois sophias logois*)</note> others read **persuasive words of human wisdom.** <note>original: πιθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγου (*pithois anthrōpinēs sophias logou*); a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:4</note>

**Page 120, verse 3.** Regarding the *Philocalia*, Hoeschel supplemented this in the Notes. **verse 8. of wisdom,** read **of power.** <note>original: potentiæ</note> **verse 10. of the one upon...** <note>original: τῆς ἐπ' αὐτ. (*tēs ep' aut.*)</note> Hoeschel’s edition: **for those who encounter it.** <note>original: τοῖς ἐπιτυγχάνουσι (*tois epityngchanousi*)</note> **verse 15. episo...** <note>fragmentary</note> Hoeschel’s edition: **to be preserved.** <note>original: ἐπισώζεσθαι (*episōzesthai*)</note> **verse 17. same reading: and he says that the...** <note>original: φησὶ δ' ὁ (*phēsi d' ho*)</note> **verse 20. most faithful** <note>original: πεπιστόταπ (*pepistotap*); a corrupt spelling</note> same reading: **faithful.** <note>original: πιστ. (*pist.*)</note> **verse 23. same reading: grace.** <note>original: χάρις (*charis*)</note> **verse 26. same reading: the woman, the prophet in.** <note>original: γυνὴ ὁ προφήτης ἐν (*gynē ho prophētēs en*)</note> **verse 27. same reading: the seventh.** <note>original: ἡ ἑβδόμη (*hē hebdomē*)</note>

**Page 121, verse 1.** in the same reading **or** <note>original: ἢ (*ē*)</note> is missing. **verse 3. under.** <note>original: ὑπὸ (*hypo*)</note> same reading: **from.** <note>original: ἀπὸ (*apo*)</note> **verse 12. who.** <note>original: οἵ (*hoi*)</note> missing in the same reading. **verse 14. under d.** <note>original: ὑπὸ δ. (*hypo d.*)</note> same reading: **from receptors.** <note>original: ἀπὸ δοχῶν (*apo dochōn*)</note> **many.** <note>original: πολλοί (*polloi*)</note> same reading: **by much.** <note>original: πολλῷ (*pollō*)</note> Read: **many**, or, **much better.** **verse 16. same reading: having shown.** <note>original: δηλωσας (*dēlōsas*)</note> **verse 17. to understand.** <note>original: ἐπίστασθαι (*epistasthai*)</note> same reading: **to attack.** <note>original: ἐπιτίθεσθαι (*epitithesthai*)</note> Another reading: **to attack.** Both are wrong. **verse 23.** another reading: **having been made genuine** <note>original: γνησιωμένης (*gnēsiōmenēs*)</note>—badly. Commonly: **of that which is becoming.** <note>original: γινομένου (*ginomenou*)</note> See Plato’s 7th Epistle.

**Page 123, verse 7.** same reading: **and good association.** <note>original: κὴ ὁμιλίαν χρηστ. (*kē homilian chrēst.*)</note> **verse 13.** another reading: **by seeking.** <note>original: τῷ ζητεῖν (*tō zētein*)</note> same reading: **to discuss together.** <note>original: τὸ συζητ. (*to syzēt.*)</note> In Plato: **and to discuss together.** **verse 17. same reading: concerning p.** **verse 19. same reading: meddlesomeness.** <note>original: πειραγία (*peiragia*) likely meant as *periergia*</note> **verse 21. private individuals.** <note>original: ἰδιωτ. (*idiōt.*)</note> same reading: **of Jews** <note>original: Ἰουδαίων (*Ioudaiōn*)</note>—badly. See Plato in the *Phaedo*. Gelenius [reads]: **of the Greeks,** as the **hearers** <note>original: κατήκοοι (*katēkooi*); those initiated into a school or mystery</note> knew before. **verse 23.** Hoeschel’s edition: **so great things.** <note>original: τηλικαῦτα (*tēlikauta*)</note> same reading: **so great things indeed.** <note>original: τηλικαῦτά γε (*tēlikauta ge*)</note> **verse 28. same reading: to be carried indeed.** <note>original: φεροῦ τὸ γὲ (*pherou to ge*)</note> corrupted.

**Page 124, verse 7. same reading: as.** <note>original: ὡς (*hōs*)</note> **verse 14. surely l.** in the same reading. **verse 17.** Hoeschel’s edition: **to have transcended.** <note>original: ὑπερβεβηκέναι (*hyperbebēkenai*)</note> **verse 22.** same reading and Gelenius: **of those who have learned much.** <note>original: πολυμαθῶν (*polymathōn*)</note> Many [read]: **of those who love learning.** <note>original: φιλομαθῶν (*philomathōn*)</note> **verse 27. same reading: itself.** <note>original: αὐτὴν (*autēn*)</note>

**Page 125, verse 4.** same reading: **toward all things or into all.** <note>original: πρὸς πάντα ἢ εἰς π. (*pros panta ē eis p.*)</note> **verse 10.** in the same reading: **l. himself.** **verse 12.** same reading: **God,** as below in verse 19. **verse 14.** Hoeschel’s edition: **having faith.** <note>original: πίστιν ἔχων (*pistin echōn*)</note> **verse 15. the faith within us.** <note>original: πίστιν τὴν ἐν ἡμῖν (*pistin tēn en hēmin*)</note> Gelenius: **or by what part of himself.** **verse 18. to similar things.** <note>original: παραπλησίοις (*paraplēsiois*)</note> same reading: **similarly.** <note>original: παραπλησίως (*paraplēsiōs*)</note> **verse 19. Lord God.** **verse 28.** same reading: **to themselves.** Otherwise [it is]: John 1:3; Hosea 10.

**Page 126, verse 7. then the light.** 2 Corinthians 3. **verse 27. he sent.** same reading. **verse 28. then.** <note>original: τότε (*tote*)</note> same reading: **thereupon.** <note>original: εἶτα (*eita*)</note> Hoeschel’s edition: **how many of it thereupon the prophet prophesying.** **verse 29.** same reading: **withdrawing.** <note>original: ἀφιστάντης (*aphistantēs*)</note> Gelenius: **of the one calling away.**

**Page 127, verse 5.** same reading: **observe.** <note>original: σκόπει (*skopei*)</note> **verse 7.** same reading: **having been said.** <note>original: λελεγμένη (*lelegmenē*)</note> **verse 11.** Hoeschel’s edition: **to the blessed one.** **verse 13. to the same.** same reading: **of this one.** Hoeschel’s edition: **concerning him.** **verse 15.** Hoeschel’s edition: **those happening upon him.** **verse 24.** these things are found in book 7, page 381.

**Page 128, verse 1.** it must be read **to defend oneself.** <note>original: ἀμύνεσθαι (*amynesthai*)</note> **verse 5. indeed.** same reading: **and itself.** Plato in the *Crito*. **verse 8. therefore.** <note>original: ἄρα (*ara*)</note> read **then?** <note>original: ἆρα (*ara*)—changing from a statement to a question</note> He [Origen] set down Plato's opinion, and we have rendered it. Its form is this:
**SOCRATES:** In no way, then, must one do wrong.
**CRITO:** Certainly not.
**SOCRATES:** Nor then, if wronged, should one return wrong, as the many think; since in no way must one do wrong.
**CRITO:** It does not appear so.
**verse 14. same reading: to him.** **verse 16. e. l.** in the same reading: **these things.** same reading: **such things.** <note>original: τοιαῦτα (*toiauta*)</note> **verse 19.** Hoeschel’s edition: **to Plato.** **verse 20.** same reading: **loosening.** <note>original: ἐπιλύων (*epilyōn*)—often meaning "explaining" or "refuting"</note> **verse 22. same reading: Moses and following.** **verse 28. same reading: that also from.**

**Page 129, verse 2.** Hoeschel’s edition: **to the one loosening.** **verse 8.** the same: **how many indeed.** **verse 18.** same reading: **with words.** **verse 22. healthy.** same reading, and **verse 25. those learning.**

**Page 130, verse 1. and to those** is missing in the same reading. **verse 8.** same reading: **of such preparations.** <note>original: τοιάσδε διασκευασίας (*toiasde diaskeuasias*)</note> Hoeschel’s edition: **of constructions.** <note>original: κατασκευασίας (*kataskeuasias*)</note> **verse 13.** same reading: **to such** and **of such.** **verse 18. to the wealthy.** <note>original: πλουσίοις (*plousiois*)</note> same reading: **to the learned.** <note>original: λογίοις (*logiois*)</note> Hoeschel’s edition: **usefully preparing these things with words**—which is completely irrelevant. **verse 20.** This is far different in the same reading: **equal health and vigor (for let it be granted) arising from things prepared in this way, or in that?** **verse 22. you suggest.** same reading, and **verse 26. to change, a thing to be reshaped.**

**Page 131, verse 5.** same reading: **only.** **verse 6. but** <note>original: δὲ (*de*)</note> is missing in the same reading. **verse 7.** Hoeschel’s edition: **to those who have looked down upon.** What then? **verse 8.** same reading: **those who the.** **verse 9.** same reading: **long.** **verse 14.** same reading: **having hinted at being made like those,** etc. **verse 17.** Hoeschel’s edition: **let them prepare.** and **19. and what sort.** **verse 23.** same reading: **of such a kind.** **verse 24. and if it is set before.** same reading: **when.** **verse 28.**

**Page 132, line 6.** **prepared,** <note>original: συνεσκευασμένος (*syneskeuasmenos*)</note> foolishly. Hoeschel's Philocalia: **the [one] would be prepared.** <note>original: συνεσκευασμένος εἴη ἂν ὁ (*syneskeuasmenos eiē an ho*)</note>

# ON THE WORKS OF ORIGEN
<note>This section provides critical notes on the text of Origen, a 3rd-century theologian. The scholar compares different manuscript versions to find the most accurate wording.</note>

**Page 276, line 1.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **discord**. <note>original: στάσις (stasis)</note> **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus was a 4th-century translator who turned Origen’s Greek into Latin, though he often edited the content for clarity or orthodoxy.</note> reads in line 18: it should certainly be read as **"he is disobedient; what need is there to harden the heart?"** <note>original: ἀπειθεῖ, τίς χρεία πωρῶσαι καρδίαν (apeithei, tis chreia porōsai kardian)</note> If, however, he resists, what need is there for his heart to be hardened, and that more than once? etc. **Line 22.** Rufinus adds **him**; except that it was indeed possible for him to be persuaded; nor would he be said to be hardened by another, unless he was not hard before. But if he was not hard by his own nature, it follows that he was not of an "earthly nature," but of such a kind as could yield, being struck by signs and powers. <note>This discussion concerns the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus, a major topic in Origen's defense of free will against Gnostic fatalism.</note>

**Page 277, line 20.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **he might receive**. <note>original: ἀνδέχοιτ’ αν</note> **Line 23.** **Those men]** refers to the followers of Basilides. <note>Basilides was an early Gnostic teacher in Alexandria.</note> **Line 24.** **Certain person]** refers to the Marcionites. <note>Followers of Marcion, who believed the God of the Old Testament was different from the God of the New Testament.</note>

**Page 278, line 14.** **Fitting]** <note>original: προσῆκουσα</note> Rufinus translates as **primitive**. **Line 24.** **With a bare head.** <note>original: γυμνῆ τῇ κεφαλῇ (gymnē tē kephalē). This is a Greek idiom meaning "shamelessly" or "openly."</note> Chrysostom uses this often, as does Gregory in his first *Apology*: **proceeding toward their desires "with a bare head," as the saying goes.**

**Page 279, line 28.** **The one who rains]** <note>original: τὸν ὕοντα</note> I would read this as **the rain**; or you might refer **the one who rains** to the one who waters.

**Page 280, line 4.** Read: **they had become**. **Line 7.** **At least]** <note>original: γ’ οὖν</note> The de Thou manuscripts read: **for**. **Line 11.** The manuscript reads: **it becomes**. **Line 20.** The manuscript reads: **that**. **Line 23.** **He was saying.** The manuscript reads: **that**.

**Page 281, line 3.** The Royal Manuscript reads: **hardening**. <note>original: σκληρυμμόν</note> **Line 9.** **Heart]** Rufinus reads: **house**. <note>original: οἰκίαν</note> **Line 26.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **by frictions**. <note>original: ἐπιτριβισμοῖς</note>

**Page 282, line 18.** **Again]** The de Thou manuscripts read: **again**. Rufinus reads: **also**. **Line 27.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **is able to**.

**Page 283, line 4.** Rufinus adds: **those who have sinned**, with whom the prophet also makes himself one, saying in Isaiah 63. **Page 284, line 4.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **to themselves**.

**Page 285, line 12.** **The immortality of the soul;** understand this as the kind Paul speaks of in 1 Corinthians 15; Rufinus understands it differently.

**Page 286, line 19.** **A fifty-year period.** Rufinus reads: **sixty years**. **Line 20.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **among them**.

**Page 287, line 8.** **By]** <note>original: ὑπὸ</note> The de Thou manuscripts read: **from**. <note>original: ἀπό</note> **Line 26.** **Creator]** <note>original: δημιουργός (dēmiourgos)</note> instead read: **farmer**. <note>original: γεωργός (geōrgos)</note> Rufinus reads: **husbandman**.

**Page 288, line 16.** The de Thou manuscripts read: **plots**.

**Page 290, line 3.** In the manuscripts: **if**. **Line 10.** **The (thing)]** The manuscripts read: **to the**. **Line 12.** Rufinus seems to have read: **it is not necessary to hear, but just as...** [meaning] this ought not to be understood in such a way.

**Page 291, line 2.** **Of me]** The manuscripts read: **the**.

**Page 292, line 1.** Read with the manuscripts and Rufinus: **thus they shall return**, they shall be converted, and so they shall be converted.

**Page 293, line 19.** The manuscripts read: **seeking such a**. **Line 19.** **Better]** read: **less**.

**Page 293, line 8.** **If indeed to themselves]** The manuscripts read: **if among themselves**. **Line 25.** The manuscripts read: **firmly**.

**Page 295, line 18.** The manuscripts read: **they had wandered**. **Line 21.** **They show]** perhaps: **it is clear that**.

**Page 296, line 6.** The manuscripts read: **in them**.

**Page 297, line 3.** The manuscripts read: **that one**. **Line 4.** **To the one who has given**. **Line 12.** **Nothing**. **Line 13.** **To the**.

**Page 298, line 13.** The manuscripts read: **in the**. **Line 23.** **Of the intermediate things]** <note>original: τῶν μέσων (tōn mesōn)</note> thus Herillus <note>A Stoic philosopher and pupil of Zeno.</note> called **the things between virtue and vice "indifferent things";** <note>original: adiaphora</note> just as Miltiades of Chios used the term **indifference**, and Zeno used **neutrals**, who also wanted there to be some category **among the intermediate things**.

**Page 299, line 11.** The manuscripts read: **and he says**. Psalm 126. **Page 300, line 11.** In the manuscripts: **not**.

**Page 301, line 23.** Read with the de Thou manuscripts: **the one who to the**.

**Page 302, line 4.** **Or voluntarily]** The manuscripts read: **through the voluntary**. **Line 8.** **Sinned]** The manuscript reads: **the commandments do away with**. Aristotle, *Magna Moralia*, Book 1, Chapter 6: **from that point all human life is subverted; in vain are the laws...**
