# NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA
<note>The *Philocalia* is an anthology of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus in the 4th century. These notes compare different editions and manuscripts to establish the correct text.</note>

### Tttt iij

[...if these things] are granted, then rebukes, praises, censures, and exhortations are employed in vain, and no justice has established rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked. <note>original: "dantur, frustra obiurgationes, laudes, vituperationes, exhortationes adhibentur, neque ulla iustitia bonis praemia & malis supplicia constituta sunt."</note> Cicero; Augustine, *City of God*, Book 5, chapter 15, etc.] The Manuscripts add: **in vain.** <note>original: μάτην (matēn)</note> And in line 18: **but indeed.** <note>original: δέ γε (de ge)</note>

**Page 303, verse 19.** **as if.** <note>original: ὡσεί (hōsei)</note> **Verse 25.** In the Manuscripts, read: **under.** <note>original: ὑπο (hypo)</note> **Last verse.** **that of God.** <note>original: τὸ θεοῦ (to theou)</note>

**Page 304, verse 7.** Manuscripts: **in the furnaces or under those things set on fire.** <note>original: ταῖς καμίνοις ἢ ὑπὸ τοῖς ἐναπτόις (tais kaminois ē hypo tois enaptois)</note> **Verse 11.** **to himself.** <note>original: ἑαυτῷ (heautō)</note>

**Page 305, verse 17.** **drawn.** <note>original: ἕλκτος (helktos)</note> Rufinus reads: **salvation.** <note>original: salutem</note>

**Page 306, verse 9.** **again]** The Royal Manuscript reads: **but to the.** <note>original: τῷ δὲ (tō de)</note> The de Thou Manuscripts read: **to the again.** <note>original: τῷ αὖ (tō au)</note> **Verse 21.** I have restored: **that which is said** <note>original: λεγόμενον (legomenon)</note> from the de Thou Manuscripts in place of **stripped.** <note>original: γυμνόμενον (gymnomenon)</note>

**Page 307, verse 3.** de Thou Manuscripts: **of this phrase.** <note>original: ταύτης τῆς λέξεως (tautēs tēs lexeōs)</note> **Verse 7.** **not from the beginning.** <note>original: οὐκ ἀρχῆθεν (ouk archēthen)</note> The Theologians <note>likely Basil and Gregory, the compilers of the Philocalia</note> interpret this one way, and Rufinus another. **Verse 11.** read: **well.** <note>original: εὖ (eu)</note> **Verse 13.** **so that]** <note>original: ὥστε (hōste)</note> Manuscripts read: **just as.** <note>original: ὥσπερ (hōsper)</note> **Verse 18.** read: **out of.** <note>original: ἐξ (ex)</note> **Verse 20.** **having taken away.** <note>original: ἀφελόντες (aphelontes)</note>

**Page 308, verse 6.** **which I was.** <note>original: ἃ ἦα (ha ēa)</note> **Verse 14.** **perhaps he teaches.** <note>original: τάχα διδάσκει (tacha didaskei)</note>

**Page 309, verse 17.** read: **stripped.** <note>original: γυμνόμενον (gymnomenon)</note> **Verse 24.** Manuscripts: **articulated.** <note>original: διαρθρωθέντα (diarthrōthenta)</note> **Verse 25.** **in the new creation.** <note>original: ἐν τῇ καινῇ κτίσει (en tē kainē ktisei)</note> You who remember you are a man, be fair to humanity. <note>original: "Qui te hominem meministi, humanitati aequus esto."</note>

**Page 310, verse 21.** Manuscripts: **to where.** <note>original: ὅποι (hopoi)</note> **Verse 25.** **the "how" is in our power** <note>original: τὸ πῶς ἐφ’ ἡμῖν (to pōs eph' hēmin)</note> is poorly written.

**Page 311, verse 8.** Manuscripts: **exhalations.** <note>original: ἀναπνώμασι (anapnōmasi)</note>

**Page 312, verse 8.** **not the.** <note>original: οὐκ τὸ (ouk to)</note> See page 254 of the edition of the book *Against Celsus*. **Verse 18.** read as: **of whatever kind indeed.** <note>original: ὁποίας δὴ (hopoias dē)</note> **Verse 21.** **wherever it might happen to be of benefit.** <note>original: ὅτῃ ποτ' ἂν τύχηι ὠφελήσοισι (hotē pot' an tychē ophelēsoisi)</note>

**Page 313, verse 5.** read: **in the administration** <note>original: ἐν διοικ. (en dioik.)</note> as on the following page. **Verse 12.** In the de Thou Manuscripts, read: **later.** <note>original: ὕστερον (hysteron)</note>

**Page 314, verse 8.** **the parts of the earth]** Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> in *On the Celestial Hierarchy* calls these **divine stewardships** <note>original: θείας ἐπιστασίας (theias epistasias)</note> from which he says one **must not depart from the formation of other nations.** <note>original: μὴ ἀφίστασθαι χρὴ τῆς τῶν ἑτέρων ἐθνῶν ἀποπλασήσεως (mē aphistasthai chrē tēs tōn heterōn ethnōn apoplasēseōs)</note> **Verse 12.** read as: **as if.** <note>original: ὡσανεὶ (hōsanei)</note> **Verse 17.** **in]** <note>original: ἐν (en)</note> de Thou Manuscripts read: **from.** <note>original: ἐξ (ex)</note> **Verse 28.** **of those things that are advantageous.** <note>original: συμφερόντων (sympherontōn)</note> de Thou Manuscripts: **advantageously.** <note>original: συμφερόντως (sympherontōs)</note>

**Page 315, verse 11.** de Thou Manuscripts: **to seem this.** <note>original: τοῦτο δοκεῖν (touto dokein)</note> read as: **the thing said.** <note>original: τὸ εἶπον (to eipon)</note> **Verse 15.** read with the de Thou Manuscripts and the cited place: **it has been distributed.** <note>original: διανένεμηται (dianenemetai)</note> **Verse 16.** others read: **I rule.** <note>original: ἄρχω (archō)</note> **Verse 26.** read as: **let him announce.** <note>original: ἐπαγγειλάτω (epangeilatō)</note> otherwise.

**Page 316, verse 3.** **Approaching]** **"With these people, it is considered prophetic to have relations with mothers."** <note>original: τούτοις ἢ ἐκ μητράσι σκοπεῖσθαι πάντειον νενόμισται (toutois ē ek mētrasi skopeisthai panteion nenomistai)</note> Strabo in Book 15. Athenagoras complains that this was wickedly charged against Christian piety: **"They falsely accuse us of three crimes: atheism, Thyestean feasts [cannibalism], and Oedipean unions [incest]."** <note>original: τρία ἐπιφημίζουσιν ἡμῖν ἐγκλήματα, ἀθεότητα, Θυέστεια δεῖπνα, Οἰδιπόδους μίξεις (tria epiphēmizousin hēmin enklēmata, atheotēta, Thyesteia deipna, Oidipodous mixeis)</note> **Verse 4.** in the cited place read: **relatives.** <note>original: οἰκείοις (oikeiois)</note> **Verse 8.** read: **in those that vanished.** <note>original: ἐν τοῖς ἐξαφ. (en tois exaph.)</note> **Verse 11.** read: **the laws are clear to everyone.** <note>original: ἐπὸ πάσης δῆλον οἱ νόμοι (epo pasēs dēlon hoi nomoi)</note> de Thou Manuscript: **friendly.** <note>original: φίλιον (philion)</note> **Verse 16.** read as: **it was blessed.** <note>original: μακάριον ἦν (makarion ēn)</note> The "was" is superfluous. For that custom <note>ritual suicide</note> was observed both at Marseilles and on the island of Ceos. Strabo in Book 10. Aelian in Book 3 of *Various History*, chapter 37. Valerius Maximus, an **eyewitness** <note>original: αὐτόπτης (autoptēs)</note> himself, in Book 3, chapter 6. At the same place, **by shame]** **"Most of the Germans die by a hanging death."** <note>original: Γερμανῶν οἱ πλεῖστοι ἀγχονιμαίῳ μόρῳ ἀποθνήσκουσι (Germanōn hoi pleistoi anchonimaiō morō apothnēskousi)</note> Bardizanes <note>a 2nd-century Syrian gnostic and scholar</note> in Book 6. The Gymnosophists of India die on the pyre; the elderly of Marseilles and Ceos by hemlock. manuscript: **passing through.** <note>original: διεξ. (diex.)</note> Manuscripts and the cited place read: **to go out.** <note>original: ξελθεῖν (xelthein)</note> **Verse 22.** **to the foreign persons.** <note>original: τοῖς ξένοις προσώ. (tois xenois prosō.)</note> Regarding human victims, see **On Ancient Human Sacrifice** <note>original: περὶ παλαιῶν ἀνθρωποθυσίας (peri palaiōn anthrōpothysias)</note> in Eusebius, Book 4 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, from Porphyry and others. **Verse 27.** read: **among the Jews.** <note>original: ἐν Ἰουδαίοις (en Ioudaiois)</note>

**Page 317, verse 6.** read: **the object of worship.** <note>original: τὸ προσκυνώμενον (to proskynōmenon)</note> de Thou Manuscript: **among the common people.** <note>original: παρὰ τοῖς δήμοις (para tois dēmois)</note> **Verse 11.** Printed Edition: **or toward the others.** <note>original: ἢ πρὸς τοῖς ἑτέροις (ē pros tois heterois)</note> **Verse 16.** **only]** read as: **no longer.** <note>original: μη’ ἔτι (mē eti)</note> **Verse 21.** read with the cited place: **the innocent.** <note>original: ἀναιτίοις (anaitiois)</note> **Verse 23.** others: **with contempt.** <note>original: καταφρονήσει (kataphronēsei)</note> de Thou Manuscript: **sentence of death.** <note>original: καταθανάτου (katathanatou)</note> **Verse 25.** read: **the just or the holy.** <note>original: τὸ δίκαιον ἢ ὁσίον (to dikaion ē hosion)</note> **Verse 26.** **but.** <note>original: δὲ (de)</note> These are missing in the cited place up to those things on page 318, **verse 11.** **if therefore indeed.** <note>original: εἴπερ οὖν (eiper oun)</note>

**Page 318, verse 11.** read: **I rejected.** <note>original: ἀπωσάμην (apōsamen)</note> The rest, which were separated from here to those things on page 320, **verse 6.** Hoeschelius <note>David Hoeschel, a German humanist and editor of Origen</note> stuffed in **"more simply"** <note>original: ἀπλώστερον (aplōsteron)</note> in the Notes. **Verse 27.** **through.** <note>original: διὰ (dia)</note> read with the printed edition: **according to.** <note>original: κατά (kata)</note> **Verse 28.** **to the** <note>original: τῷ γ. (tō g.)</note> in many Manuscripts.

### NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA

**Page 342, verse 1.** In the Manuscripts: **was.** <note>original: ἦν (ēn)</note> **Verse 22.** **powers. Not of the individual, but of the essence itself and of the power.** <note>original: δυνάμεις. οὐκ τῆς καθ' ἕκαστον, αὐτῆς οὐσίας ἐς δυνάμεως (dynameis. ouk tēs kath’ hekaston, autēs ousias es dynameōs)</note> See Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 11. <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a Christian theologian and philosopher; this reference suggests Origen’s text aligns with later celestial hierarchies.</note>

**Page 343, verse 7.** **we shall repeat.** <note>original: ἐπαληψόμεθα (epalēpsometha)</note> The Manuscripts read: **we shall examine.** <note>original: ἐπασκεψόμεθα (epaskepsometha)</note> **Verse 20.** **the things of the... the p. p.** <note>Note: These appear to be abbreviations for a specific phrase in the Greek text.</note>

**Page 344, verse 9.** The second de Thou Manuscript: **he might do.** <note>original: ποιήση (poiēsē)</note> **Verse 18.** **it is.** <note>original: ἔστιν (estin)</note> Both read: **it shall be.** <note>original: ἔσται (estai)</note>

**Page 345, verse 19.** de Thou Manuscripts: **slipping.** <note>original: ὀλισθαίνοντα (olisthainonta)</note> **Verse 20.** Manuscripts: **that one.** <note>original: ἐκείνη (ekeinē)</note> **Verse 18.** **He reaches** or **God touches.** <note>original: ἐφάπτεται (ephaptetai); the author notes the Latin "attingit Deus."</note>

**Page 347, verse 7.** In the Royal Manuscript: **truly.** <note>original: ἀληθῶς (alēthōs)</note> Manuscript [pò]: de Thou Manuscripts: **if.** <note>original: εἱ (ei)</note> **Verse 11.** Royal Manuscript: [phro. de gr.] de Thou Manuscripts: **but before.** <note>original: πρὸ δὲ (pro de)</note>

**Page 348, verse 15.** Royal Manuscript: <gloss>**you know**</gloss> <note>original: ἐπίστασθε (epistasthe)</note> and it is likely both are correct.

**Page 350, verse 4.** **concerning.** The de Thou Manuscripts add **beautiful** <note>original: καλῆ (kalē)</note> in vain. **Verse 20.** These things, which are muddled, I would read in this manner: **and that which is toward what we have, of intensity,** etc. <note>original: κ. τὸ πρὸς οἷς ἐχομεν, σφοδρότητος (k. to pros hois echomen, sphodrotētos)</note> **Verse 23.** **to become.** <note>original: γενέσθαι (genesthai)</note> Royal Manuscript: **to be about to be.** <note>original: ἔσεσθαι (esesthai)</note> **Verse 29.** de Thou Manuscripts: **we shall be.** <note>original: ἐσόμεθα (esometha)</note>

**Page 351, verse 7.** [pon]: de Thou Manuscripts: **him.** <note>original: αὐτὸν (auton)</note> and **verse 9**, **here.** <note>original: ἐνταῦθα (entautha)</note>

**Page 352, verse 1.** Read: **of men.** <note>original: ἀνθρώπων (anthrōpōn)</note> de Thou Manuscripts: **to a man.** <note>original: ἀνθρώπῳ (anthrōpō)</note> **Verse 10.** *The Philocalia of H...*: **thus he thought...** book c. page 74. **Verse 19.** Read with the published edition: **of the same.** <note>original: τῆς αὐτῆς (tēs autēs)</note> **Verse 23.** Missing in the published edition and in Gelenius’s interpretation: **powerfully or even not to happen.** <note>original: δυνατῶς ἢ καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι (dynatōs ē kai mē genesthai)</note> Whence the whole sentence **limps.** <note>The editor means the sentence is grammatically or logically incomplete without these words.</note>

**Page 353, verse 1.** Read: **when.** <note>original: πότε (pote)</note> **Verse 15.** **as.** <note>original: ὡς (hōs)</note> *Philocalia H...*: **to the.** <note>original: τῇ (tē)</note> **Verse 17.** **it is necessary to know.** <note>original: ἰστέον (isteon)</note> In the same: **of the useful.** <note>original: χρησιμῶν (chrēsimōn)</note> **Verse 20.** In the published edition it is read corruptly: **the word concerning the Jew Nau.** <note>original: λόγον τὸν περὶ τοῦ Ἰουδαίου ναῦ (logon ton peri tou Ioudaiou nau)</note> **Verse 11.** *Philocalia H...*: **What is said to someone in the Psalms: God.** <note>original: Τί τινι λέγεται ἐν ψαλμοῖς ὁ θεός (Ti tini legetai en psalmois ho theos)</note> **Verse 28.** [eirē.]: published edition: **the things written.** <note>original: γεγραμμένα (gegrammena)</note>

**Page 354, verse 4.** de Thou Manuscripts and published edition: **to the same wickedness.** <note>original: αὐτῆ κακίαν (autē kakian)</note> **Verse 5.** published edition: **of which things he says.** <note>original: ὧν φησιν (hōn phēsin)</note> **Verse 8.** **he was able.** <note>original: ἐδύνατο (edynato)</note> *Philocalia H...* adds: **he says.** <note>original: φησί (phēsi)</note> **Verse 9.** published edition: **mercy.** <note>original: ἔλεον (eleon)</note> **Verse 12.** published edition and *Philocalia H...*: **he handed over.** <note>original: παρέδωκεν (paredōken)</note> **Verse 13.** de Thou Manuscripts and published edition add: **in the prophecy.** <note>original: τῆ ἐν προφητεία (tē en prophēteia)</note> **Verse 14.** published edition: **the manner in the stated form.** <note>original: χρησό- τῶ εἰρημένῳ τύπῳ τὸν τρόπον (chrēso- tō eirēmenō typō ton tropon)</note> **Verse 21.** published edition: **where leaping.** <note>original: ἧ πηδῶν (hē pēdōn)</note> Another manuscript: **furrow.** <note>original: αὐλακα (aulaka)</note> **Verse 24.** **the one who grew.** <note>original: ὁ φὺς (ho phys)</note> de Thou Manuscripts incorrectly read: **serpent.** <note>original: ὄφις (ophis)</note> Which they write was applied to **Laius** because of the similarity of the sound. <note>Laius was the father of Oedipus; the author is noting a scribe's pun or phonetic error between "serpent" and a word related to Laius's story.</note> **Verse 26.** published edition: **through blood.** <note>original: δι' αἱμάτων (di’ haimatōn)</note> **Verse 27.** *Philocalia H...*: **in types.** <note>original: τύποις (typōis)</note> **Verse 29.** published edition: **the furrow of children.** <note>original: παίδων ἄλοκα (paidōn aloka)</note>

**Page 355, verse 1.** **For it would not.** <note>original: οὐκ ἂν γὰρ (ouk an gar)</note> This is missing in the *Philocalia H...*, the published edition, and Gelenius’s interpretation, from that point until: **I might guard against.** <note>original: φυλαξαίμην (phylaxaimēn)</note> **Verse 5.** In place of which, *Philocalia H...* has: **to the one who has accepted.** <note>original: τῶ καταδεξαμένῳ (tō katadexamenō)</note> **Verse 10.** **the lazy argument.** <note>original: ἀργὸς λόγος (argos logos)</note> Cicero, in *On Fate*:
> **Nor will that "lazy argument" hinder us, as it is called; for a certain argument is named by philosophers the *lazy argument* (argos logos), which if we were to obey, there would be nothing at all for us to do in life. For they ask: If it is your fate to recover from this disease, etc.** <note>original Latin: Nec nos impediet illa ignaua ratio, quæ dicitur: appellatur enim quiddam à philosophis ἀργὸς λόγος, cui si pareamus, nihil est omnino, quod agamus in vita: sic enim interrogant: si fatum tibi est ex hoc morbo conualescere, &c.</note>
Yet Agesilaus foolishly obeyed this during a disease and recovered. Plutarch, in his *Sayings*. <note>Agesilaus II was a King of Sparta; the author is contrasting philosophical fatalism with historical anecdotes.</note> **Verse 11.** published edition: **through the [fact] that, being said.** <note>original: διὰ τῆς ὅτι, λεγόμενος (dia tēs hoti, legomenos)</note> **Verse 14.** published edition: **whenever he...** <note>original: ὅποτε ἐπιι. (hopote epii.)</note> **Verse 15.** **but.** <note>original: δέ (de)</note> published edition: **at least.** <note>original: γε (ge)</note> **Verse 23.** others: **either but.** <note>original: εἴτε δέ (eite de)</note> **Verse 27.** published edition: **it will be placed beside.** <note>original: παραθέσεται (parathestetai)</note> **Last verse.** **you might come together with.** <note>original: συνελθῃς (synelthēs)</note> **Whether you have been with a woman, or whether you have not been.** According to Cicero.

**Page 356, verse 23.** In the published edition: **not.** <note>original: μή (mē)</note> **Verse 28.** published edition: **by the sound.** <note>original: ὑπ' ἠκοῦ (hyp' ēkou)</note> *Philocalia H...*: **and she follows.** <note>original: ἡ δὲ ἀκολουθεῖ (hē de akolouthei)</note>

**Page 357, verse 2.** **rock** <note>original: πέτρᾳ (petra)</note> is missing in the published edition and in Gelenius. **Verse 5.** published edition: **own.** <note>original: ἰδιάν (idian)</note> **Verse 6.** In the published edition: [l. pa.] **Verse 13.** books and *Philocalia H...*: **in the dish.** <note>original: ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ (en tō trybliō)</note> **Verse 15.** **but.** <note>original: δέ (de)</note> Manuscripts: **indeed.** <note>original: δή (dē)</note>

**Page 358, verse 7.** de Thou Manuscripts: **having taken.** <note>original: λαβόντα (labonta)</note> **Verse 24.** **birth,** read **origin.** <note>The author corrects the Latin term *partus* to *ortus*.</note>

**Page 359, verse 16.** Read: **that.** <note>original: ὅτι (hoti)</note> Manuscript [cc.]: **according to.** <note>original: κατὰ (kata)</note>

**Page 360, verse 4.** [l. mon p.] **Verse 5.** The second de Thou Manuscript: **of the present.** <note>original: ἐνεστῶτος (enestōtos)</note> **Verse 21.** Manuscripts: **for just as.** <note>original: ὥσπερ γὰρ (hōsper gar)</note> **Verse 27.** [tō cc. po.]

**Page 361, verse 9.** **prayer.** <note>original: προσευχῆ (proseuchē)</note> Most things very similar to these are found in the book truly [a testament...]

# NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA <note>The *Philocalia* is a famous collection of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus in the 4th century to preserve his most important theological and philosophical insights.</note>

**Page 382, verse 5.** **the word.** <note>original: λέξαν (lexan)</note> Printed books: **to have been gathered.** <note>original: συλλελοίσθαι (sulleloisthai)</note> **Verse 10.** **if even upon.** <note>original: εἰ κι ἐπὶ (ei kai epi)</note> The writing of the Royal Codex was this: **if even to take care... to add.** <note>original: εἰ κι ἐπιμ. δ´ ἐπιποιεῖν (ei kai epim. d. epipoiein)</note> Marginal note: **use those who take care... to do.** <note>original: χρ. οἱ κι ἐπιμ. δ´ π´ ποιεῖν (chr. hoi kai epim. d. p. poiein)</note> **Verse 21.** **of a temple.** <note>original: νεώς (neōs)</note> In the place cited: **temples.** <note>original: ναούς (naous)</note>

**Page 388, verse 5.** **that substance which belongs to all** <note>original: ἅ πᾶσιν ἔστιν ἡ οὐσία (ha pasin estin hē ousia)</note> is missing in the printed books. **Verse 6.** **the physician.** <note>original: ὁ ἰατρός (ho iatros)</note> ] **a physician.** <note>original: ἰατρός (iatros)</note> **Verse 9.** **and these.** <note>original: καὶ ταῦτα (kai tauta)</note> Books: **and those things to the evil.** <note>original: κἀκεῖνα τῷ κακά (kakeina tō kaka)</note> **Verse 11.** **it will be.** <note>original: ἔσται (estai)</note> & **Verse 26.** Manuscripts and books: **it is within.** <note>original: ἔνεστιν (enestin)</note> **Verse 27.** **of substance.** <note>original: οὐσίας (ousias)</note> Cited books: **of cause.** <note>original: αἰτίας (aitias)</note>

Nor can there truly be any doubt that from there the greatest theologians <note>Likely referring to Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note> made their excerpts; that this was their own observation, and not that of some transcriber, is sufficiently proved to me both by its form and by the fact that it is found in three manuscripts—I do not know if it is in all. Therefore, through these restorers, Origen will not lose his claim to his own property.

Jerome. **Verse 10.** Manuscripts: **to himself.** <note>original: ἑαυτῷ (heautō)</note> **Verse 11.** **he pleased.** <note>original: ηὐδοκ (ēudok)</note> Common edition: **God was pleased.** <note>original: εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεός (eudokēsen ho theos)</note> **Verse 16.** **the.** <note>original: τὸν (ton)</note> Manuscripts: **to the,** <note>original: τῷ (tō)</note> and **predestined.** <note>original: προωρισμένῳ (proōrismenō)</note> & so forth.

# ON ORIGEN'S WORKS

**Page 400, verse 22.** **to him the.** <note>original: αὐτῷ ἡ (autō hē)</note> **Verse 27.** another reading in the Thuanus manuscript: **I was departing.** <note>original: ἀπήιων (apēiōn)</note>

**Page 401, verse 3.** **to wake up beforehand.** <note>original: προαπνίσαι (proapnisai)</note> **Verse 13.** **the [thing] around.** <note>original: ἡ περί (hē peri)</note> **Verse 15.** **not even any who.** <note>original: οὐδ' πις ὁ (oud' tis ho)</note> **Verse 18.** **we are considered.** <note>original: νομιζόμεθ' (nomizometh')</note> **Verse 28.** <term>foreknowledge of God</term> <note>original: πρόγνωσις τοῦ Θεοῦ (prognōsis tou Theou). This refers to the theological debate over whether God knowing the future forces it to happen.</note> **Verse 29. but since he was about to]** There is a very wise commentary by Justin Martyr <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher and apologist.</note> in his *Responses*, number 58: **It is not because foreknowledge is the cause of what is to come that it happens, but because it is going to happen, foreknowledge exists. For the future does not follow from foreknowledge, but foreknowledge follows from the future; and in no way is the one who foreknows the cause of the betrayal, but the betrayal is the cause of the Lord's foreknowledge.** The same reasoning regarding the devil and the first man is found, he says, both here in Origen and in his commentary on *Genesis*, and was subsequently available to everyone who followed: to Athanasius in his *Oration on the Passion*: **The things that happen do not happen because they say they will; rather, they say they will happen because they are going to happen,** etc. Just as **we are seen because we happen to be there, and it is not that we happen to be there because we are seen.** So too John Chrysostom in his work *On the Obscurity of Prophecies*, where he speaks of Judas: **It was not because Christ foretold it that he became a traitor, but because he was going to be a traitor, Christ foretold it.** Also in his 60th *Homily on Matthew*; and in Jerome, Augustine, Cyril of Alexandria, and others. The same **opinion.** <note>original: γνώμη (gnōmē)</note>

**Page 402, verse 17.** **of logic.** <note>original: λογικῆς (logikēs)</note> And one may understand this as "logical contemplation," which is found in Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics*.

**Page 403, verse 7.** read **he heals.** <note>original: παίνει (painei), likely from ἰαίνει (iainei)</note> as below in **verse 9.** **he might excel.** <note>original: προύχη (prouchē)</note> **Verse 29.** **let them answer.** <note>original: ἀποκρινάσθωσαν (apokrinasthōsan)</note>

**Page 404, verse 5.** **upon the] not of the [thing] being given.** <note>original: οὐκ τῆς διδομένης (ouk tēs didomenēs)</note>

**Page 407, verse 17.** **of preparation.** <note>original: κατασκευῆς (kataskeuēs)</note> **Verse 24.** read with the manuscripts **virtue.** <note>original: ἀρέτη (aretē)</note>

**Page 408, verse 5.** **from not,** etc. these are missing in the Thuanus manuscripts. **Verse 8.** the abbreviation **p.cc.p.** does not appear.

**Page 409, verse 2.** **by] "by"** is correct. <note>original: ὑπὸ (hypo)</note> **Verse 4.** **fond of learning... manuscripts: fond of oars.** <note>original: φιλοκῶπες (philokōpes)</note> **Verse 10.** **word] place.** <note>original: τόπον (topon)</note> **Verse 24.** **good.** <note>original: ἀγαθός (agathos)</note> **Verse 29.** manuscripts: **and if indeed.** <note>original: κὴ εἰ δή π. (kai ei dē p.)</note>

**Page 410, verse 10.** **those men]** He refers to Plato and Aristotle, to whom this division [of goods] belongs: **Of goods, some belong to the soul, some to the body, and some are external.** These are indeed peculiar to Plato, further divided into three kinds: **Some are possessed, some shared, and some inherent.** They are reduced to those four kinds which the same author established: first, **possessing virtue**; second, **virtue** itself; third, **things of such a kind** etc.; and fourth, **flute-playing, acting,** and the like. Then there is this two-fold division from Book 1 of the *Laws*: **Goods are twofold: some are human, and some are divine.** Theodoret discusses this at length in Book 6 of *On Providence*. Finally, there is the division: **of goods, some are for their own sake, others for the sake of something else,** which Aristotle took from his Master [Plato]. Of all these, **we say those concerning the soul are the most authoritative.** (Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 1, Chapter 8). Zeno and the Stoics felt differently. Basil says in *Epistle 42*: **Only the lasting good is serious and praiseworthy, and this is the honor that comes from God.** To which his brother [Gregory of Nyssa] adds a similar thought in his *Oration on the Dead*: **Of all things, only this should be declared truly good: that which is always and for all established equally in the nature of the Good, always the same, and not changing according to external circumstances.** Philo says the same in *On the Sobriety of Noah*. This is Origen's meaning.

**Page 411, verse 6.** **beautiful... manuscripts: of letters.** <note>original: γραμμάτων (grammatōn)</note>

**Page 412, verse 27.** **the [plural]] to which.** <note>original: οἷ (hoi)</note>

**Page 414, verse 22.** **they [unclear]] they had been judged.** <note>original: ἐκέκριντο (ekekrinto)</note> **Verse 28.** **blindness.** <note>original: πύφλωσιν (typhlōsin)</note> **Verse 24.** **of those who have preoccupied.** <note>original: προκατειληφότων (prokateilēphotōn)</note>

**Page 415, verse 18.** **I might grieve,** and **19. Grieve.** <note>original: λυποῦ (lypou)</note> **Verse 20.** **badly.** <note>original: κακῶς (kakōs)</note>

<header>NOTES ON THE PHILOCALIA.</header>

**Page 416, verse 20. a small bed.** <note>original Greek: σκιμπόδιον (skimpodion)</note> [Or read] **a banquet.** <note>original Greek: συμπόσιον (symposion)</note> **Verse 28. desolate places.** <note>original Greek: ῥήμοις (rhēmois)</note>

**Page 418, verse 8. to the virtuous man.]** <note>original Greek: τῷ δὲ σπουδαίῳ (tō de spoudaiō)</note> While some thought those who claim everything belongs to the virtuous man are speaking in paradoxes, Moses considers wisdom so outstanding and sought-after that he believes not only the entire world is its worthy inheritance, but even the Ruler of all things. **Plato the Jew** <note>This refers to Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who so combined Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture that he was nicknamed "the Jewish Plato."</note> in his work *On Husbandry*. **Verse 16. is it then?** <note>original Greek: ἆρα (ara)</note> Read with the manuscripts: **untimely.** <note>original Greek: ἄκαιρον (akairon)</note> **Verse 27. of it.** <note>original Greek: αὐτῆς (autēs)</note> I restored from the Thuanus manuscripts: **to have become completions, how are they not evils for him?** <note>original Greek: συμπληρώματα γεγονέναι, πῶς οὐκ αὐτῷ κακά</note>

**Page 419, verse 18. cities.** <note>original Greek: πόλη (polē)</note> The manuscripts wrongly read **much.** <note>original Greek: πολὺ (poly)</note>

**Page 420, verse 18. from...** <note>original Greek: ἐκ ληων (ek lēōn)</note> It should be read as **must be said from.** <note>original Greek: ἐκ λεκτέον (ek lekteon)</note>

**Page 421, verse 20. into.** <note>original Greek: εἰς (eis)</note> Read **if.** <note>original Greek: εἰ (ei)</note>

**Page 424, verse 3.** The manuscripts read **sneering** <note>original Greek: μυκτήριον (muktērion), literally "nostril," used to denote a sneer or mockery.</note>, as also below in verse 9. **Verse 20. of the fullness.** <note>original Greek: πλειώματος (pleiōmatos)</note>

**Page 425, verse 1. until] which.** <note>original Greek: ἕως] οὗ (heōs hou)</note> **Verse 27. cruelty.** <note>original Greek: ἀπηνίαν (apēnian)</note>

**Page 430, verse 28. of so many impious [ones].** <note>original Greek: τοσούτων ἀσεβής (tosoutōn asebēs)</note>

**Page 431, verse 8. they might confess.** <note>original Greek: ὁμολογήσωσιν (homologēsōsin)</note>

**Page 433, verse 2. as,** and so forth. The manuscripts read **just as letting go.** <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἀφιε (hōsper aphie)</note> **Verse 15. to him]** read with the manuscripts **to the.** <note>original Greek: τῷ (tō)</note> **Verse 29. you will not scrape]** <note>original Greek: οὐ καταξεῖς (ou kataxeis)</note> Origen read this with the Hebrew text as **you will scrape,** which his own explanation confirms.

**Page 436, verse 23. of whom** or **to whom.** <note>original Greek: ὧν ἡ οἷς (hōn ē hois)</note>

**Page 437, verse 23. seed-producing.** <note>original Greek: γονοθρόοις (gonothroois)</note>

**Page 438, verse 8.** We have restored **slower** <note>original Greek: βραδύτερον (bradyteron)</note> in place of **shorter.** <note>original Greek: βραχύτερον (brachyteron)</note> **Verse 15. they are choked.** <note>original Greek: καταπνιπῶνται (katapnipōntai)</note> **Verse 20. from so great a war... if not in such a war.** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοσ. πολ. εἰ μή ἐν τοσούτῳ πολέμῳ</note> Here too, Origen is excessively merciful. <note>The editor is noting Origen's controversial tendency toward "Universalism"—the hope that even the most wicked might eventually be saved after a long period of correction.</note>

**Page 439, verse 3. the** <note>original Greek: τῷ (tō)</note> is redundant. **Verse 20.** delete **iron.** **Verse 21.** delete **in.** **Verse 28.** read **for correction.**

**Page 440, verse 21.** In the manuscripts: **the hardness.** <note>original Greek: ἡ σκληρότης (hē sklērotēs)</note>

**Page 441, verse 17. to God] to Christ.** <note>original Greek: θεῷ] χριστῷ (theō / christō)</note>

**Page 443, verse 2. still he was burning.** <note>original Greek: ἔτι δ' ἐκάιν (eti d' ekain)</note> The common edition reads: **still he was driving** or **was he already praised?** <note>original Greek: ἔτι δ' ἤλαυνε εἰ ἤδη αἰνήθη; (eti d' ēlaune ei ēdē ainēthē)</note>

**Page 444, verse 10. of the sight.** <note>original Greek: τῆς ὄψεως (tēs opseōs)</note>

**Page 445, verse 4. he might find,** as Augustine skillfully writes to the priest Sixtus in Letter 105: "God does not harden hearts by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy." And in his commentary on Psalm 77: *For when God is said to perform this most unjust and wicked action, he does so not by instigating and inspiring, but by abandoning the soul.* These matters are handled differently in the second Homily on the Song of Songs, translated by Jerome. **Verse 7. among others]** <note>original Greek: ἐν ἄλλοις (en allois)</note> Neither these nor the remaining words are found in the Thuanus manuscripts. **Verse 9. he might be healed.** <note>original Greek: ἰαθῇ (iathē)</note> On this point, recall what was said on page 285.

**Page 446. verse 19.** The common edition reads: **Do you think me not...** <note>original Greek: οἴει δὲ με μή (oiei de me mē)</note> From Job 40. Many manuscripts reject the word **not.**

**Page 447, verse 2. the good circles.** <note>original Greek: οἱ χρηστοὶ κύκλοι (hoi chrēstoi kykloi)</note> Similar things, if not the very same, are discussed at greater length on pages 281 and 282.

**Page 449, verse 3. fall.** <note>original Greek: πτῶσιν (ptōsin)</note> Which is the prophecy of Simeon: **Behold, this child is destined for the fall,** etc., in Luke chapter 2. **Verse 15.** commonly **Chorazin**; others read **Chorozaim.**

**Page 452, verse 4.** Origen, although he surpassed everyone in his other books, in his commentary on the *Song of Songs*, he surpassed even himself.

<header>ON ZACHARIAS</header>

# ON THE DIALOGUE OF ZACHARIAS
## NOTES.

<margin>Page 457</margin> **Of Zacharias.** <note>original Greek: Ζαχαρίου (Zachariou)</note> In the *Acts of the Fifth Synod*, according to Agapetus, he is named third, the Metropolitan of Mitylene, in Act 1.
**SCHOLASTIC.** <note>original Greek: ΣΧΟΛΑΣΤΙΚΟΥ (Scholastikou)</note> At first, this was nothing other than the "leader of a school," <note>original Greek: σχολῆς προηγούμενος (scholēs proēgoumenos)</note> as noted by Dionysius of Halicarnassus in his letter to Ammaeus. Of this sort were the "scholarly characters" <note>original Greek: σχολικοί χαρακτῆρες (scholikoi charaktēres)</note> of declaimers and rhetoricians, as well as "skill in public speaking." <note>original Greek: περὶ δημοσίοις δεινότης (peri dēmosiois deinotēs)</note> There were also "scholastic fellow-contestants," "fellow-students," and "school-mates." <note>original Greek: συναγωνισταί, συσχολασταί, συμβοιτηταί</note> Seneca says in the preface to his third book: *the scholastics looked at me to see who I was, I who had such thick necks* <note>A reference to the physical robustness of a man from the countryside compared to the pale, "shadowy" students of the city.</note>—a name with which Cicero was also mocked when he first returned home from Greece, according to Plutarch. There, indeed, the Scholastics are "living creatures at whom any child might laugh," as Arrian says in Book 1 of his *Discourses*. He speaks of *scholastic and shadowy letters* <note>meaning academic exercises that lack real-world application</note>; and Isaeus, that torrential rhetorician, had passed his sixtieth year and was "still a scholastic." Pliny mentions in Book 2: Scholastics like Socrates, Evagrius, Severus, and many other most famous men. Mutaeus of Marseille is called "a scholastic in speech" by Gennadius. For the same author, Salvian wrote with a "scholastic and open style." A "Scholastic" could be one skilled in Church affairs, an assessor, an advocate, or finally, one most knowledgeable in the Scriptures, from which the name of the Ecclesiastical office was born; but that arose in a later century. Here, however, the title is given to Zacharias not for an office, but for his eloquence, owing to the exquisite elegance of his Platonic "furniture" <note>a metaphor for vocabulary and rhetorical style</note> with which his whole work shines.

**THE CHRISTIAN.** <note>original Greek: ΧΡΙΣΤΙΑΝΟΥ (Christianou)</note> For this reason, it would be childish to suspect this is a name of rank or Ecclesiastical office here. For who does not see that he is distinguished by this mark from those other "shadow-dwelling" Scholastics who were merely craftsmen of declamations?

<margin>Page 459.</margin> **More [Platonic].** <note>original Greek: Τινικώτερον (Tinikōteron), likely a corruption of Πλατωνικώτερον (Platonikōteron)</note> The arrangement of the dialogue is no different from that of Theophrastus; both are Platonic. But this one is by a man who has "thoroughly drunk in Plato." <note>original Greek: τὸν Πλάτωνα πάνυ πεπωκότος</note> **Verse 6. that.** <note>original Greek: ὅτι (hoti)</note> Perhaps it should be **still.** <note>original Greek: ἔτι (eti)</note> **Verse 9. mother... to the law.** <note>original Greek: μητ. τῷ νόμῳ (mēt. tō nomō)</note> Eunapius calls this very city of Berytus <note>modern-day Beirut, famous for its Roman law school</note> the "mother of the law." **Verse 13. if anywhere.** <note>original Greek: εἴπου (eipou)</note> We have rendered this as **from a drinking party.** <note>original Greek: ἐκ πότου (ek potou)</note> **Verse 16. justice]** <note>original Greek: δίκαιον (dikaion)</note> [Meaning] **warm, legal.** Pollux, Book 8, Chapter 1. Here "justice" is nothing other than **power.** <note>original Greek: δύναμις (dynamis)</note> For to know the laws is not to know the words, but their *power* [the intent behind them], according to Book 2 of the *Basilica*, 13. I would also say it means **the reasoning**, <note>original Greek: τὸν λογισμόν (ton logismon)</note> were it not cautioned in title 19 of the same book that *it is not possible to provide a reason for all laws, therefore one should not seek a reason for them.*

<margin>Page 460, verse 1.</margin> **To Proclus.** <note>original Greek: Πρόκλῳ (Proklō)</note> He was the master of Ammonius, who often used the "theorems of the blessed Dionysius," <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> and in these very dry words. He was a Lycian, a disciple of Syrianus and Plutarch the son of Nestorius, and a fellow student of Domninus. **Verse 2. unphilosophical.** <note>original Greek: ἀφιλοσόφου (aphilosophou)</note> This refers to the man who, in eighteen arguments against the Christians, contended that the world was **uncreated** <note>original Greek: ἀγένητον (agenēton)</note> and **incorruptible** <note>original Greek: ἄφθαρτον (aphtharton)</note>; John Philoponus wrote back in reply to these. **Verse 5.** We have restored **making** <note>original Greek: ποιῶν (poiōn)</note> in place of **to make.** <note>original Greek: ποιῆν (poiēn)</note> **Verse 7. Of Ammonius.]** <note>original Greek: Ἀμμωνίου (Ammoniou)</note> Called "Ammonius the Small, son of Hermeias" by others. He was the teacher of John the Grammarian, who confesses to have composed his commentaries on the *Posterior Analytics* from their conversations.

<margin>Page 462, verse 8.</margin> **Of Eustathius.** <note>original Greek: Εὐστάθιου (Eustathiou)</note> This is a gloss that has been conveniently inserted. Bery-

<meta>The catchword "Bery-" refers to the city Berytus (Beirut) which is discussed on the next page regarding its famous law school.</meta>

<header>NOTES ON THE DIALOGUE.</header>

At the council with Photius of Tyre, Eusebius, Bishop of Beirut <note>original: Βηρυτίων (Bērytiōn)</note> and Callipolis, presided and signed the decree. Eustathius, the most devout bishop, is mentioned frequently in the acts of the Council; Nicephorus makes highly honorable mention of him in Book 1.

**Page 464, line 4.** "more blessed." <note>original: μακαριώτερον (makariōteron)</note> He looked toward this passage in the fifth book of Plato’s *Laws*: "Truth is the most useful thing for all, and blessed and happy is he who participates in it from the very beginning." <note>original: ἥτις... μέτοχος εἴη</note> But it would be a task of small reward to want to trace every little thing back to Plato, since almost everything here is derived from him. **Line 29.** "limit/boundary," <note>original: βλῆμα (blēma)</note> which is properly "a boundary" <note>original: ὅρος (horos)</note>. **Same line.** "in a reaping manner," <note>original: θριστικῶς (thristikōs)</note> obviously. Philostratus says in Book 7, chapter 8: "Fortune is a light-speaking thing to those who reap and lift up." <note>original: κουφολόγον οἱ θρισταὶ χρῆμα καὶ ἐξαίρειν ἡ τύχη</note> Dio Chrysostom, in his 12th Oration, calls the same people "peacocks variegated with reputation and fellow-sounding disciples like feathers." <note>original: ταὼς ποικίλους δόξη καὶ μαθηταῖς ἑταιροθρόοις ὡς πτεροῖς</note> But how little do these things matter compared to Plato and Isocrates?

**Page 465, line 22.** "how the 'well done'" <note>original: πῶς τὸ καλῶς (pōs to kalōs)</note>] From the exact words of Plato’s *Timaeus*.

**Page 466, line 4.** "how or from what things." <note>original: πῶς τίνων (pōs tinōn)</note> In the margin of the Royal Codex <note>a manuscript from the French royal collection</note> it was written: "Saint Maximus says that the Son, being the eternal Creator, creates by the consubstantial Word and Spirit whenever He wills. And do not ask: by what reason did God create now, since He is always good?" <note>original: φησὶ ὁ ἅγιος Μάξιμος... ἀεὶ ἀγαθὸς ὑπάρχων;</note> But there is almost no one among the ancient Fathers who has not debated this question.

**Page 468, last line.** read *earum* <note>Latin: "of them" (feminine)</note>.

**Page 469.** "spider's web" <note>original: δραχίαν (drachian), likely for ἀραχνίαν</note> in this manner Aristo compared the arguments of Dialecticians to spider webs: they are not useful for anything, yet are highly technical; just as Zaleucus said of laws.

**Page 473, last line.** "through Socrates." <note>original: διὰ Σωκράτους (dia Sōkratous)</note> In the *Phaedo*, following Pythagoras, who forbids one to leave the post and station of life without the command of the general—that is, God. See Cicero’s *On Old Age*.

**Page 477, line 4.** The Royal Codex had "he confesses" <note>original: ὁμολογεῖ (homologei)</note>; it should be read as "you (plural) confess." <note>original: ὁμολογεῖτε (homologeite)</note>

**Page 478, line 8.** "disorderly." <note>original: ἀτακτην (ataktēn)</note> For it immediately degenerates into Mob Rule <note>original: Ochlocratiam</note>, when:
> Reckless liberty has thrown the city into confusion,
> And license has loosened the ancient reins.

<margin>Line 12.</margin> "Of Monarchy"] <note>original: Μοναρχίας (Monarchias)</note> On which Ostanes wisely speaks in Herodotus regarding the options presented—even if all were the best—of a perfect democracy, an oligarchy, and a Monarch: "I say this latter far excels the others," etc. Plato plainly and openly defends Monarchy. One should consult Isocrates' *To Nicocles*, Aristotle's *Politics* Book 3, and Lactantius Book 1.

**Page 479, line 24.** We have restored "silence," <note>original: ἀφωνία (aphōnia)</note> which the scribe had excluded in favor of "in silence." <note>original: ἐν ἀφωνίᾳ (en aphōnia)</note>

**Page 480, line 26.** "and Plato"] <note>original: καὶ Πλάτωνά (kai Platōna)</note> for he was reconciling Aristotle with Plato, emulating the elder Ammonium.

**Page 481, line 6.** "Earthly" <note>original: Γέαιος (Geaios)</note> and "Earth-like" <note>original: Γέοιος (Geoios)</note> are written in various ways.

**Page 486, line 27.** "to create" <note>original: δημιουργῆ (dēmiourgē)</note> had to be rewritten in place of "he creates." <note>original: δημιουργεῖ (dēmiourgei)</note>

**Page 487, line 4.** restored for "mixed things." <note>original: κεκρασμένα (kekrasmena)</note> **Line 10.** We made "you might benefit" <note>original: ὠφέλης (ōphelēs)</note> out of "concerning the." <note>original: περὶ τῆς (peri tēs)</note>

**Page 488, line 5.** read, *blooming with time or old age*. Or *blooming beyond time*. **Line 10.** "wax"] <note>original: κηρὸν (kēron)</note> From the *Odyssey*, Book 12:
> "In order, I smeared it upon the ears of all my companions." <note>original: Ἑξείης δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐπὶ οὔατα πᾶσιν ἄλειψα</note> **Line 17.** read *smeared around*.
> "They touch the rims and the cups all around
> With the sweet and yellow flavor of honey." <note>A famous quote from Lucretius explaining how difficult philosophy is made palatable, like medicine in a honeyed cup.</note>

<margin>Line 21.</margin> "the women." <note>original: αἱ γυναῖκες (hai gynaikes)</note> An old and well-known saying. Plutarch. **Line 27.** "outside." <note>original: ἔξω (exō)</note> Book 10 of the *Laws*.

**Page 489, line 26.** should be read as "having begotten together." <note>original: συναπογεννήσας (synapogennēsas)</note>

**Page 492, line 6.** "it is fitting"] <note>original: πρέπει (prepei)</note> read "is turned or changed." <note>original: ὠϊατρέπειται (ōiatrepeitai)</note>
"Shining, unperturbed, running the same course, undying it journeys." <note>original: αἰγλανὴς ἀγάρακτος ὁμόδρομος ἀσβρὸς ὁδεύει</note> Nonnus, Book 29 of the *Dionysiaca*. <note>Nonnus of Panopolis was a 5th-century poet; his *Dionysiaca* is the longest surviving poem from antiquity.</note>
**Line 18.** "concerning time"] <note>original: ἐπὶ χρόνου (epi chronou)</note> Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential theologian.</note> in Question 6 on *Genesis* wishes this to pertain to shadow, light, body, and a place that is not at all bright; as does Andrew of Crete in his 4th Oration on Gregory. **Last line.** "in an age." <note>original: ἐν ἐᾶ (en ea)</note>

> For nothing else can it be, except air deprived of light,
> That which we are accustomed to call a shadow.

Lucretius, Book 4. <note>Lucretius was a Roman poet and philosopher known for *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things).</note>

**Page 493, line 15.** "wall"] <note>original: τείχει (teichei)</note> Philoponus uses these exact words from Proclus. <note>Philoponus and Proclus were influential late antique philosophers who often debated the eternity of the world.</note> **Line 17.** "image"] <note>original: εἴδωλον (eidōlon)</note> like the shadows of the dead, "images of those who have toiled" <note>original: εἴδωλα καμόντων (eidōla kamontōn)</note> in Homer. In Plato's *Phaedo*, "shadow-like apparitions." <note>original: σκιοειδῆ φαντάσματα (skioeidē phantasmata)</note> **Line 25.** "for by measure"] <note>original: μέτρω γὰρ (metrō gar)</note> See Aristotle in Book 4 of the *Physics*. But Plato seems to call "the very motion of the heavens 'time'." <note>original: τὴν τῆ οὐρανοῦ φορὰν χρόνον (tēn tē ouranou phoran chronon)</note> **Line 29.** "toward"] <note>original: πρὸς (pros)</note> see Porphyry's *Introduction*, chapter 7.

**Page 494, line 1.** "in which"] <note>original: ἐν ᾧ (en hō)</note> These are Aristotle's subtleties in chapter 13, Book 4 [of the *Physics*] and Book 1 of *On the Heavens*: "in time all things are born and pass away." <note>original: ἐν χρόνῳ πάντα γίνεται καὶ φθείρεται (en chronō panta ginetai kai phtheiretai)</note>

**Page 497, line 10.** We wrote [this] instead of "law-treasury." <note>original: νομοθητήκης (nomothētēkēs)</note>

**Page 500, line 25.** "as he says"] <note>original: ὡς φησί (hōs phēsi)</note> in the *Hexaemeron* <note>A series of homilies on the six days of creation.</note>, Homily 1: "That whose parts are subject to corruption and change, such is the form of the whole also," and so forth, as above.

**Page 502, line 18.** Thus commonly "arises in"; <note>original: ἐγγίνεται (enginetai)</note> perhaps it should be "be born in." <note>original: ἐγγενέθῃ (engennēthē)</note> **Line 28.** read "you may wash away." <note>original: eluas</note>

**Page 505, line 14.** "to himself"] <note>original: ἑαυτῷ (heautō)</note> it had been written "to herself." <note>original: ἑαυτῇ (heautē)</note> **Same line.** "by thought."] <note>original: κτ᾿ ἔννοι (kat' ennoi)</note> God dwelt within himself, dwells within himself, was within himself, is within himself. Augustine on Psalm 122. "For just as in a man there is an internal word in the mind." <note>original: καθάπερ γὰρ ἀνθρωπός ἐστὶν ἐν νῷ λόγος ἐνδιάθητος</note> Philo believes God dwells in the "Word" <note>original: λόγῳ (logō)</note> in his treatise *On Migration*. <note>original: περὶ ἀποικίας (peri apoikias)</note> **Same line.** "place"] <note>original: ἔννον (ennon)</note> perhaps "place; since he is a place to himself, and God is himself full and sufficient for himself." <note>original: τόπον· ἐπεὶ αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ τόπος, & αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ πλήρης καὶ ἱκανὸς ὁ θεός</note> The same author in *Allegories of the Law*.

**Page 506, line 13.** We have adopted "in" <note>original: ἐν (en)</note> instead of "from." <note>original: ἀφ (aph)</note> **Line 17.** read "he might conceive." <note>original: ἐννοείη (ennoeiē)</note>

**Page 507, line 11.** Basil. **Same line.** "They acknowledge God as the cause from himself, but as a cause unchangeably, as the body is the cause of the shadow and the radiator is the cause of the brightness." <note>original: ἐξ αἴτιον μὲ αὐτό ὁμολογοῦσι τὸν θεόν, αἴτιον δ᾿ ἀπαρατρέπτως, ὡς τῆς σκιᾶς τὸ σῶμα καὶ τῆς λαμπηδόνος τὸ ἀπαύγαζον</note> **Line 25.** "offspring of time"] <note>original: χρ. γένημα (chr. genēma)</note> perhaps "fruitful." <note>original: γόνιμα (gonima)</note>

**Page 519, line 13.** "not" <note>original: μή (mē)</note> absolutely had to be supplied. The manuscript has "to one having." <note>original: ἔχοντι (echonti)</note> Either "having" <note>original: ἔχον (echon)</note>—which I would approve—or "to one having."
**Page 520, line 18.** "let them perish" <note>original: ἐρρέτωσαν (erretōsan)</note> in the *Analytics*. <note>A reference to Aristotle’s logical treatises, the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics*.</note>
**Page 522, line 2.** read "insofar as." <note>original: quatenus</note>
**Page 528, line 8.** "from" <note>original: ἐκ (ek)</note> we have inserted.
**Page 530, last line.** "cause"] <note>original: αἰτίαν (aitian)</note> The more scrupulous Latin authors almost always shrink from this word. <note>The translator suggests that Latin writers avoid the Greek term for 'cause' or 'reason' due to its specific philosophical or theological baggage.</note>
**Page 531, line 4.** "Gregory the Stunted"] <note>original: Κολόβος Γρηγόριος (Kolobos Grēgorios)</note> see the *Peaceful Discourse* 2, oration 13. Out of all these and such great Theologians, Gregory observes in his *Life* that "only this one was revealed as a Theologian after John the Evangelist." <note>In the Eastern Orthodox tradition, the title "Theologian" is reserved for very few, primarily St. John the Evangelist and St. Gregory of Nazianzus.</note> **Line 13.** "three"] <note>original: τρία (tria)</note> One may be permitted to say "three" <note>in the masculine gender, referring to persons</note>, but it would be a matter of religious concern to say "three" <note>in the neuter gender, which might imply three separate substances</note>.
**Page 532, line 9.** "the" <note>original: τῷ (tō, dative case)</note> instead of "of the." <note>original: τῆς (tēs, genitive case)</note>
**Page 553, line 3.** "after the intelligible things." <note>original: μετὰ τὰ νοητὰ (meta ta noēta)</note> Indeed, the school of theologians has rejected this opinion.
**Page 536, line 3.** "of the proverb"] <note>original: παροιμίας (paroimias)</note> from the Homeric line:
->How God always leads like to like.<- <note>original: ὡς αἰεὶ τὸν ὅμοιον ἄγει θεὸς ὡς τὸν ὅμοιον</note>
Plato in the *Symposium*: "For the old saying holds true, that like always approaches like." <note>original: ὁ γὰρ παλαιὸς λόγος εὖ ἔχει, ὡς ὅμοιον ὁμοίῳ αἰεὶ πελάζει</note> Who does not know this?
**Line 15.** read "oh!" <note>original: ἰὼ (iō)</note> **Last line.** Who would doubt to read "likewise" <note>original: αὑτὼς (hautōs)</note> instead of "himself"? <note>original: αὐτός (autos)</note>
**Page 541, line 1.** "having reported." <note>original: ἀπαγγειλάμενον (apangeilamenon)</note> No one would deny it should be read as "having been freed" <note>original: ἀπαλλαγμένον (apallagmenon)</note> or "having been anointed." <note>original: ἀπαλλειμμένον (apalleimmenon)</note>
**Page 543, line 4.** "the great"] <note>original: ὁ μέγας (ho megas)</note> thus Theodoret in Oration 4: "Basil the Great, the light-bearer of the world." <note>St. Basil the Great was a 4th-century bishop and one of the three 'Cappadocian Fathers' who defined early Christian doctrine.</note>
**Page 546, line 14.** I have restored "we are perceived" <note>original: νοούμεθα (nooumetha)</note> in place of "we are sick/ailing." <note>original: νοτοῦμεν (notoumen)</note> This is also more conveniently read above on page 541, line 2: "Lest we think ourselves immortal, let us remember we are men; born, as that author says, under the mortal condition."
**Page 549, last line.** should be read as "they desired together." <note>original: συνεπεθύμουν (synepethymoun)</note>
**Page 550, line 7.** "of those things being cultivated"] <note>original: γεωργουμένων (geōrgoumenōn)</note> taken from Gregory, like most things in this text. Oration 1: "In this, it is the particular characteristic of supreme goodness to make the good, which is ours, not only sown by nature, but also cultivated by choice in the movements of both aspects of our free will."
**Page 553, line 26.** "indissoluble." <note>original: ἀδιαλύτην (adialytēn)</note> It was incorrectly read as "dissoluble." <note>original: διαλύτην (dialytēn)</note>
**Page 555, line 20.** "reasonable"] <note>original: εὔλογον (eulogon)</note> the phrase "unreasonable reasonable" <note>original: ἄλογον εὔλογον (alogon eulogon)</note> had cast it out of its place.
**Page 556, line 6.** "having shed feathers"] <note>original: πτεροῤῥυηστάσας (pterorrhystasas)</note> write "having shed feathers." <note>original: πτεροῤῥυησάσας (pterorrhystasas)</note> This is indeed a word used by Aristophanes, but here it is the plain speech of Plato in the *Phaedo* and *Phaedrus*. <note>Aristophanes was a comic playwright; Plato's 'Phaedo' and 'Phaedrus' are famous dialogues exploring the soul.</note>
**Page 557, line 9.** I wrote "O begotten one" <note>original: γεγεννημένε (gegennēmene)</note> in the manner of the fathers "who hold the same opinion." <note>original: ὁμοδόξων (homodoxōn)</note>

<header>ON THE WORKS OF ANASTASIUS THE PRESBYTER</header>

<meta>catchword: but not <note>original: ἀλλ' οὐκ (all’ ouk)</note></meta>

## TO CELEBRATED OPINIONS
### NOTES ON THE SOUL.

**OPINIONS.** <note>original: ΔΟΞΑΙ</note> Another manuscript (manuscript Th.) bears the title "On the Opinions Concerning the Soul." <note>original: περὶ τῶν τῆς ψυχῆς δοξῶν</note> That title should have been preferred. Whether you call these "helpful lessons," <note>original: χρηστομαθείας</note> "summaries," <note>original: ἐπιτομάς</note> or "selections," <note>original: ἐκλογὰς</note> you would not be far from the truth, since they contain a choice selection from the abundance of Plato and Aristotle and create a sound and holy compendium of the doctrine of the soul. Nor are they separated from the treatise of Anastasius by any great interval. Since they appear anonymously, they cannot long lack a name for the sake of industriousness and diligence. Perhaps work should have been done to ensure they shine with the gift of new light and added adornment, if our circumstances and time permitted; however, this sample of notes will show how many and how foul the stains that have been wiped away, which suggests that it was not our will that failed us, but the time and the assistance of the manuscripts. **Line 10.** "of the mind." <note>original: διανοίας</note> Intellect.

### FROM GENESIS.

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a figure and foliage.</image-desc>
*And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years. pages 330 & 335.* <note>original Latin: "Et sint in signa..." referring to the creation of the heavenly bodies in Genesis 1:14.</note>

*And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars: and God set them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine upon the earth, and preside over the day and night. 112.* <note>Genesis 1:16-17.</note>

<margin>2</margin>
*From every tree that is in paradise, you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat of it: for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death. 85 & 86.* <note>Genesis 2:16-17. The phrase "die by death" is a literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom often translated as "surely die."</note>

<margin>11</margin>
*And the whole earth was of one lip, and one voice for all: and it came to pass, when they moved from the East, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and dwelt there. 322.* <note>Genesis 11:1-2. The Latin "labium" (lip) refers to a common language.</note>

*Come, let us make bricks, and bake them with fire. 24.* <note>Genesis 11:3.</note>

*The Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built; and the Lord said, Behold, it is one race and one lip for all: and they have begun to do this: and now nothing will be lacking for them, that they might do whatever they have undertaken to do. Come, and descending let us confound their tongues, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor. And the Lord scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth: and they ceased building the tower: therefore its name was called Confusion, because there the Lord God confounded the lips of the whole earth, and from there the Lord God scattered them over the face of the earth. 322.* <note>Genesis 11:5-9. The name "Confusion" translates the Latin "confusio," referring to Babel.</note>

<margin>49</margin>
*The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes for whom things are reserved. 6.* <note>Genesis 49:10. This is a famous Messianic prophecy; the "thigh" (original: "femore") is a euphemism for lineage or loins.</note>

## From Exodus.

<margin>4</margin> *Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord?* 281. <note>original Latin: "surdastrum," a late Latin term for one somewhat deaf or mute.</note>
*I will harden Pharaoh's heart.* p. 274. & 289. p. 347.
*The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart.* 428. 429. 431. 434. 444. <note>These page numbers refer to Origen's extensive discussions on free will and how God is said to "harden" a heart.</note>
*But you shall say to Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son; and I said to you, let my people go, that they may serve me; but if you will not let them go, behold: I will kill your firstborn son.* 278. p. 450. p. 451.

<margin>24</margin> *Moses alone shall come near to God; the others shall not come near.* 257.

The margin "8" likely refers to chapter 26 or 27 in some numbering systems, or is a printer's error for chapter 25.</note>

## From the Second Book of Maccabees.

<margin>6</margin> *I exhort all who read this book not to be discouraged because of these calamities, but to consider that these things that happen are not for destruction, but for the discipline of our race. For the Lord, sustaining us, does not wait as he does with other nations, so that when their sins have finally been filled up, he may then take vengeance on them; so he has also decided concerning us, who has educated his people through calamity—* <note>original: "Adhortor omnes, qui librum hunc legunt..." *For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who suppress the truth in injustice, because that which can be known about God is manifest to them; for God has manifested it to them. # EXTRACT OF THE PRIVILEGE.

<note>A "privilege" was a legal monopoly granted by the monarch to a printer or author, preventing others from reprinting the work for a set period. It is the ancestor of modern copyright.</note>

BY privilege of the King on the 15th of March 1618, signed BY LALANE, permission is granted to PIERRE DE FORGE, Bookseller at the University of Paris, to print or have printed a book titled: *The Philocalia of Origen on the obscure passages of Holy Scripture, excerpted from various commentaries of Origen by the Holy Fathers Basil the Great and Gregory the Theologian. The Disputation of Zacharias the Scholastic, later Bishop of Mitylene, on the Creation of the World against the Philosophers. The Disputation of Anastasius the Presbyter on Mount Sinai on the creation of man in the image and likeness of God. And sentences on the Soul: all now published for the first time in Greek from the Royal Library by the labor and study of* JOANNES TARINUS *of Angers, who also produced the Latin translation and illustrated it with notes.* And prohibitions are made to all Booksellers, Printers, sellers of books, and all persons of whatever quality and condition they may be, from printing, selling, and distributing it within the Kingdom of France, during the time and space of nine years, counting from the day that the said book shall have finished being printed, under penalty of a thousand livres fine; and confiscation of the counterfeit copies, and of all expenses, damages, and interests. As is more at length contained in the said letters and privilege.
